# Labels name a tuple's elements.
position(): (line: int, column: int) {
    return (line: 3, column: 7);
}

struct Token {
    var text: String = "";
    var at: (line: int, column: int);
}

main(): int {
    var p = position();
    assert(p.line == 3 && p.column == 7, "read by label");
    assert(p.0 == 3, "positions still work");

    # Labeled and unlabeled tuples convert to each other.
    var plain: (int, int) = p;
    assert(plain.1 == 7, "same elements");

    # A labeled value carries its labels into the variable's type.
    var end = (line: 4, column: 1);
    assert(end.line == p.line + 1, "labeled literal");

    var t = Token();
    t.at = (5, 6);
    assert(t.at.column == 6, "a labeled field");
    return 0;
}
  • Labels belong to the type you write, not to the value. A labeled tuple and an unlabeled one with the same element types are the same type, so each converts to the other freely.
  • Either every element has a label or none does, and labels in one tuple must differ.
  • Labels do not pass through a type argument: Optional<(line: int, column: int)> is the same type as Optional<(int, int)>, so its value() returns an unlabeled tuple. Declare a labeled variable to name the elements again.
  • var p = (line: 3, column: 7); gives p the labeled type (line: int, column: int). A labeled value takes at least two elements.
  • A labeled value initializing or returned as a labeled type must use its labels in order: (column: 7, line: 3) where a (line: int, column: int) is expected is an error, not a swap. An unlabeled value, or a labeled one going to an unlabeled type, converts by position.
  • A destructuring assignment lists places alone: (a, b) = (b, a);, never (x: a, y: b) = ....

Destructuring

var (a, b) = value; declares one variable for each element of a tuple:

struct Point {
    var x: int = 0;
    var y: int = 0;
}

min_max(values: Array<int>): (int, int) {
    var low = values[0];
    var high = values[0];
    for (var v in values) {
        if (v < low) {
            low = v;
        }
        if (v > high) {
            high = v;
        }
    }
    return (low, high);
}

main(): int {
    var values = Array<int>();
    values.append(4);
    values.append(-2);
    values.append(9);

    # Destructure the result into new variables.
    var (low, high) = min_max(values);
    assert(low == -2 && high == 9, "both ends");

    # `_` skips an element; a binding may state its type.
    var (_, top: long) = min_max(values);
    assert(top == 9, "only the maximum");

    # `const` makes every binding constant.
    const (first, last) = (values[0], values[2]);
    assert(first == 4 && last == 9, "constants");

    # Assign to existing places. The right side is evaluated first,
    # so this swaps.
    var a = 1;
    var b = 2;
    (a, b) = (b, a);
    assert(a == 2 && b == 1, "swapped");

    var p = Point();
    (p.x, p.y) = min_max(values);
    assert(p.x == -2 && p.y == 9, "fields are places too");
    return 0;
}
  • The number of names must match the number of elements.
  • _ skips an element.
  • A name may state its type, var (_, top: long) = …; the element converts to it. Without one, the variable takes the element’s type.
  • const (a, b) = … declares constants.
  • Patterns nest: var (id, (name, age)) = … takes an element that is itself a tuple apart.
  • A for loop destructures each element: for (var (name, count) in pairs).
  • (a, b) = value; assigns to places that already exist: variables, fields (p.x) and array elements. The whole right side is evaluated before any assignment, so (a, b) = (b, a) swaps.

Tuples and references

A tuple is a value, like a number. It is not an object on the heap, and copying it copies its elements. An element that is a reference is shared, not copied, exactly as if you had assigned it to a variable:

  • Building a tuple from a variable adds a reference to the object; building it from a function result takes over that result’s reference.
  • A tuple holds its references until it goes out of scope or is replaced, then releases them.
  • Destructuring moves each element into its variable. After var (a, b) = pair();, a holds the only reference to its object, just as it would after var a = make();.

A tuple is thread-safe when all its elements are, so a module-scope const origin: (int, long) = (0, 0); is allowed.

Collections, comparing and printing

A tuple works anywhere a type does, including as a type argument: Array<(int, String)>, HashMap<(int, int), String>. Iterating a HashMap yields (key, value) tuples:

main(): int {
    # A tuple can be a key: here, a grid position.
    var grid = HashMap<(int, int), String>();
    grid[(0, 0)] = "start";
    grid[(2, 3)] = "goal";
    assert(grid[(2, 3)] == "goal", "looked up by value");

    # Tuples compare element by element.
    assert((1, "a") == (1, "a"), "equal");
    assert((1, "a") != (1, "b"), "different");

    # A HashMap yields (key, value) tuples; destructure them in the loop.
    var ages = HashMap<String, int>();
    ages["ada"] = 36;
    ages["grace"] = 85;
    var total = 0;
    for (var (name, age) in ages) {
        total += age;
    }
    assert(total == 121, "every entry");

    # An array of tuples.
    var pairs = Array<(String, int)>();
    pairs.append(("x", 1));
    pairs.append(("y", 2));
    for (var (name, count) in pairs) {
        print((name, count));
    }
    return 0;
}
  • == and != compare element by element. Each element compares the way it would on its own: a type with an == operator (such as String) uses it, and any other struct compares by identity (the same object).
  • A tuple can be a HashMap key or a HashSet member. Its hash combines the hashes of its elements, so equal tuples hash equally.
  • print((1, "two")) prints (1, two).
  • copy(t) (see Copying a value) copies each element: a struct element as copy would copy it on its own, anything thread-safe as is.

Matching tuples

A match over a tuple tests all of its elements at once. A tuple pattern lists a pattern for each element: (Rock, Scissors), (Number(v), 1), (4, column). Write the tuple in the match itself with double parentheses, match ((a, b)), or match a tuple value, match (at).

# `match` takes a tuple apart, testing every element at once.
enum Move {
    Rock,
    Paper,
    Scissors,
}

# Who wins: 1 for the first player, 2 for the second, 0 for a draw.
winner(first: Move, second: Move): int {
    match ((first, second)) {
        (Rock, Scissors), (Paper, Rock), (Scissors, Paper) => {
            return 1;
        }
        (Rock, Rock), (Paper, Paper), (Scissors, Scissors) => {
            return 0;
        }
        else => {
            return 2;
        }
    }
}

enum Token {
    Number(value: int),
    Word(text: String),
}

# Literals, cases with values, bound names and `_` mix in one pattern.
describe(token: Token, line: int): String {
    return match ((token, line)) {
        (Number(v), 1) => "a number on the first line",
        (Word(text), _) => text,
        (_, _) => "another number",
    };
}

main(): int {
    assert(winner(Move.Rock, Move.Scissors) == 1, "rock blunts scissors");
    assert(winner(Move.Paper, Move.Scissors) == 2, "scissors cut paper");
    assert(winner(Move.Paper, Move.Paper) == 0, "a draw");

    assert(describe(Token.Word("hi"), 3) == "hi", "a word binds its text");
    assert(describe(Token.Number(7), 1) == "a number on the first line", "a literal element");

    # A name binds its element; `is` tests one pattern.
    var at = (4, 2);
    if (at is (4, column)) {
        assert(column == 2, "bound by the pattern");
    }
    return 0;
}
  • Each element takes a case of its enum (Rock, Word(text)), a literal (1, "x", true), another tuple pattern, _ for any value, or a name.
  • A name binds its element, unless the element is an enum with a case of that name, which it then matches. So in (Circle, other) over two shapes, Circle is a case and other holds the second shape.
  • An arm’s patterns bind the same names, each at the same element: (x, 0), (0, x) is an error, since x would mean a different element depending on which pattern matched.
  • The arms must handle every value unless there is an else. A missing value is named with an example: match on '(Shape, int)' does not handle '(Line, _)'. Only enum cases and true/false can be listed in full; other literals need a pattern with _ or a name at that element.
  • A pattern that the arms before it already cover is an error, and an else after arms that cover everything is a warning.
  • value is (4, column) tests one tuple pattern, and binds its names as the whole condition of an if or while, as for enums.

Collection literals

A collection literal writes an array, a map or a set in one expression:

trait Shape {
    area(): int;
}

struct Square {
    int side;

    construct(side: int) {
        this.side = side;
    }
}

extend Square with Shape {
    area(): int {
        return side * side;
    }
}

total(values: long[]): long {
    long sum = 0;
    for (var value in values) {
        sum += value;
    }
    return sum;
}

main(): int {
    # An array literal is an Array of its elements' type.
    var primes = [2, 3, 5, 7];
    assert(primes.count() == 4 && primes[3] == 7, "an Array<int>");

    # A trailing comma lets a long literal put one element per line.
    var operators = [
        "===",
        "!==",
        "=>",
    ];
    assert(operators[1] == "!==", "an Array<String>");

    # Where an Array type is expected, the elements convert to its element type.
    assert(total([1, 2, 3]) == 6, "an Array<long> argument");
    Shape[] shapes = [Square(2), Square(3)];
    assert(shapes[1].area() == 9, "elements convert to the trait type");

    # A map literal is a HashMap; a repeated key keeps its last value.
    var ages = ["Ada": 36, "Alan": 41];
    assert(ages["Alan"] == 41, "a HashMap<String, int>");

    # An array literal where a HashSet is expected makes a set.
    HashSet<String> keywords = ["if", "else", "if"];
    assert(keywords.count() == 2, "duplicates are kept once");

    # [] and [:] are empty, where the type is declared.
    long[] none = [];
    HashMap<String, int> nobody = [:];
    assert(none.empty() && nobody.count() == 0, "empty collections");
    return 0;
}

Arrays

  • [a, b, c] is a new Array<T> holding the elements in order. A trailing comma is allowed: [a, b, c,].
  • With no other type to go by, T is the first element’s type, and every later element converts to it the way an argument converts to a parameter: [1, 2] is an Array<int>, and [1, "a"] is an error.
  • Where an array type is expected (a declared variable, a parameter, a return value, an assignment), T is that type’s element type instead, and every element converts to it: long[] a = [1, 2];, Shape[] s = [square, circle];.
  • Nested literals are typed the same way: long[][] grid = [[1], [2, 3]];.
  • [] is an empty array. It needs a declared type (long[] none = [];), since it has no element to take a type from:
main.pep:2:13: error: empty array literal has no element type; declare the variable's type or write 'Array<T>()'
    2 |     var a = [];
      |             ^~

Maps

  • [k1: v1, k2: v2] is a new HashMap<K, V> holding the entries. K and V come from the first entry, or from the HashMap<K, V> a declared variable, parameter or return type expects.
  • A key written twice keeps its last value, as two insert calls would.
  • [:] is an empty map, and needs a declared type: HashMap<String, int> none = [:];.

Sets

There is no separate set literal. An array literal where a HashSet<K> is expected converts to one through HashSet’s implicit constructor, which keeps each element once: HashSet<String> keywords = ["if", "else"];.

Types of specializations

A literal never changes a collection’s type after it is built: Array<int> and Array<long> are different types, and neither converts to the other.

main.pep:2:21: error: cannot initialize variable 'a' of type 'Array<long>' with a value of type 'Array<int>'
    2 |     Array<long> a = Array<int>();
      |                     ^~~~~~~~~~

Function types and closures

Functions in Pepper are values. You can store a function in a variable, a field or an array, pass it to another function, and return it. This lets you choose behavior at run time: a sort order, a callback, a step in a pipeline. A function value is a named function, a method, a constructor, or a closure: an anonymous function written where it is used.

Function types

A function type is written (parameter types) => return type:

TypeMeaning
(int) => inttakes an int, returns an int
(String, int) => booltakes a String and an int, returns a bool
() => voidtakes nothing, returns nothing
(int) => (int) => inttakes an int, returns an (int) => int

=> is right-associative, so the last row is a function that returns a function. A function type can be used anywhere a type can: for variables, parameters, return types, struct fields, generic arguments such as Array<(int) => int>, and type aliases.

Written with shared in front, as in shared () => void, a function type is thread-safe: its values can be passed to other threads. See Sharing function values between threads.

Referring to a named function

The name of a free function, written without a call, is a value of that function’s type. Calling a function value calls the function:

# Function types and references to named functions.
square(x: int): int { return x * x; }
negate(x: int): int { return -x; }

# A parameter can take a function: its type is '(parameter types) => return type'.
apply(f: (int) => int, x: int): int {
    return f(x);
}

twice(f: (int) => int, x: int): int {
    return f(f(x));
}

# Generic functions can take function values too.
apply_twice<T>(f: (T) => T, x: T): T {
    return f(f(x));
}

main(): int {
    # A function's name without a call is a value of its function type.
    var f = square;                 # f: (int) => int
    assert(f(3) == 9, "call through a local");

    var g: (int) => int = negate;   # the type can be written out
    assert(g(4) == -4, "explicit function type");

    # Function variables can be reassigned to another function of the same type.
    f = negate;
    assert(f(6) == -6, "reassigned");

    assert(apply(square, 5) == 25, "pass a function as an argument");
    assert(twice(square, 3) == 81, "(3 * 3) * (3 * 3)");
    assert(twice(negate, 7) == 7, "negating twice");
    assert(apply_twice<int>(square, 2) == 16, "generic");
    return 0;
}
  • var f = square; infers f’s type, (int) => int, from the function. An overloaded name, or an overloaded method (p.move), needs a declared type instead, which picks the member.
  • A function-typed variable can be reassigned to any function of the same type.
  • A parameter of function type, such as f: (int) => int, lets the caller pass in the behavior. Generic functions can take function parameters too.

Methods, constructors and generic functions

Methods, constructors and specializations of generic functions are values too:

# Methods, constructors and generic functions used as values.
struct Point {
    int x;
    int y;
    construct(this.x = 0, this.y = 0) {}

    norm(): int {
        return x + y;
    }

    shifted(dx: int): Point {
        return Point(x + dx, y);
    }
}

larger<T>(a: T, b: T): T {
    return a > b ? a : b;
}

combine(f: (int, int) => int, a: int, b: int): int {
    return f(a, b);
}

main(): int {
    var p = Point(3, 4);

    # A bound method: the method of one object, which it keeps alive.
    var norm = p.norm;
    assert(norm() == 7, "bound method");

    # An unbound method takes the object as its first argument.
    var norm_of: (Point) => int = Point.norm;
    assert(norm_of(Point(1, 1)) == 2, "unbound method");

    # A struct's name is its constructor.
    var make: (int, int) => Point = Point;
    assert(make(5, 6).y == 6, "constructor");

    # A generic function with its type arguments names one specialization.
    assert(combine(larger<int>, 2, 9) == 9, "generic function");

    var steps = Array<(int) => Point>();
    steps.append(p.shifted);
    steps.append(Point(10, 0).shifted);
    assert(steps[1](5).x == 15, "methods in an array");
    return 0;
}
WrittenTypeCalls
p.norm() => intp.norm(), on the object p referred to when the value was made
Point.norm(Point) => intnorm on the object passed as the first argument
Point.origin (a static method)() => PointPoint.origin()
Point(int, int) => Pointthe constructor
Box<int>(int) => Box<int>the constructor of Box<int>
larger<int>(int, int) => intthe specialization larger<int>
  • Bound methods. p.norm keeps a reference to the object, like a closure () => p.norm() that captured p, so the object lives as long as the value does. The expression before the . is evaluated once, when the value is made. Inside a method, write this.norm; a bare norm is not a value. Storing this.norm in a field of this would be a reference cycle, and is an error, as for closures.
  • Traits and extensions. A method declared in an extension works the same way, and so does a method of a trait-typed value (shape.area), which calls through the trait.
  • Generic functions need their type arguments: larger<int>, not larger.
  • A type with a constructor that takes no arguments. Box<int> on its own names the constructor only when the constructor needs at least one argument; otherwise it is a call, Box<int>(). The same goes for a generic function whose parameters all have defaults.

Storing and returning functions

Function values go wherever other values go: struct fields, arrays, module-level variables and return values. A type alias gives a long function type a short name, and can have type parameters of its own.

# Function values in fields, arrays, globals, and return values.

import async;

square(x: int): int { return x * x; }
negate(x: int): int { return -x; }
increment(x: int): int { return x + 1; }

struct Transform {
    var op: (int) => int;
    construct(this.op = square) {}
    run(x: int): int { return op(x); }
}

# Choose a function at run time and return it.
pick(squared: bool): (int) => int {
    if squared {
        return square;
    }
    return negate;
}

# A module-level function variable. Every module-level variable is const
# and thread-safe: an Atomic lets it change, and a function type every thread
# can reach is declared shared.
const handler = async.Atomic<shared (int) => int>(increment);

# A type alias can name a function type, even a generic one.
type Combine<T> = (T, T) => T;
add(a: int, b: int): int { return a + b; }
fold(values: int[], combine: Combine<int>, start: int): int {
    var total = start;
    for (var v in values) {
        total = combine(total, v);
    }
    return total;
}

# A function that returns nothing has the return type void.
const events = async.Atomic<int>(0);
record(n: int) { events.fetch_add(n); }

main(): int {
    var t = Transform();
    assert(t.run(4) == 16, "the default op squares");
    t.op = negate;
    assert(t.op(4) == -4, "call through a field");

    var pipeline = Array<(int) => int>();
    pipeline.append(increment);
    pipeline.append(square);
    pipeline.append(negate);
    var value = 2;
    for (var step in pipeline) {
        value = step(value);
    }
    assert(value == -9, "-((2 + 1) * (2 + 1))");
    assert(pipeline[1](5) == 25, "call an array element");

    assert(pick(true)(5) == 25, "call a returned function directly");
    var chosen = pick(false);
    assert(chosen(5) == -5, "call a stored returned function");

    assert(handler.load()(1) == 2, "global function value");
    handler.store(square);
    assert(handler.load()(3) == 9, "replaced global");

    var numbers = Array<int>();
    numbers.append(1);
    numbers.append(2);
    numbers.append(3);
    assert(fold(numbers, add, 10) == 16, "10 + 1 + 2 + 3");

    var callback: (int) => void = record;
    callback(2);
    callback(5);
    assert(events.load() == 7, "void function values");
    return 0;
}
  • Fields. A field of function type is called like a method: t.op(4). Inside the struct, op(x) and this.op(x) both call it.
  • Arrays. pipeline[1](5) indexes the array and calls the element.
  • Module-level variables. Every module-level variable is const and thread-safe (see Module-scope variables), so one whose function changes is an Atomic of a shared function type: handler.load()(1) calls the current function and handler.store(square) replaces it.
  • Return values. pick(true)(5) calls the function that pick returns.
  • void results. A function without a return value has a function type ending in => void, such as (int) => void.

Closures

A closure literal is a parameter list, =>, and a body. The body is an expression or a block:

# Closure literals: anonymous functions that capture values.
struct Counter {
    int count;
    construct(this.count = 0) {}
    add(n: int) { count += n; }
}

apply(f: (int) => int, x: int): int {
    return f(x);
}

# A closure can outlive the function that made it: it keeps its own copy
# of 'n'.
make_adder(n: int): (int) => int {
    return (x) => x + n;
}

struct Scaler {
    int factor;
    construct(this.factor = 1) {}

    # Inside a method, a closure can use 'this' and the struct's members.
    scaler(): (int) => int {
        return (x) => x * factor;
    }
}

main(): int {
    # Parameter types written out: the closure's type is (int) => int.
    var double = (x: int) => x * 2;
    assert(double(21) == 42, "expression body");

    # With a function type to fill, the parameter types can be left out.
    var add: (int, int) => int = (a, b) => a + b;
    assert(add(40, 2) == 42, "types from the variable");
    assert(apply((x) => x * x, 5) == 25, "types from the parameter");

    # A block body, with the return type written after the parameters.
    var clamp = (x: int, low: int, high: int): int => {
        if x < low { return low; }
        if x > high { return high; }
        return x;
    };
    assert(clamp(7, 0, 5) == 5, "block body");

    # Captured values.
    var add_five = make_adder(5);
    assert(add_five(10) == 15, "captured parameter");
    var offset = 100;
    var shift = (x: int) => x + offset;
    assert(shift(1) == 101, "captured local");

    # A captured struct is shared, so the closure can change the object.
    var counter = Counter();
    var bump = () => counter.add(1);
    bump();
    bump();
    assert(counter.count == 2, "shared struct");

    var triple = Scaler(3).scaler();
    assert(triple(4) == 12, "captured this");

    # A closure can return a closure.
    var adder: (int) => (int) => int = (a) => (b) => a + b;
    assert(adder(2)(3) == 5, "curried");
    return 0;
}

  • Parameter types. (x: int) => x * 2 writes the parameter type. When the closure goes straight into a slot of function type (a typed variable, a parameter, an assignment, a return, a field), the types come from that slot, so (a, b) => a + b is enough. A parameter of a generic function counts too: passing (x) => x + 1 to apply<T>(f: (T) => T, x: T) with x an int types the closure’s x as int (see Generics). With no slot to take them from, a parameter without a type is an error:

    main.pep:2:14: error: cannot infer the type of parameter 'x'; write it: (x: Type) => ...

  • Return type. It is inferred from the body, or from the slot. To write it, put it after the parameters: (x: int): long => x.

  • Body. An expression body is the value the closure returns. A block body uses return like a function. A closure whose type returns void can have an expression body such as () => counter.add(1); the value is discarded.

  • Calling. A closure is called like any function value, and can be called where it is written: ((x: int) => x + 1)(2).

Captured values

A closure can use the local variables and parameters around it. It keeps a copy of each one it uses, made when the closure is created, so it can outlive the function that created it (make_adder above).

A captured variable must never be assigned, before or after the closure is created, inside the closure or outside it. Then the copy and the variable can never differ:

var count = 0;
var f = () => count;
count = 5;   # error

main.pep:4:5: error: cannot assign to 'count' because a closure captures it
main.pep:3:19: note: captured here; a closure keeps a copy, so the variable must not change

The rule applies to ++, -- and compound assignments too. Only the variable is fixed: a captured struct is a reference to the same object, so the closure can call its methods and change its fields (counter above). To share a changing number, capture a struct that holds it, such as a Counter or an Atomic<int>.

this in methods

A closure written in a method can use this, the struct’s fields and its methods. It captures this (one reference to the object), never a copy of the fields, so it sees the fields’ current values.

Storing such a closure in a field of the same object would make the object and the closure keep each other alive forever (a reference cycle), so that direct case is an error:

main.pep:4:15: error: storing a closure that captures 'this' in field 'measure' of 'this' creates a reference cycle that is never freed

Capture a weak reference to the object instead.

Type checking

A function value must match the type it flows into exactly: the same parameter types in the same order and the same return type. The aliases of a primitive type count as the same type, so (i32) => i32 and (int) => int match. A mismatch in an initializer, an assignment, an argument or a return is a compile error, as is calling a function value with the wrong number of arguments:

square(x: int): int { return x * x; }

main(): int {
    var f: (String) => int = square;   # error
    return f(1, 2);                    # error
}

error: variable 'f' expects a function of type (String) => int, but was given a function of type (int) => int
a function of type (String) => int takes 1 argument(s), but 2 were given

These two errors do not show a source location yet.

Sharing function values between threads

A plain function type such as () => void can hold any function value, including a closure that captures a String or an Array. Such values stay on the thread that made them: their reference counts are plain increments, like those of a struct that is not [Shared] (see What threads can share).

A function type written with shared in front, such as shared () => void or shared (long) => void, is thread-safe. Its reference counts are atomic, and its values hold only thread-safe state, so any thread may copy, call and drop them. It goes wherever a thread-safe type is required: the body of a thread (ThreadBody is shared () => void), a field of a [Shared] struct, a module-scope variable, or async.Atomic<shared (int) => int>.

# shared function types: function values that threads can share.
import async;

const total = async.Atomic<long>(0);

# A named function holds no state, so it is always thread-safe.
add_one() {
    total.fetch_add(1);
}

# A [Shared] struct's fields must be thread-safe: a function field is shared.
[Shared]
struct Task {
    const weight: long;
    const run: shared (long) => void;
    construct(this.weight = 1, this.run = (n: long) => {}) {}
}

# A plain function type takes any function of the same signature.
apply(f: (long) => long, x: long): long {
    return f(x);
}

main(): int {
    # A closure converts to a shared type when everything it captures is
    # thread-safe: here nothing but the module-scope Atomic.
    var add: shared (long) => void = (n: long) => { total.fetch_add(n); };
    var task = Task(10, add);

    # A thread body is a shared () => void. This closure captures a
    # [Shared] struct.
    var worker = async.Thread.spawn(() => { task.run(task.weight); });
    var other = async.Thread.spawn(add_one);
    worker.join();
    other.join();
    assert(total.load() == 11, "both threads ran");

    # A shared value can be used where a plain one is expected.
    var step: long = 5;
    var add_step: shared (long) => long = (x: long) => x + step;
    assert(apply(add_step, 1) == 6, "shared value passed as plain");

    # A plain closure may capture anything, but stays on this thread.
    var name = "worker";
    var greet = () => name + " done";
    assert(greet() == "worker done", "plain closure");
    return 0;
}

  • What converts to shared. A named function, which holds no state; a method, constructor or generic function value with nothing captured, such as Point.norm or Box<int>; and a closure literal (or a bound method such as p.norm) whose captured values are all thread-safe: numbers, Atomic<T> and other [Shared] structs, shared function values, and the rest of that list. The value must be written where the shared type is expected, so that it is made thread-safe from the start.

  • What does not. A closure that captures a value that is not thread-safe is reported at the capture, with a note at the captured variable:

    main.pep:5:46: error: closure passed as 'shared () => void' captures 'name' of type 'String', which is not thread-safe
    5 |     var t = async.Thread.spawn(() => { print(name); });
      |                                              ^~~~
main.pep:4:9: note: capture a thread-safe value instead, such as an 'async.Atomic<T>' or a '[Shared]' struct
    4 |     var name = "worker";
      |         ^~~~

    A closure in a method that uses this or a member captures this, so it is thread-safe only in a [Shared] struct. A value that already has a plain type (a variable, a parameter, a call result) never becomes shared, even when it holds nothing:

    main.pep:3:32: error: cannot initialize variable 'f' of type 'shared () => void' with a value of type '() => void'
    3 |     var f: shared () => void = g;
      |                                ^

  • From shared to plain. A shared value converts to the plain type of the same signature anywhere: shared (long) => long can be passed to a parameter of type (long) => long. The conversion allocates a small plain function value that holds the shared one and calls it, so the plain copy counts with plain increments while the shared value keeps its atomic ones.

  • Inference. A variable initialized with a closure, such as var f = () => 1;, has a plain type. Write the type to make it shared: var f: shared () => int = () => 1;.

  • shared is special only directly before a function type; elsewhere it is an ordinary name.

Null function values

A function-typed variable or field that has never been assigned is null. Calling it stops the program with the message called a null function value:

var handler: (int) => int;
handler(1);   # panics: called a null function value

Names and shadowing

A local variable, parameter or field with the same name as a free function hides the function inside its scope. Inside a function with a parameter named square, square means the parameter, not the function.

Memory

A function value is a reference, like a struct value, and follows the same reference-counting rules (see Memory and reference counting). Referring to a named function allocates nothing: every reference to square shares one static function object. A method, constructor or generic function value allocates one small object, like a closure; a bound method’s object holds a reference to its receiver.

Creating a closure allocates one object holding the captured values, like constructing a struct. Copying the closure adds a reference to that object, and when the last reference goes, the object releases what it captured.

A plain function value’s counts are plain increments; a shared one’s are atomic, like a [Shared] struct’s (see Sharing function values between threads).

What is not supported yet

  • Generic functions without type arguments and extern functions cannot be referenced as values. larger alone is not a value even where the expected type would pick larger<int>. To use an extern function as a value, wrap it in a closure: (x: int) => abs(x).
  • Generic methods cannot be referenced as values: b.map<long> is not a value. Wrap the call in a closure: (f: (int) => long) => b.map(f).
  • A bare method name inside a method (var f = norm;) is not a value; write this.norm.
  • Closures in trait default methods cannot use this or the members of the struct yet.
  • Closures that capture values as C callbacks. A C function pointer (extern (P) => R) takes a named function or a closure that captures nothing; see Calling C.

Overloading

Several free functions in one file can share a name when their parameter lists differ. Each call picks the one whose parameters fit its arguments best:

# Overloaded free functions: one name, several parameter lists.

import io;

describe(n: long): String { return "a number"; }
describe(x: double): String { return "a fraction"; }
describe(s: String): String { return "some text"; }
describe(s: String, times: int): String { return "text, repeated"; }

# An exact match beats a widening, which beats a conversion; an
# `[Implicit]` constructor comes last.
size(p: io.Path): int { return 1; }
size(n: long): int { return 2; }

main(): int {
    var small: int = 7;
    assert(describe(small) == "a number", "int widens to long");
    assert(describe(2.5) == "a fraction", "exact match");
    assert(describe("hi") == "some text", "a literal promotes to String");
    assert(describe("hi", 3) == "text, repeated", "picked by argument count");

    assert(size(4) == 2, "an integer literal fits a long");
    assert(size("notes.txt") == 1, "only io.Path takes a String, by its [Implicit] constructor");
    return 0;
}

The functions of one name in one file are an overload set, and each is a member of it. Methods of one name in a struct are a set too, and so are its static methods, its operators, its constructors, and the methods its extensions add.

Declaring overloads

  • The parameter lists must differ in the number or the types of the parameters. Parameter names and default values do not count, and neither does the return type:

    main.pep:2:1: error: functions that differ only in their return type cannot be overloaded
    2 | f(x: int): long { return 2; }
      | ^
main.pep:1:1: note: previous declaration is here
    1 | f(x: int): int { return 1; }
      | ^

    Two functions with the same parameter types and the same return type are a redefinition of 'f'.

  • One file, one set. A file’s own functions hide an imported function of the same name, as before; overloads do not merge across files.

  • One visibility per set. The members are all exported or all private, so a set is imported or hidden as a whole:

    util.pep:2:1: error: overloads of 'scale' must all be exported or all be private
    2 | scale(x: double): double { return x * 3.0; }
      | ^~~~~
util.pep:1:8: note: other overload declared here
    1 | export scale(x: int): int { return x * 2; }
      |        ^~~~~

    Importing the name (import [scale] from util, or the whole file) brings every member, and import [scale as grow] renames the whole set.

  • extern functions do not overload: a C function has one symbol. Wrap it in a Pepper function to give it company.

How a call picks a member

A member is viable when the call has between its required and total number of parameters and each argument converts to its parameter. For each argument, the conversion has a rank, best first:

RankWhat converts
exactthe same type; a string literal to __ptr<char>
promotionan integer widening that loses nothing (int to long, u8 to int; the narrower target ranks better, so a short picks int over long), float to double, an integer literal to any integer type it fits, a struct to a trait it declares, __null to a reference, a string literal to String
conversionany other numeric conversion (bool included), and pointer conversions
implicit constructora value to a struct whose [Implicit] constructor takes it

One viable member is better than another when none of its arguments ranks worse and at least one ranks better, as in C++. The call picks the member that is better than every other viable one. When there is none, the call is an error that lists the candidates:

main.pep:3:22: error: call to 'f' is ambiguous
    3 | main(): int { return f(1); }
      |                      ^
main.pep:1:1: note: candidate function
    1 | f(x: long): int { return 1; }
      | ^
main.pep:2:1: note: candidate function
    2 | f(x: short): int { return 2; }
      | ^

An integer literal fits every integer type that holds its value equally well, so f(1) above is ambiguous; an int member would take it exactly. Two widenings to types of the same width (a ushort to long and ulong) are ambiguous too; convert the argument yourself (f(n as long)). When no member is viable, each note says why:

main.pep:5:12: error: no matching function for call to 'f'
    5 |     return f(s);
      |            ^
main.pep:1:1: note: candidate function not viable: no known conversion from 'String' to 'int' for 1st argument
    1 | f(x: int): int { return 1; }
      | ^
main.pep:2:1: note: candidate function not viable: requires 2 arguments, but 1 was provided
    2 | f(x: int, y: int): int { return 2; }
      | ^

The member picked decides the call’s type, so var x = half(9.0); is a double when half(x: double): double is picked. In the editor, hovering the call shows the member it picked and how many others the set has, and go-to-definition goes to that member.

Generic members

A set can mix generic and non-generic members. A generic member is viable when its type arguments can be inferred from the call, and ranks as an exact match for the arguments that inferred them. When a generic and a non-generic member tie, the non-generic one wins. Writing type arguments (describe<int>(7)) considers only the generic members:

# Generic and non-generic overloads, and overloads called from generic code.

# A non-generic overload wins a tie with a generic one.
describe<T>(value: T): String { return "something"; }
describe(value: int): String { return "an int"; }

# Generic overloads can differ in their number of parameters.
last<T>(a: T): T { return a; }
last<T>(a: T, b: T): T { return b; }

kind(n: int): String { return "number"; }
kind(s: String): String { return "text"; }

# Each specialization resolves `kind` for its own `T`.
label<T>(value: T): String { return kind(value); }

main(): int {
    assert(describe(7) == "an int", "non-generic wins the tie");
    assert(describe(1.5) == "something", "only the generic fits");
    assert(describe<int>(7) == "something", "type arguments pick generic overloads");

    assert(last(1) == 1, "one argument");
    assert(last(1, 2) == 2, "two arguments");

    assert(label(3) == "number", "label<int> calls kind(int)");
    assert(label("x") == "text", "label<String> calls kind(String)");
    return 0;
}

A call inside a generic function or a generic struct’s method whose argument types depend on a type parameter is resolved again for each specialization, so label<String> above calls kind(s: String).

An override such as describe<Point>(p: Point) belongs to the generic member with the same number of type parameters and parameters; it is not a member itself.

Methods and operators

A struct’s methods of one name are an overload set, and a call picks among them the same way, whether it is written m.add(x), this.add(x), or add(x) inside a method. Static methods overload among themselves (Money.of(250)), and operators are methods, so +(Money) and +(int) can coexist:

# Overloaded methods, static methods and operators.

struct Money {
    var cents: long;

    construct(long cents = 0) {
        this.cents = cents;
    }

    # Methods of one name in a struct overload like free functions.
    add(other: Money): Money { return Money(cents + other.cents); }
    add(dollars: int, cents: int): Money { return Money(this.cents + dollars * 100 + cents); }

    # Static methods overload among themselves.
    static of(cents: long): Money { return Money(cents); }
    static of(text: String): Money { return Money(text.size() as long); }

    # Operators are methods, so they overload by operand type too.
    +(other: Money): Money { return add(other); }
    +(more: int): Money { return Money(cents + more); }
}

main(): int {
    var a = Money.of(250);
    var b = a.add(1, 5);                  # add(int, int)
    assert(b.cents == 355, "two ints");
    assert(a.add(b).cents == 605, "a Money");

    var c = a + b + 10;                   # +(Money), then +(int)
    assert(c.cents == 615, "operators");
    assert(Money.of("four").cents == 4, "static of(String)");

    # A method used as a value takes the member its type names.
    var plus: (Money) => Money = a.add;
    assert(plus(a).cents == 500, "method value");
    return 0;
}

  • A static method and an instance method may not share a name, since a bare of(x) inside a method could mean either:

    main.pep:3:12: error: static method 'get' cannot share its name with an instance method of 'S'
    3 |     static get(x: String): int { return 2; }
      |            ^~~
main.pep:2:5: note: previous declaration is here
    2 |     get(x: int): int { return 1; }
      |     ^~~

  • In a generic struct, each specialization resolves its own calls: in Holder<int>, has(x: T) takes an int. Two members that become the same after substitution (has(x: T) and has(x: String) in Holder<String>) are only an error when a call cannot tell them apart.

  • A method as a value (m.add, Money.of) picks its member from the expected function type, like a free function below; without one the error is cannot infer the type of 'f' from overloaded method 'Money.add'.

Extensions and traits

An extension’s methods join the struct’s overload set of their name, and a trait may declare several methods of one name. Each of a trait’s overloads is implemented by the conforming type’s method with the same parameter types, and a call through a value of the trait type picks among the trait’s members the same way:

struct Square {
    var side: int = 0;

    construct(this.side = 0) {}

    area(): int {
        return side * side;
    }
}

# An extension's methods join the struct's overload set of their name.
extend Square {
    area(scale: int): int {
        return area() * scale;
    }
}

# A trait may declare overloads too; each is its own member.
trait Shape {
    area(): int;
    area(scale: int): int;

    # A default joins the conforming type's set of its name.
    describe(): int {
        return area() * 100 + area(2);
    }
}

# Each trait member is implemented by the method with its parameter types.
extend Square with Shape {}

total(shape: Shape): int {
    return shape.area() + shape.area(10);
}

main(): int {
    var square = Square(3);
    assert(square.area(2) == 18, "the extension's overload");
    assert(total(square) == 99, "each call through the trait takes its own member");
    assert(square.describe() == 918, "the default body calls both");
    return 0;
}
  • An extension member with a body method’s parameters is redefinition of 'area', with a note at the method it repeats.
  • A call sees only the extensions visible in its file (see Visibility): a private extension’s overload is never a candidate in another file, so importing a file can add candidates to a call. If an added candidate makes a call ambiguous, the error’s notes point at each candidate, the extension’s included.
  • A trait’s default method is copied into a conforming type that lacks a method with its parameter types, even when the type has other methods of that name; the copy joins their set.
  • A missing overload is named with its parameter types: 'Square' does not implement 'area(int)', required by trait 'Shape'.

Constructors

A struct may declare several constructors. A call Span(...) picks among them exactly as a call picks among functions:

struct Span {
    var start: int = 0;
    var length: int = 0;

    # Constructors overload like functions: each takes its own parameters.
    construct(this.length = 0) {}

    construct(start: int, end: int) {
        this.start = start;
        length = end - start;
    }

    construct(text: String) {
        length = text.length() as int;
    }
}

main(): int {
    assert(Span().length == 0, "no arguments");
    assert(Span(5).length == 5, "one int");

    var middle = Span(2, 7);
    assert(middle.start == 2 && middle.length == 5, "two ints");

    assert(Span("pepper").length == 6, "a String");

    # As a value, the expected function type picks the constructor.
    var make: (int, int) => Span = Span;
    assert(make(1, 4).length == 3, "the (int, int) constructor");
    return 0;
}
  • Two constructors with the same parameter types are constructor of 'Span' cannot be redeclared, with a note at the first.
  • No constructor fits is no matching constructor for initialization of 'Span', and a tie is call to constructor of 'Span' is ambiguous; the notes point at each candidate constructor.
  • A generic struct’s constructors resolve in each specialization: Pair<int>(1, 2) picks among Pair<int>’s constructors.
  • At most one constructor may be [Implicit]: an implicit conversion needs one constructor to call.
  • [Deprecated] on one constructor warns only at the calls that resolve to it.
  • A constructor as a value (var make: (int, int) => Span = Span;) picks its member from the expected function type, like a function below.

Overloaded functions as values

The name of an overload set, written without a call, is a value only where the expected function type picks one member exactly: a typed variable, an argument, a return from a function with a declared return type, or an assignment. A closure whose parameters have no types, passed to an overloaded function, picks the member whose function parameter has its number of parameters:

# An overloaded function used as a value, and closures passed to overloads.

twice(n: int): int { return n * 2; }
twice(s: String): String { return s + s; }

apply(f: (int) => int, n: int): int { return f(n); }

# Overloads that differ in the type of a function parameter.
run(f: (int) => int): int { return f(10); }
run(f: (int, int) => int): int { return f(10, 20); }

main(): int {
    # The declared type picks the overload.
    var doubler: (int) => int = twice;
    assert(doubler(4) == 8, "twice(int)");

    # So does the parameter it is passed to.
    assert(apply(twice, 5) == 10, "twice(int) again");

    # A closure without parameter types picks the overload of its arity.
    assert(run((a) => a + 1) == 11, "one parameter");
    assert(run((a, b) => a + b) == 30, "two parameters");
    return 0;
}

Without an expected type, the compiler asks for one:

main.pep:4:13: error: cannot infer the type of 'g' from overloaded function 'f'
    4 |     var g = f;
      |             ^
main.pep:1:1: note: candidate function
    1 | f(x: int): int { return 1; }
      | ^
main.pep:2:1: note: candidate function
    2 | f(x: long): int { return 2; }
      | ^
main.pep:4:13: note: declare the type, for example 'var g: (int) => int = f;'
    4 |     var g = f;
      |             ^

An expected type that matches no member is address of overloaded function 'f' does not match required type '(bool) => int'.

What is not supported yet

  • Unary operators cannot be declared at all yet.
  • extern functions do not overload.
  • Overloads across files do not merge: a file’s own functions of a name hide an imported set of that name.

Structs

A struct groups related values into one named type, and gives that type behavior through methods. Pepper has no classes and no inheritance: a struct holds data, methods and extensions add behavior, and traits describe what a type can do.

Every struct value is a reference to an object, so assigning a struct or passing it to a function shares the object rather than copying it. The memory chapter explains exactly when objects are created and destroyed.

Declaring a struct

Declare a struct with struct, a name, and its fields in braces. Struct names are PascalCase by convention.

# A struct groups related values into one type.
struct Point {
    var x: int = 0;
    var y: int = 0;
}

# Fields can also be declared C-style, with the type first.
struct Counter {
    int count;          # no initializer: starts at zero
    String label = "clicks";
}

main(): int {
    # Without a constructor, `Point()` makes a Point with every field
    # at its initial value.
    var p = Point();
    assert(p.x == 0 && p.y == 0, "fields start at their initializers");

    p.x = 3;
    p.y = 4;
    assert(p.x * p.x + p.y * p.y == 25, "fields can be read and written");

    var c = Counter();
    assert(c.count == 0, "a numeric field without an initializer is zero");
    assert(c.label == "clicks", "a String field can have an initializer");

    # A struct value is a reference: `q` names the same Point as `p`.
    var q = p;
    q.x = 10;
    assert(p.x == 10, "p and q are the same object");
    assert(p === q, "=== tests whether two references name the same object");
    assert(!(p === Point()), "a new Point is a different object");
    return 0;
}

Things to notice:

  • A field is declared like a variable: var x: int = 0; or, C-style, int x = 0;. The initializer is optional.
  • A field without an initializer starts at its type’s default: zero for numbers, false for bool, and null for a struct type such as String or another struct. Reading a field through a null reference crashes the program, so give struct-typed fields a value before you use them.
  • A struct with no constructor can be created with its name and empty parentheses, Point(). There is no new keyword at the call site.
  • p.x reads a field and p.x = 3 writes it.
  • a === b is true when a and b refer to the same object, and a !== b when they do not. See Comparing structs for ==.

A struct can have a field whose type is a struct declared later in the file, a field of its own type, or fields that lead back to it through other structs (a Team holding a Player that holds the Team). A struct-typed field holds a reference, so a linked list or a tree is just a struct that names itself:

# A field can hold the struct's own type: each Link points at the next one.
struct Link {
    var value: int;
    var next: Link;

    construct(this.value = 0) {}
}

# Two structs can refer to each other, in either declaration order.
struct Team {
    var name: String;
    var lead: Player;

    construct(this.name = "") {}
}

struct Player {
    var name: String;
    # A weak back pointer: the team owns its lead, so the player's link
    # back to the team must not keep the team alive (see the memory chapter).
    var team: Weak<Team>;

    construct(this.name = "") {}
}

sum(first: Link): int {
    var total = 0;
    var link: Link = first;
    while (link !== __null) {
        total = total + link.value;
        link = link.next;
    }
    return total;
}

main(): int {
    var list = Link(1);
    list.next = Link(2);
    list.next.next = Link(3);
    assert(sum(list) == 6, "the list holds 1, 2 and 3");
    assert(list.next.next.next === __null, "the last link has no next");

    var team = Team("Owls");
    team.lead = Player("Ada");
    team.lead.team = Weak<Team>(team);
    with (var t = team.lead.team) {
        assert(t.name == "Owls", "the player reaches its team");
    }
    return 0;
}

Objects that refer to each other in a loop keep each other alive, so make back pointers such as a child’s parent a Weak<T> (see Cycles leak).

Constructors

A constructor sets up a new object. Declare it with construct, followed by its parameters and a body. Callers create the object by calling the struct’s name like a function.

struct Rect {
    var width: int;
    var height: int;
    var area: int;

    # `this.width = 1` declares a parameter that is stored straight into the
    # field `width`; `1` is its default when the caller leaves it out.
    construct(this.width = 1, this.height = 1) {
        area = width * height;
    }
}

struct Temperature {
    var celsius: float;

    # Ordinary parameters work too, written like a function's: `name: Type`.
    construct(fahrenheit: float = 32.0) {
        celsius = (fahrenheit - 32.0) * 5.0 / 9.0;
    }
}

main(): int {
    var r = Rect(3, 4);
    assert(r.width == 3 && r.height == 4, "arguments fill the fields");
    assert(r.area == 12, "the constructor body runs after the fields are set");

    var tall = Rect(2);
    assert(tall.width == 2 && tall.height == 1, "omitted arguments use their defaults");

    var unit = Rect();
    assert(unit.area == 1, "every parameter has a default, so Rect() works");

    var boiling = Temperature(212.0);
    assert(boiling.celsius == 100.0, "212 F is 100 C");
    assert(Temperature().celsius == 0.0, "the default is 32 F");
    return 0;
}
  • A parameter written this.width = 1 stores its argument directly into the field width, before the body runs. The = 1 is required: it is the value used when the caller omits that argument.
  • Ordinary parameters are written as in a function, name: Type, with an optional default: fahrenheit: float = 32.0. The C-style form, float fahrenheit = 32.0, is accepted too.
  • Inside the body, fields are in scope by name. Use this.name when a parameter has the same name as a field.
  • A struct may declare several constructors with different parameter lists; a call picks one by its arguments, as for any overloaded function. At most one of them may be [Implicit]. A struct has at most one destructor.

A this.field parameter must have a default. Leaving it out is an error:

struct Point {
    var x: int;
    construct(this.x) {}
}

main.pep:3:21: error: expected '='
    3 |     construct(this.x) {}
      |                     ^

A struct without a constructor accepts no arguments:

main.pep:7:13: error: too many arguments to 'Point': expected 0, have 2
    7 |     var p = Point(1, 2);
      |             ^~~~~

Note: new is the older, deprecated spelling of construct. It still compiles, with a warning that offers the fix (see Deprecations).

Implicit conversions

A constructor marked [Implicit] also converts. Wherever a value flows into a place whose type is the struct, and the value has the constructor’s parameter type, the compiler calls the constructor for you:

struct Celsius {
    var degrees: double;

    # `[Implicit]` lets a `double` become a `Celsius` wherever one is expected.
    [Implicit]
    construct(double degrees) {
        this.degrees = degrees;
    }
}

struct Label {
    var text: String;

    # Without `[Implicit]`, callers write `Label("...")` themselves.
    construct(String text) {
        this.text = text;
    }
}

describe(t: Celsius): String {
    return (t.degrees > 30.0) ? "hot" : "mild";
}

main(): int {
    assert(describe(35.0) == "hot", "an argument converts");
    var today: Celsius = 21.5;            # a typed variable converts
    assert(describe(today) == "mild", "already a Celsius");

    var label = Label("kitchen");         # no conversion: call the constructor
    assert(label.text == "kitchen", "explicit constructor call");

    var n = 12.0;                         # no slot type: stays a double
    assert(n == 12.0, "untyped local");
    return 0;
}

The standard library uses this for io.Path, which converts from a String, so dir.join("logs") and io.File.open("notes.txt") work without writing io.Path(...), and for Error, so Result<int>.err("bad input") works.

  • Where it applies: a variable’s initializer when the variable’s type is written, an assignment, a function, method or constructor argument (operators and a[i] = value included), a call through a function value, and a return from a function with a declared return type.
  • Where it does not: the receiver of a method call ("docs".join("x") does not turn "docs" into a Path), a var whose type is inferred (var n = 12.0; stays a double), and __null, which stays a null reference.
  • One conversion per value. The value must already have the constructor’s parameter type, or reach it by a widening that loses nothing: a smaller integer to a larger one, an integer literal that fits, float to double, or a struct to a trait it declares. Conversions never chain: if Tag converts from Name and Name from String, a String does not become a Tag.
  • Overloads prefer anything else. Among overloads, a member that takes the value as it is, or by any other conversion, beats one that needs an [Implicit] constructor.
  • Each conversion is a constructor call, so it allocates a new object. The VS Code extension shows the call as an inlay hint around the converted value, and hovering the value names the constructor. The converted value is a temporary like any constructor call’s result: it is released after the call it was passed to (see Memory and reference counting).
  • Only a constructor that can be called with one argument may be [Implicit]: one parameter, or a first parameter followed by parameters that all have defaults. It may not convert from the struct itself or, in a generic struct, from a bare type parameter (construct(T value)):
main.pep:2:5: error: 'Implicit' constructor of 'Span' must be callable with one argument
    2 |     [Implicit]
      |     ^~~~~~~~~~

Conversions are opt-in: a constructor without [Implicit] never runs on its own. When a value would fit such a constructor, the type error says so:

main.pep:6:27: error: cannot pass a value of type 'String' as argument 1 of 'show', which has type 'Label'
    6 | main(): int { return show("x"); }
      |                           ^~~
main.pep:3:5: note: 'Label' has a constructor from 'String': call 'Label(...)', or mark the constructor [Implicit]
    3 |     construct(String text) { this.text = text; }
      |     ^~~~~~~~~

Destructors

A destructor runs when an object is destroyed, which happens when the last reference to it goes away. Declare it with destruct and a body, with no parentheses. Use it to release something the object holds that Pepper does not manage for you, such as a file handle from C.

import async;

# A module-scope counter: const, and changed through an Atomic.
const closed = async.Atomic<int>(0);

struct Connection {
    var name: String;

    construct(this.name = "") {}

    # The destructor runs once, when the last reference to the object goes
    # away. Use it to release whatever the object holds.
    destruct {
        closed.fetch_add(1);
    }
}

main(): int {
    {
        var c = Connection("db");
        assert(closed.load() == 0, "still in use");
    }
    # `c` went out of scope at the closing brace.
    assert(closed.load() == 1, "the destructor ran at the end of the block");
    return 0;
}

You never call a destructor yourself. After it runs, Pepper releases the object’s fields, so a destructor can still read them. The memory chapter lists every point where an object can be destroyed.

Methods

A method is a function declared inside a struct. You call it on an object with a dot, v.length_squared(), and inside it this refers to that object.

struct Vector {
    var x: int = 0;
    var y: int = 0;

    construct(this.x = 0, this.y = 0) {}

    # A method: name, parameters, then the return type after `:`.
    length_squared(): int {
        # Fields can be named directly inside a method...
        return x * x + y * y;
    }

    # ...or through `this`, the object the method was called on.
    dot(other: Vector): int {
        return this.x * other.x + this.y * other.y;
    }

    # Methods can change fields, and can call other methods.
    scale(factor: int) {
        x = x * factor;
        y = y * factor;
    }

    # The return type can also come first, C-style.
    bool is_zero() {
        return length_squared() == 0;
    }

    # A static method belongs to the type, not to one object: there is
    # no `this`. Call it on the type name.
    static unit_x(): Vector {
        return Vector(1, 0);
    }
}

main(): int {
    var v = Vector(3, 4);
    assert(v.length_squared() == 25, "method call");
    assert(v.dot(Vector(1, 1)) == 7, "method with an argument");

    v.scale(2);
    assert(v.x == 6 && v.y == 8, "a method can modify its object");

    assert(Vector().is_zero(), "methods can be called on a temporary");
    assert(Vector.unit_x().x == 1, "static method called on the type");
    return 0;
}
  • Methods are written like functions: name(parameters): ReturnType { ... }. Leave out the return type for a method that returns nothing. The C-style form, bool is_zero() { ... }, works too.
  • Inside a method, the object’s fields and other methods can be named directly (x, length_squared()), or through this (this.x). A parameter or local with the same name as a field hides the field; use this. to reach the field.
  • A method can change the fields of its object. Because struct values are references, the caller sees the change.
  • Calling a method does not copy the object or add a reference to it. The result of a method call is a new reference, like any function result.
  • Several methods can share a name when their parameters differ; each call picks the best fit (see Overloading).

Static methods

A method marked static belongs to the type rather than to one object. It has no this, and you call it on the type name: Vector.unit_x(). Static methods are the usual way to offer named constructors, such as the standard library’s Result<int>.ok(42).

Inside the struct, any method, static or not, can call a static method by its bare name: unit_x() in a method of Vector means Vector.unit_x().

# Static methods belong to the type; inside it, they are called by name.
struct Vector {
    var x: double = 0.0;
    var y: double = 0.0;
    construct(this.x = 0.0, this.y = 0.0) {}

    static unit_x(): Vector {
        return Vector(1.0, 0.0);
    }

    # A static method calls another by its bare name.
    static scaled_unit_x(factor: double): Vector {
        var unit = unit_x();
        return Vector(unit.x * factor, unit.y * factor);
    }
}

main(): int {
    var v = Vector.scaled_unit_x(3.0);
    assert(v.x == 3.0 && v.y == 0.0, "called on the type name outside it");
    return 0;
}

Operators

A struct can define what the operators do for it. Declare a method whose name is the operator, written like any other method: ==(other: Money): bool. The C-style form with the return type first, bool ==(Money other), is accepted too.

struct Money {
    var cents: int = 0;

    construct(this.cents = 0) {}

    # `a == b` calls `a.==(b)`. Without this method, `==` on two structs
    # compares identity, like `===`.
    ==(other: Money): bool {
        return cents == other.cents;
    }

    # `!=` is derived from `==` when the struct does not define it.

    # `a < b` calls `a.<(b)`.
    <(other: Money): bool {
        return cents < other.cents;
    }

    # `a + b` calls `a.+(b)` and returns a new Money.
    +(other: Money): Money {
        return Money(cents + other.cents);
    }

    # `-a` calls `a.-()`: a unary operator takes no parameters.
    -(): Money {
        return Money(0 - cents);
    }

    # `a - b` calls `a.-(b)`. The unary and binary `-` overload each other,
    # told apart by their number of parameters.
    -(other: Money): Money {
        return Money(cents - other.cents);
    }

    # `a += b` needs its own method; it is not rewritten to `a = a + b`.
    +=(other: Money): Money {
        cents += other.cents;
        return this;
    }
}

struct Shelf {
    var slots: Array<String>;

    construct() {
        slots = Array<String>();
        slots.append("empty");
        slots.append("empty");
    }

    # An indexer with one parameter handles reads: `shelf[i]`.
    [](index: int): String {
        return slots[index];
    }

    # An indexer with two parameters handles writes: `shelf[i] = value`.
    [](index: int, value: String): String {
        slots[index] = value;
        return value;
    }
}

main(): int {
    var price = Money(250);
    assert(price == Money(250), "== compares cents");
    assert(price != Money(100), "!= compares cents");
    # `===` and `!==` always compare identity: equal cents, different objects.
    assert(price !== Money(250), "!== compares identity");
    var same = price;
    assert(same === price, "=== is true for the same object");

    var total = price + Money(50);
    assert(total.cents == 300, "+ makes a new value");
    assert(price.cents == 250, "+ left its operands alone");

    assert(price < total, "< compares cents");

    var refund = -price;
    assert(refund.cents == -250, "unary - calls -()");
    assert((total - price).cents == 50, "binary - calls -(other)");

    total += Money(25);
    assert(total.cents == 325, "+= updated total in place");

    var shelf = Shelf();
    shelf[1] = "books";
    assert(shelf[1] == "books", "indexer write, then read");
    assert(shelf[0] == "empty", "the other slot is unchanged");
    return 0;
}

When the left operand is a struct that declares the operator, a + b becomes the call a.+(b). The right operand is the method’s single parameter, and it can be any type. These binary operators can be defined:

KindOperators
Arithmetic+ - * / % **
Bitwise& | ^ >>
Bitwise shifts<< >>
Comparison and logical== != < <= > >= && ||
Compound assignment+= -= *= /= %= <<= >>= &= |= ^=

Keep these rules in mind:

  • An operator can be declared once per right-operand type (+(Money) and +(int)), and a + b picks by b’s type, as for any overloaded method.
  • Each operator is its own method, with one exception: when a struct defines == but not !=, a != b means !(a == b). += is not rewritten to a = a + b; define each one you want to use.
  • Comparison operators must return bool; any other return type is an error (comparison operator '==' must return 'bool', not 'String'). Logical operators should return bool too. Arithmetic, bitwise and compound assignment operators usually return the struct’s own type; a compound assignment usually changes this and returns it.
  • The left operand decides: a + b uses the method on a’s type. An expression with a number on the left and a struct on the right, such as 2 * v, is not supported.
  • Operators that start with < (<, <=, <<, <<=) can only be declared in the name: Type form, <(other: V): bool: in the C-style form the parser reads bool < as the start of generic arguments.

The result of an operator has the type its method returns, so with -(other: V): int, var r = a - b; is an int.

Unary operators

A unary operator is a method with no parameters; its operand is this.

OperatorDeclarationop x calls
Negation-(): Vx.-()
Bitwise complement~(): Vx.~()
Logical not!(): boolx.!()
Truth test!!(): boolx.!!() (see below)

The C-style form works here too: V -(), bool !!(). ! and !! must return bool (truth-test operator '!!' must return 'bool', not 'int'), and !, ~ and !! take no parameters. -a on a number is unchanged. A struct may declare both a unary -() and a binary -(other: V): they overload each other, told apart by their number of parameters.

Truth tests and conditions

A condition asks a value “true or false?”. For bool the answer is the value, for a number it is “not zero”, and for a raw pointer (__ptr<T>) or a function value it is “not null”. A struct answers through its truth-test operator, !!(): bool, like C++’s operator bool:

# A struct that declares `!!(): bool` can be used as a condition.
struct Budget {
    var cents: int = 0;

    construct(this.cents = 0) {}

    # The truth test: `if (budget)` calls `budget.!!()`.
    !!(): bool {
        return cents > 0;
    }
}

struct Label {
    var text: String;

    construct(this.text = "") {}
}

spend(budget: Budget, amount: int): int {
    var spent = 0;
    # A condition, an operand of `&&`, and the operand of `!` all call `!!`.
    while (budget && amount > 0) {
        budget.cents -= 1;
        amount -= 1;
        spent += 1;
    }
    if (!budget) {
        print("budget used up");
    }
    return spent;
}

main(): int {
    var budget = Budget(3);
    assert(spend(budget, 2) == 2, "spent 2 of 3");
    assert(budget ? true : false, "a ternary condition calls !! too");
    assert(spend(budget, 5) == 1, "only 1 left");
    assert(!!budget == false, "!!x calls the truth test");

    # A struct without `!!` is not a condition: `if (label)` is an error.
    # Compare with `__null` to ask whether a reference is set.
    var label: Label;
    assert(label === __null, "no Label yet");
    label = Label("sale");
    assert(label !== __null, "now there is one");
    return 0;
}

These are the boolean contexts. In each, a struct value x becomes x.!!():

  • the condition of if, else if and while;
  • the condition of condition ? a : b;
  • each operand of &&, ||, and and or (unless the struct declares && or || itself, which then takes the whole operation);
  • the operand of !: without its own ! method, !x is !(x.!!()).

!!x is the truth test itself: on a struct it calls x.!!(); on a bool or a number it is still two negations. Optional declares !!, so if (found) asks whether an optional holds a value.

A struct that does not declare !! cannot be used as a condition at all:

main.pep:6:9: error: 'Node' cannot be used as a condition: declare '!!(): bool' on it, or compare with '__null'
    6 |     if (node) {
      |         ^~~~

A struct value is a reference, but a condition never tests it for null. To ask whether a reference is set, compare it with __null (node !== __null), or better, use an Optional for a value that may be missing. A trait value is treated the same way: it is a condition only when its trait declares !!.

Comparing structs

Without an == method, a == b on two structs compares identity: it is true only when both refer to the same object, exactly like a === b. The same goes for !=. Define == when two distinct objects with the same contents should count as equal, as String and Array do; != then follows from it. === and !== always compare identity, whatever methods the struct declares, so "a" + "b" == "ab" is true while "a" + "b" === "ab" is false.

Indexers

An indexer lets you write object[index]. Declare it as a method named []:

  • With one parameter, [](index: int): String, it handles reads: shelf[i].
  • With two parameters, [](index: int, value: String): String, it handles writes: shelf[i] = value. The second parameter is the value being stored.

The C-style form, String [](int index), is accepted too.

A struct can have both. With both, compound assignment through an index (counts[i] += 1) reads with the first and writes with the second. Array and String are indexed this way.

Enums and match

An enum is a type with a fixed set of named cases. A value of the enum holds exactly one of them. Use an enum where you would otherwise pass an integer code or a string, so the compiler checks that only the listed cases flow through, and that a match handles each one.

There are two kinds:

  • In an enum whose cases carry nothing (Red, Green), each case is an integer. Such an enum is a value type, like int.
  • When a case carries values (Circle(radius: int)), the enum is a reference type, like a struct. See Cases that carry values.
# An enum names a fixed set of cases; a slot of the enum type holds one.
enum Suit {
    Clubs,
    Diamonds,
    Hearts,
    Spades,
}

# A representation sets the stored integer type; a case may give its value.
enum Status: u8 {
    Ok,
    NotFound = 44,
    Failed,
}

struct Card {
    Suit suit;
    int rank = 1;
}

main(): int {
    var card = Card();
    assert(card.suit == Suit.Clubs, "a slot starts at the case whose value is 0");
    card.suit = Suit.Hearts;
    assert(card.suit != Suit.Spades, "cases compare with == and !=");

    # 'as' turns a case into its integer; the reverse is not allowed.
    assert((Suit.Hearts as int) == 2, "cases number from 0");
    assert((Status.Failed as int) == 45, "numbering continues after an explicit value");
    assert(sizeof<Status>() == 1, "Status is stored as a u8");
    return 0;
}

Declaring an enum

enum Name { ... } lists the cases, separated by commas; a comma after the last case is optional. Case names are PascalCase, like types (see naming conventions).

Each case is an integer. The first case is 0 and each case after it is one more than the one before. A case can give its own value with = value, and numbering continues from there:

enum Status: u8 {
    Ok,             # 0
    NotFound = 44,  # 44
    Failed,         # 45
}

A value must be an integer constant: a literal such as -1 or 0x20, or a character such as 'y'. Two cases cannot have the same value.

The type after the colon is the representation, the integer type the enum is stored as. It can be any integer type (u8, short, int, long, and so on). Without one, the enum is stored as an int. Every case value must fit in the representation.

A case can carry a [Target] attribute, so a platform can have cases that others lack. A dropped case does not renumber the others.

Using enum values

This section is about enums whose cases carry nothing.

Name.Case is a value of the enum type. Such an enum is a value type, like int: it is copied, not reference counted, and it can be stored in locals, fields, arrays and module-scope constants, and passed to and returned from functions.

  • == and != compare two values of the same enum. No other operator applies to an enum.
  • An enum does not mix with integers or with other enums: int x = Color.Red and Color c = 0 are errors, and so is comparing a Color with a Size.
  • value as int (or any integer type) gives a case’s integer value. The reverse, 1 as Color, is an error, since the integer may not name a case; name the case, or use from_value.
  • A slot of an enum type that is not given a value (a field, or a local declared without one) holds the case whose value is 0, or the first case when no case is 0.
  • sizeof<Name>() is the size of the representation.
  • An enum works wherever an integer does: as a HashMap key or HashSet element, in an Atomic<Name>, and in an extern function’s signature, where C sees the representation (an int unless the enum names another).

Cases that carry values

A case can carry values, declared like parameters: Circle(radius: int). An enum with such a case is a reference type: each value is an object, reference counted like a struct.

# Cases that carry values: each case is a constructor, and a `match`
# pattern binds the values of the case it matches.
enum Shape {
    Circle(radius: int),
    Rect(width: int, height: int),
    Square(side: int),
    Point,

    area(): int {
        match (this) {
            Circle(r) => { return 3 * r * r; }
            Rect(w, h) => { return w * h; }
            Square(s) => { return s * s; }
            Point => { return 0; }
        }
        return 0;
    }
}

# A generic enum can name itself: a list is empty, or a value and the rest.
enum List<T> {
    Empty,
    Cons(head: T, tail: List<T>),
}

length(list: List<String>): int {
    match (list) {
        Empty => { return 0; }
        # `_` skips a value.
        Cons(_, tail) => { return 1 + length(tail); }
    }
    return 0;
}

main(): int {
    var shapes = Array<Shape>();
    shapes.append(Shape.Circle(2));
    shapes.append(Shape.Rect(3, 4));
    shapes.append(Shape.Point);
    var total = 0;
    for (var s in shapes) {
        total += s.area();
    }
    assert(total == 24, "12 + 12 + 0");

    # Several patterns in one arm bind the same names.
    var side = 0;
    match (Shape.Square(5)) {
        Rect(w, _), Square(w) => { side = w; }
        else => {}
    }
    assert(side == 5, "a square's side");

    var names = List<String>.Cons("a", List<String>.Cons("b", List<String>.Empty));
    assert(length(names) == 2, "two names");
    assert(names.name() == "Cons", "name() spells the case");
    return 0;
}
  • Name.Case(values...) makes a new value, like a constructor call, and Name.Case alone is a case that carries nothing. An enum’s values are made only by its cases: Shape(...) is an error.
  • A case that carries values must be given them: Shape.Circle without (radius) is an error.
  • The values are fixed once made. There is no way to change them, so a value can be shared freely. To change one, make a new value.
  • Each case that carries nothing is a single object that every use shares. It is never freed and costs no allocation, however often it is used.
  • A slot of the enum type that is not given a value holds null, as a struct slot does. === and !== compare identity.
  • An enum can have type parameters (enum List<T>), and its cases can hold the enum itself, directly or through other types, so lists and trees are enums.
  • The enum can be [Shared] when every value its cases carry is thread-safe (see What threads can share). An enum whose cases carry nothing is stored as an integer and is always thread-safe. It can conform to a trait with extend Name with Trait, like a struct, and its methods can come from an extend block too.
  • Cases cannot have explicit values (= 3), and the enum has no representation type (: u8), since its values are not integers.

Methods

An enum can declare methods after its cases. Inside a method, this is the value the method was called on, and a bare call of another method of the enum (next()) calls it on this. A static method is called on the enum itself (Light.first()).

# An enum can declare methods after its cases; `this` is the value.
enum Light: u8 {
    Red,
    Amber,
    Green,

    may_go(): bool {
        return this == Light.Green;
    }

    next(): Light {
        match (this) {
            Red => { return Light.Green; }
            Amber => { return Light.Red; }
            Green => { return Light.Amber; }
        }
        return this;
    }

    # A bare call of another method acts on `this`.
    after_two(): Light {
        return next().next();
    }

    static first(): Light {
        return Light.Red;
    }
}

main(): int {
    var light = Light.first();
    assert(!light.may_go(), "red means stop");
    assert(light.next().may_go(), "green follows red");
    assert(light.after_two() == Light.Amber, "then amber");

    # Every enum has name() and from_value().
    assert(light.name() == "Red", "name() spells the case");
    var found = Light.from_value(2);
    assert(found.is_ok() and found.value() == Light.Green, "2 is Green");
    assert(!Light.from_value(7).is_ok(), "no case has the value 7");

    # Enums key hash maps and fill atomics, like integers.
    var waits = HashMap<Light, int>();
    waits[Light.Red] = 30;
    assert(waits[Light.Red] == 30, "an enum is a hash key");
    return 0;
}

For an enum whose cases carry nothing, this is passed by value, like an int: a method cannot change the value it was called on. Return a new case instead, as next() does. For an enum whose cases carry values, this is the object, as in a struct’s method; its values still cannot change.

Built-in methods

Every enum has these methods without declaring them, and cannot declare methods of the same names:

MethodWhat it does
value.name()Returns the case’s name as written ("Red"), a String. Every enum has it.
Name.from_value(n)Returns a Result<Name>: Ok with the case whose value is n, or an Err when no case has it. n has the enum’s representation type. Only enums whose cases carry nothing have it.

from_value is the checked way back from an integer (from a file, a C library or the network) to a case, since as only goes the other way.

match

match (value) { ... } runs the arm for the case that value holds:

# 'match' runs the arm of the case a value holds, and must handle every case.
enum Light {
    Red,
    Amber,
    Green,
}

next(light: Light): Light {
    match (light) {
        Red => { return Light.Green; }
        Amber => { return Light.Red; }
        Green => { return Light.Amber; }
    }
    return light;
}

may_go(light: Light): bool {
    match (light) {
        Green => { return true; }
