        else => { return false; }
    }
    return false;
}

wait_seconds(light: Light): int {
    match (light) {
        Red, Amber => { return 30; }
        Light.Green => { return 0; }
    }
    return 0;
}

main(): int {
    var light = Light.Red;
    var changes = 0;
    while (!may_go(light)) {
        light = next(light);
        changes += 1;
    }
    assert(changes == 1, "red turns green");
    assert(wait_seconds(Light.Amber) == 30, "one arm handles two cases");
    assert(wait_seconds(light) == 0, "a pattern may name the enum");
    return 0;
}
  • Each arm is one or more patterns, separated by commas, then => and a block. A pattern is a case name (Red) or the case qualified by its enum (Light.Red).
  • A pattern for a case that carries values can bind them: Rect(w, h) declares w and h in its arm, holding the case’s values in order. The bindings are const. _ skips a value. A pattern binds all of its case’s values or, written without parentheses (Rect), none.
  • Patterns that share an arm must bind the same names, with the same types (Rect(w, _), Square(w)).
  • An else => { ... } arm, last, handles every case the other arms do not.
  • The arms must handle every case. A missing case is an error that names it, located at match; the language server offers a quick fix that adds an empty arm for each missing case. An else that can never run, because the other arms handle every case, is a warning.
  • Handling a case twice is an error.
  • In a match statement, break, continue and return inside an arm act on the enclosing loop or function, as they would inside an if.

The value is evaluated once, before any arm runs. A match on a null value of an enum whose cases carry values panics with match on a null 'Name'.

match expressions, is, and literal patterns

# `match` produces a value, `is` tests one case, and a `match` on an
# integer, character, `bool` or `String` compares with literals.
enum Shape {
    Circle(radius: int),
    Rect(width: int, height: int),
    Point,
}

enum List {
    Empty,
    Cons(head: int, tail: List),
}

area(s: Shape): int {
    return match (s) {
        Circle(r) => 3 * r * r,
        Rect(w, h) => w * h,
        Point => 0,
    };
}

keyword(word: String): int {
    return match (word) {
        "import" => 1,
        "export", "extern" => 2,
        else => 0,
    };
}

main(): int {
    var total = area(Shape.Rect(2, 3)) + keyword("extern");

    # `is` binds only in the block of the `if` or `while` it is the
    # condition of.
    var s = Shape.Circle(1);
    if (s is Circle(r)) {
        total += r;
    }

    var list = List.Cons(1, List.Cons(2, List.Empty));
    while (list is Cons(head, tail)) {
        total += head;
        list = tail;
    }

    var point = Shape.Point is Point;
    if (point && !(s is Rect)) {
        total += 100;
    }

    # A `match` on an integer needs an `else`: literals cannot list every
    # value.
    var size = match (total) {
        0 => "none",
        1, 2, 3 => "few",
        else => "many",
    };
    assert(size == "many", "total is past three");
    assert(total == 6 + 2 + 1 + 3 + 100, "every step adds up");
    return 0;
}
  • A match that produces a value can go wherever a value can: after var x =, return, in an argument. Each arm is patterns => value, and arms are separated by commas (one after the last is allowed). It follows the rules above: a pattern binds names for its arm’s value, and the arms must handle every case unless there is an else. The value has the first arm’s type, and every other arm’s value must convert to it. A closure in an arm’s value cannot use a name the arm binds; use a match statement there.
  • value is Pattern is a bool: whether value holds that case (d is Line, !(d is Text)). It takes any one pattern. When it is the whole condition of an if or while, its bindings are declared in that block only: if (d is Text(t)) { ... } reads t inside the braces, and while (list is Cons(head, tail)) { ... } examines list again on every iteration. Anywhere else, is cannot bind names. is is a keyword only between a value and a pattern, so it stays usable as a name (token.is(text)).
  • Literal patterns: a match on an integer, a character, a bool or a String compares with literals (1, -1, 'a', true, "import"), using ==. Literals cannot list every value, so such a match needs an else arm, except on a bool that handles both true and false. Matching the same literal twice is an error. A match on an enum takes its case names, not literals, and a match on int takes literals, not names.

Current limits

  • Optional is not an enum yet, so it cannot be matched. Result is one (Ok(value), Err(error)).
  • An enum whose cases carry nothing cannot be generic. The methods of any enum cannot be generic yet. An enum cannot declare operators or indexers yet; == and != are built in for enums whose cases carry nothing.
  • A case’s values bind names only: a pattern cannot nest inside a case (Some(Text(t))) or compare its values (Text("")) yet. Patterns nest inside tuple patterns ((Text(t), 0)). Patterns cannot match ranges (1..9) or have guards yet. A literal pattern is a literal, not a named constant.
  • A match cannot examine floating-point values.
  • An enum whose cases carry nothing cannot be extended (extend Color { ... }); declare its methods inside it. So it cannot conform to a trait either, and a trait value is a reference to an object, which such an enum’s value is not.

Memory and reference counting

Pepper frees memory for you, without a garbage collector and without ownership annotations. Every struct object keeps a count of the references to it, and the object is destroyed the moment that count drops to zero. Because the rules are simple and the same everywhere, you can always tell when an object will be destroyed and its destructor will run.

If you know C++, the whole model fits in one sentence: every struct value behaves exactly like a std::shared_ptr<T> passed by value.

Values and references

Numbers, bool, and the other primitive types are plain values: assigning one copies it, as in C. So is a tuple, whose elements are copied the way each element would be on its own.

Everything else, including your own structs, String, Array, HashMap, and function values, is a reference to an object on the heap. Assigning a reference, passing it to a function, or storing it in a field or an array shares the object. Nothing is copied.

struct Account {
    var balance: int = 0;
}

# The parameter is another reference to the caller's object, so changes to
# its fields are visible to the caller.
deposit(account: Account, amount: int) {
    account.balance += amount;
}

# Rebinding the parameter itself only changes this function's reference.
replace(account: Account) {
    account = Account();
    account.balance = 999;
}

main(): int {
    var mine = Account();
    var yours = mine;               # shares the object; nothing is copied
    yours.balance = 50;
    assert(mine.balance == 50, "assignment shares the object");

    deposit(mine, 25);
    assert(mine.balance == 75, "a function can change the shared object");

    replace(mine);
    assert(mine.balance == 75, "rebinding a parameter does not affect the caller");

    # To get an independent object, make a new one and copy the fields.
    var copy = Account();
    copy.balance = mine.balance;
    copy.balance = 0;
    assert(mine.balance == 75, "the copy is a separate object");
    return 0;
}
  • var yours = mine; makes a second reference to the same Account. Changes through either name are visible through both.
  • A parameter is one more reference to the caller’s object. The function can change the object’s fields, but assigning a new object to the parameter only changes the function’s own reference.
  • To get an independent object, create a new one. Pepper does not copy structs for you; some library types offer a method for it, such as Array’s clone().

A struct-typed variable or field that has not been given a value, such as var next: Account;, is null: it refers to no object. Reading a field or calling a method through a null reference crashes the program. Use === or !== to check whether two references name the same object, or whether one is null (next === __null). A struct is not a condition by itself, so if (next) is an error unless the struct declares the truth test !! (see Truth tests and conditions). For a value that may be absent, prefer Optional<T>, whose type says so.

When objects are destroyed

A reference is held by whatever stores it: a local variable, a parameter, a field, an element of a container, or a temporary value in the middle of an expression. Each of those releases its reference exactly once, when it goes away. When the last reference is released, the object is destroyed: its destructor runs, and then its fields release their own references, which may destroy further objects in turn.

import async;

# A module-scope counter: const, and changed through an Atomic.
const destroyed = async.Atomic<int>(0);

struct Tracked {
    var name: String;
    construct(this.name = "") {}
    destruct {
        destroyed.fetch_add(1);
    }
}

struct Holder {
    var item: Tracked;
}

make(name: String): Tracked {
    var t = Tracked(name);
    return t;                   # the caller receives the object
}

main(): int {
    # 1. A local is released when its scope ends.
    {
        var a = Tracked("a");
    }
    assert(destroyed.load() == 1, "a was destroyed at the end of its block");

    # 2. While another reference exists, the object stays alive.
    var b = Tracked("b");
    var also_b = b;
    b = Tracked("b2");          # b lets go of the first object...
    assert(destroyed.load() == 1, "...but also_b still holds it");
    also_b = b;                 # the last reference moves away
    assert(destroyed.load() == 2, "the first object is destroyed now");

    # 3. Fields and containers hold references too.
    var holder = Holder();
    {
        var c = Tracked("c");
        holder.item = c;
    }
    assert(destroyed.load() == 2, "holder.item keeps c alive after its scope");
    holder = Holder();          # the old Holder dies and releases c
    assert(destroyed.load() == 3, "releasing the holder released its field");

    var list = Array<Tracked>();
    list.append(Tracked("d"));
    assert(destroyed.load() == 3, "the array holds d");
    list.clear();
    assert(destroyed.load() == 4, "clearing the array released d");

    # 4. Returned objects belong to the caller; unused results are
    #    destroyed right away.
    var e = make("e");
    assert(destroyed.load() == 4, "e is alive in main");
    make("temporary");
    assert(destroyed.load() == 5, "a result nobody keeps is destroyed immediately");
    return 0;
}

Concretely, a reference is released when:

  • A local variable goes out of scope, at the closing brace of the block that declared it, or when the function returns.
  • A variable or field is overwritten. b = Tracked("b2"); releases the object b held before, after taking the new one. Assigning a variable to itself (a = a) changes nothing.
  • A parameter’s function returns. The function held its parameters for as long as it ran.
  • The object that holds a field is destroyed, or a container removes an element (clear(), overwriting list[i], and so on). remove_at() and pop() are the exception: they hand the container’s reference to the caller, so var x = list.remove_at(0); leaves the count unchanged.
  • A temporary is no longer needed. A result that is not stored anywhere, like the one from make("temporary");, is released at the end of the statement. The same goes for a call result passed straight to another function, and for the object in make().name.

Returning a local hands its reference to the caller, so the object survives the function. Calling a method on an object does not add a reference to it: inside the method, this refers to the caller’s object.

Cycles leak

Reference counting cannot free a cycle: objects that refer to each other, directly or through a chain, keep each other’s counts above zero even after nothing else refers to them. Their destructors never run and their memory is never freed.

import async;

# A module-scope counter: const, and changed through an Atomic.
const destroyed = async.Atomic<int>(0);

struct Person {
    var name: String;
    var friends: Array<Person>;

    construct(this.name = "") {
        friends = Array<Person>();
    }

    destruct {
        destroyed.fetch_add(1);
    }
}

main(): int {
    # Two people who list each other as friends form a cycle: each keeps
    # the other alive, so neither is ever destroyed.
    {
        var ann = Person("Ann");
        var bob = Person("Bob");
        ann.friends.append(bob);
        bob.friends.append(ann);
    }
    assert(destroyed.load() == 0, "the cycle leaked both objects");

    # Break the cycle before letting go, and both are destroyed.
    {
        var cat = Person("Cat");
        var dan = Person("Dan");
        cat.friends.append(dan);
        dan.friends.append(cat);
        dan.friends.clear();    # Dan no longer holds Cat
    }
    assert(destroyed.load() == 2, "without the cycle, both were destroyed");
    return 0;
}

To avoid a cycle, make one direction of it a weak reference (next section), or break the cycle yourself before the last outside reference goes away: clear the container, or overwrite the field, that closes the loop.

A closure holds a reference to every struct it captures, including this, so a closure stored inside an object it captures closes a cycle too. The compiler reports the direct case, a method storing a closure that captures this in a field of this.

Weak references

A Weak<T> points at an object without keeping it alive. Use it for back pointers: a child’s parent, a document’s folder, an observer’s subject. The owner holds strong references down the tree, and everything that points back up holds a Weak<T>, so there is no cycle.

import async;

# A module-scope counter: const, and changed through an Atomic.
const destroyed = async.Atomic<int>(0);

struct Folder {
    var name: String;
    var files: Array<Document>;

    construct(this.name = "") {
        files = Array<Document>();
    }

    destruct {
        destroyed.fetch_add(1);
    }
}

struct Document {
    var title: String;
    # A weak back pointer: the folder owns its documents, not the other way
    # round, so there is no cycle.
    var folder: Weak<Folder>;

    construct(String title, Folder folder) {
        this.title = title;
        this.folder = Weak<Folder>(folder);
    }

    destruct {
        destroyed.fetch_add(1);
    }

    String path() {
        with (var f = folder) {
            return f.name + "/" + title;
        } else {
            return "(deleted)/" + title;
        }
        return "";
    }
}

main(): int {
    var kept = Document("draft", Folder("none"));
    {
        var home = Folder("home");
        var notes = Document("notes", home);
        home.files.append(notes);
        assert(notes.path() == "home/notes", "the folder is alive");
        kept = notes;
    }
    # The folder went away with `home`; the weak pointer did not keep it.
    assert(kept.path() == "(deleted)/notes", "the folder is gone");
    assert(kept.folder.expired(), "and the weak reference knows it");
    return 0;
}
  • Weak<T>(object) makes the weak reference. It does not change the object’s reference count.
  • A with block reaches the object: with (var f = folder) { ... } binds f to an ordinary strong reference for the length of the block. When the object has already been destroyed, the body is skipped and the else block runs. See Scoped blocks with with.
  • expired() reports whether the object has been destroyed.
  • The object is destroyed on time. When its last strong reference goes, its destructor runs and its fields are released, even if weak references remain. Only the object’s small header stays allocated until the last weak reference is gone.

In C++ terms, a struct value is a std::shared_ptr<T> and Weak<T> wraps the built-in __weak<T>, a std::weak_ptr<T>: Weak<T>(object) is weak_ptr(object), and entering it with with is lock(). A weak reference made while an object is still inside its constructor cannot be upgraded until the constructor returns, as with weak_from_this() in C++.

References and threads

Reference counts are plain, fast increments, so a struct’s objects must stay on one thread. A struct declared [Shared] has atomic counts instead, and its references can be copied and dropped on any thread. The compiler requires such a struct’s fields to be const and thread-safe. See What threads can share.

Function values follow the same split: a plain function type such as () => void has plain counts and stays on one thread, and a shared function type such as shared () => void has atomic counts.

Copying a value with copy

copy(value) makes a copy of a value that shares no object that is not thread-safe with the original, so the copy can go to another thread: pass copy(x) to a channel to send a value you keep using.

var names = Array<String>();
names.append("ada");
var copied = copy(names);
copied[0].append(" lovelace");   # names[0] is still "ada"
  • Every struct object the value reaches is copied once. An object referenced twice is copied once and stays shared inside the copy, and a cycle becomes the same cycle among the copies.
  • Thread-safe objects are not copied: a [Shared] struct or a shared function value in the original is the same object in the copy. For a thread-safe value, copy returns the value itself.
  • A weak reference to an object that was copied points at its copy. A weak reference to an object outside the copied value becomes null.
  • A struct is copied field by field, without running its constructor.

A struct with a destructor or a raw pointer (__ptr<T>) field is not trivially copyable: copying its fields would share what it owns, such as a buffer it frees. Such a struct says how to copy itself by implementing Copyable<T>, with a copy(Copies copies) method that builds the copy and copies each value it holds with copies.copy(value). String, Array, HashMap and HashSet implement it. String.copy() also copies a single String; it replaces the deprecated clone(). Array.clone() is unchanged: it copies the Array but shares its elements.

Copying a value that reaches a struct that is not trivially copyable and does not implement Copyable<T> is an error at the copy call. It names the struct, shows each field on the way to it, says why it cannot be copied, and shows a Copyable<T> to fill in (the editor offers to insert it):

main.pep:14:13: error: cannot copy 'Log' because it contains 'Handle', which is not trivially copyable
   14 |     var c = copy(log);
      |             ^~~~
main.pep:9:5: note: 'Log' reaches it through field 'out'
    9 |     Handle out;
      |     ^~~~~~
main.pep:1:8: note: 'Handle' has a destructor, so copying its fields would release what it owns twice
    1 | struct Handle {
      |        ^~~~~~
note: implement 'Copyable<Handle>' to say how to copy it:
    extend Handle with Copyable<Handle> {
        Handle copy(Copies copies) {
            # Build the copy; copy each struct field with copies.copy(field).
            panic("copying 'Handle' is not implemented");
            return this;
        }
    }

Some types cannot be copied at all: an io.File owns an operating-system handle, so the error says to send its path instead. A plain function value cannot be copied, because it may capture anything; declare it shared. A trait value cannot be copied yet.

Handing a reference over with move

move(x) gives up x’s reference: the call returns the same object, and x is left null. Nothing is copied and no count changes. It is how a value built in a local variable goes to a channel, a Mutex or another [Move] parameter, which takes a new value, without the cost of copy(x):

var lines = Array<String>();
lines.append("first");
var log = async.Mutex<Array<String>>(move(lines));   # lines is now null

move is an ordinary function from the prelude (runtime/copy.pep), but the compiler checks every call:

  • Only a local variable can be moved (move(h.s) is an error), and only when it holds the one reference to a new value: nothing else refers to it or to anything it reaches. A parameter can be moved only when it is [Move], since the caller handed its value over.

    main.pep:8:24: error: 'a' cannot be moved: 'b' also references its value
    8 |     names.replace(move(a));
      |                        ^
note: only a variable that holds the one reference to a new value can hand it over; pass 'copy(...)' instead

  • A moved variable cannot be read again until it is assigned a new value, including on the next pass through a loop:

    main.pep:8:12: error: 'a' is used after its value was moved
    8 |     return a.count();
      |            ^
main.pep:7:19: note: 'a' was moved here; assign it a new value before using it again
    7 |     names.replace(move(a));
      |                   ^~~~

The runtime also moves values out of raw memory (move(buffer[head])), which is a promise the compiler cannot check: only runtime files may do it. The parameter of move is marked [MoveSource], which is also only allowed in the runtime, so a hand-off always shows at the call as move(x); a function of your own that takes over its argument uses [Move].

Summary

CodeWhat happens to references
var b = a;b takes a new reference to a’s object.
b = c;b takes a reference to c’s object, then releases its old one.
f(a)The parameter takes a reference for the duration of the call.
return a;The caller receives a reference to a’s object.
a.method()No change: this refers to a’s object.
f(move(a))No change: a’s reference goes to the call, and a is left null.
make(); (result unused)The result is released at the end of the statement.
var w = Weak<T>(a);No change to a’s count; w does not keep the object alive.
var c = copy(a);c refers to new objects; a’s count does not change.
end of a blockEvery local declared in the block releases its reference.

Generics

Generics let you write a struct or a function once and use it with many types. Add type parameters in angle brackets after the name, then use them like any other type name. The standard library’s Array<T>, HashMap<K, V>, and Result<TValue, TError> are all ordinary generic structs written this way.

Pepper generics work like C++ templates: each distinct set of type arguments, such as Stack<int> or Stack<String>, produces its own copy of the code, compiled for those exact types. There is no runtime cost for using them.

Generic structs

# `T` is a type parameter: each use such as `Stack<int>` or
# `Stack<String>` makes a separate, fully typed version of the struct.
struct Stack<T> {
    var items: Array<T>;

    construct() {
        items = Array<T>();
    }

    push(item: T) {
        items.append(item);
    }

    pop(): T {
        return items.pop();
    }

    peek(): T {
        # Inside the struct, T can be used like any other type name.
        var top: T = items.last();
        return top;
    }

    is_empty(): bool {
        return items.empty();
    }
}

# Several parameters are separated by commas.
struct Entry<K, V> {
    var key: K;
    var value: V;
    construct(K key, V value) {
        this.key = key;
        this.value = value;
    }
}

main(): int {
    var numbers = Stack<int>();
    numbers.push(1);
    numbers.push(2);
    assert(numbers.peek() == 2, "peek looks at the top");
    assert(numbers.pop() == 2, "last in, first out");
    assert(numbers.pop() == 1, "then the first");
    assert(numbers.is_empty(), "empty again");

    var words = Stack<String>();
    words.push("hello");
    assert(words.pop() == "hello", "the same code works for Strings");

    var e = Entry<String, int>("answer", 42);
    assert(e.key == "answer" && e.value == 42, "two type parameters");
    return 0;
}
  • Name the type parameters after the struct’s name: struct Stack<T>, struct Entry<K, V>. Inside the struct, fields, parameters, return types, and locals can all use them.
  • Name the type arguments whenever you use the struct: Stack<int>(), var s: Stack<String>;.
  • Stack<int> and Stack<String> are different types.

Note: Inside a generic struct, var top = items.last(); cannot infer a type that involves a type parameter yet, and fails with unknown type name 'T'. Write the type out: var top: T = items.last();.

Generic functions

A free function takes type parameters the same way:

larger<T>(a: T, b: T): T {
    if (a > b) {
        return a;
    }
    return b;
}

struct Circle {
    var radius: int = 1;
    area(): int { return 3 * radius * radius; }
}

struct Square {
    var side: int = 2;
    area(): int { return side * side; }
}

# The body can use anything the type argument provides: this works for
# any T that has an `area()` method returning a number.
total_area<T>(shapes: Array<T>): int {
    var sum = 0;
    for (var shape in shapes) {
        sum += shape.area();
    }
    return sum;
}

main(): int {
    # Type arguments come from the arguments, or can be written out.
    assert(larger(3, 9) == 9, "ints");
    assert(larger<float>(2.5, 1.5) == 2.5, "floats");

    var circles = Array<Circle>();
    circles.append(Circle());
    circles.append(Circle());
    assert(total_area(circles) == 6, "circles");

    var squares = Array<Square>();
    squares.append(Square());
    assert(total_area<Square>(squares) == 4, "squares");
    return 0;
}

Pepper infers the type arguments from the arguments, so larger(3, 9) calls larger<int>. You can always write them out, larger<float>(2.5, 1.5), and must when the arguments do not determine every type parameter, for example one that appears only in the return type:

main.pep:4:13: error: cannot infer the type arguments of 'make' from its arguments; write them: make<T>(...)
    4 |     var b = make();
      |             ^~~~
main.pep:1:1: note: declared here
    1 | make<T>(): Box<T> { return Box<T>(); }
      | ^~~~

Inference works through closures in both directions. In transform(words, (w) => w.size()), where transform<T, U>(items: Array<T>, f: (T) => U), words gives T, which types the closure’s parameter w, and the closure’s result gives U.

Because each use is compiled for its concrete types, the body may use any operator, field, or method that the type arguments provide. total_area<T> calls shape.area(), so it works with any T that has an area() method returning a number, and using it with a type that lacks one is a compile error inside total_area. To state the requirement up front, and have the compiler report it where the function is used, give T a constraint.

Generic methods

A method can have type parameters of its own, in a struct, a generic struct, an extension, or a trait’s default method. They are inferred at each call like a function’s, or written after the method name:

struct Box<T> {
    T value;
    construct(T v) { value = v; }

    # A method with a type parameter of its own: `U` is chosen per call.
    map<U>(f: (T) => U): Box<U> {
        return Box<U>(f(value));
    }
}

main(): int {
    var b = Box<int>(4);

    # `U` comes from what the closure returns...
    var tens = b.map((x) => x * 10);
    assert(tens.value == 40, "tens");

    var text = tens.map((x) => "forty");
    assert(text.value == "forty", "text");

    # ...or is written after the method name.
    var wide = b.map<long>((x: int): long => x + 1);
    assert(wide.value == 5, "wide");
    return 0;
}
  • Write the type arguments with no space before < or after >: b.map<long>(f). With a space, a.b < c is a comparison.
  • A generic method cannot be called through a trait value, since each of its uses is compiled separately. Call it on the concrete type.
  • The iterator adapters map and filter are generic default methods of Iterator<T>; see Iteration.

Default type arguments

A type parameter can have a default, written Name=Type. When a use leaves that argument out, the default fills it in:

struct Measurement<TValue, TUnit=String> {
    var value: TValue;
    var unit: TUnit;
}

main(): int {
    # `Measurement<float>` fills TUnit with its default, String.
    var length = Measurement<float>();
    length.value = 2.5;
    length.unit = "m";
    assert(length.unit == "m", "TUnit defaulted to String");

    # Any argument can still be given explicitly.
    var count = Measurement<int, int>();
    count.unit = 7;
    assert(count.unit == 7, "TUnit given as int");

    # The standard library's Result uses a default the same way:
    # Result<int> means Result<int, Error>.
    var ok = Result<int>.ok(42);
    assert(ok.value() == 42, "Result with the default error type");
    return 0;
}

Arguments are matched to parameters in order, so put the parameters that have defaults last. The standard library declares struct Result<TValue, TError=Error>, so Result<int> means Result<int, Error>. See Error handling with Result.

Constraints

A type parameter can require a trait: write the trait after a colon, T: Shape. Every type argument for T must then conform to Shape. Several constraints are joined with &, and a constrained parameter can still have a default, written after them:

trait Shape {
    area(): int;
}

trait Named {
    name(): String;
}

struct Circle {
    var radius: int = 1;
    area(): int { return 3 * radius * radius; }
}

extend Circle with Shape {}

struct Square {
    var side: int = 2;
    area(): int { return side * side; }
    name(): String { return "square"; }
}

extend Square with Shape {}
extend Square with Named {}

# Every T must conform to Shape.
total_area<T: Shape>(shapes: Array<T>): int {
    var sum = 0;
    for (var shape in shapes) {
        sum += shape.area();
    }
    return sum;
}

# Several constraints are joined with `&`.
label<T: Shape & Named>(item: T): String { return item.name(); }

# A constrained parameter can have a default, which must conform too.
struct Gallery<TTag, TShape: Shape = Square> {
    var items = Array<TShape>();
    add(item: TShape) { items.append(item); }
    total(): int { return total_area(items); }
}

main(): int {
    var circles = Array<Circle>();
    circles.append(Circle());
    circles.append(Circle());
    assert(total_area(circles) == 6, "circles");
    assert(label(Square()) == "square", "label");

    # Gallery<String> is Gallery<String, Square>.
    var gallery = Gallery<String>();
    gallery.add(Square());
    assert(gallery.total() == 4, "default");

    # A trait type conforms to its own trait.
    var shapes = Array<Shape>();
    shapes.append(Circle());
    shapes.append(Square());
    assert(total_area(shapes) == 7, "trait values");
    return 0;
}

Constraints work on generic structs, enums whose cases carry values, functions, methods, traits and type aliases. A constraint may name the parameters before it in the same list: sum<T, I: Iterator<T>>(values: I).

A type argument conforms to a trait when:

  • it is a struct declared to have the trait with extend Circle with Shape. For a generic struct, extend Box<T> with Shape makes every Box<X> conform, and extend Box<int> with Shape only Box<int>. A generic trait must match exactly: extend Counter with Iterator<int> conforms to Iterator<int>, not to Iterator<long>. Having the right methods is not enough; the extension is what declares it.
  • it is the trait type itself (Array<Shape> passed as Array<T> with T: Shape), as long as every member of the trait can be called through a value of the trait type (see traits as types).
  • it is a type parameter constrained by that trait: inside wrap<T: Shape>, Gallery<String, T> is allowed.

Numbers, bool, enums, pointers, tuples and function types conform to no trait.

The Shared constraint

T: Shared is built in: it requires a type that is safe to share between threads, by the same rule as a field of a [Shared] struct. The types that conform are listed in What threads can share; no extend can make another type conform. It gives T no methods, and it joins other constraints with & (T: Shared & Named):

import async;

[Shared]
struct Settings {
    const workers: int;
    construct(this.workers = 1) {}
}

# A cell that any thread may read: its value must be thread-safe.
[Shared]
struct Cell<T: Shared> {
    const value: T;
    construct(value: T) { this.value = value; }
}

share<T: Shared>(value: T): Cell<T> { return Cell<T>(value); }

main(): int {
    var count = share(3);
    var settings = share(Settings(4));
    assert(count.value == 3 and settings.value.workers == 4, "shared cells");

    # The runtime states the same rule: spawn<T: Shared>.
    async.run(() => {
        var task = async.spawn<Settings>(() => { return Settings(2); });
        assert(task.join().value().workers == 2, "spawned");
    });
    return 0;
}

The standard library states the rule this way where it applies: spawn<T: Shared>, run_blocking<T: Shared> and Lazy<T: Shared>, so async.spawn<String>(...) is reported at String, with a note saying why it is not thread-safe ('String' is not declared [Shared]). In a constraint, Shared always means this built-in, so a trait cannot be named Shared. A generic that passes its own T to one of these (say run_blocking<T>) needs T: Shared too.

The compiler checks every use: a type argument you write, one it infers from a call, a default, and a concrete override. The error points at the type argument, or at the call argument the type came from:

main.pep:11:21: error: 'Circle' does not conform to trait 'Shape', required by 'T' in 'Gallery'
   11 |     var g = Gallery<Circle>();
      |                     ^~~~~~
main.pep:7:19: note: constraint declared here
    7 | struct Gallery<T: Shape> {
      |                   ^~~~~
main.pep:4:8: note: declare it with 'extend Circle with Shape'
    4 | struct Circle {
      |        ^~~~~~

A type parameter passed on to a constrained one must carry the constraint itself: wrap<T>(item: T): Gallery<String, T> is an error that suggests T: Shape. The language server offers both the extension and the constraint as quick fixes.

  • A constraint must name a trait: T: Point, with Point a struct, is an error.
  • An extension of a constrained struct keeps its constraints: extend Gallery<TTag, TShape> needs no TShape: Shape of its own. You may restate them as documentation, extend Gallery<TTag, TShape: Shape>. A constraint the struct does not have makes a constrained extension.
  • In an overload set, a generic member whose inferred type arguments do not meet its constraints is not viable, and the error lists why.
  • A constrained name is always a type parameter, never an override’s type argument: describe<Point: Shape> declares a generic function whose parameter happens to be named Point.

Inside a constrained generic

The compiler also checks the generic itself, once, whether or not anything uses it: inside largest<T: Shape & Ordered>, a value of type T offers exactly what Shape and Ordered declare. It may:

  • call their instance methods and operators (item.area(), best < item),
  • call their static members through the parameter (T.unit()),
  • convert to one of their trait types (var shape: Shape = item;),
  • be stored, passed, returned, and compared with ==, !=, === and !==.
trait Shape {
    area(): int;
    scaled(by: int): this;
    static unit(): this;
}

trait Ordered {
    <(other: this): bool;
}

struct Square {
    var side: int = 1;
    construct(this.side = 1) {}
    area(): int { return side * side; }
    scaled(by: int): Square { return Square(side * by); }
    static unit(): Square { return Square(1); }
    <(other: Square): bool { return side < other.side; }
}

extend Square with Shape {}
extend Square with Ordered {}

# Inside the body, a T offers what Shape and Ordered declare.
largest<T: Shape & Ordered>(items: Array<T>): T {
    var best = items[0];
    for (var item in items) {
        if (best < item) {
            best = item;
        }
    }
    return best;
}

# Static members are called through the parameter.
unit_area<T: Shape>(): int { return T.unit().area(); }

# A T converts to the trait types of its constraints.
as_shape<T: Shape>(item: T): Shape {
    var shape: Shape = item.scaled(2);
    return shape;
}

main(): int {
    var squares = Array<Square>();
    squares.append(Square(2));
    squares.append(Square(3));
    assert(largest(squares).side == 3, "largest");
    assert(unit_area<Square>() == 1, "static member");
    assert(as_shape(Square(3)).area() == 36, "conversion");
    return 0;
}

Anything else is an error at the member or operator, even before any use: a field, a method no constraint declares, a constructor T(), a call of a constraint’s method with the wrong number or types of arguments, or initializing, assigning or returning a T as another type. (Passing a T to a function that takes another type is still reported in each specialization.)

main.pep:5:45: error: no member named 'perimeter' in 'T'
    5 | total<T: Shape>(item: T): int { return item.perimeter(); }
      |                                             ^~~~~~~~~
main.pep:5:10: note: 'T' is constrained by 'Shape', which has no member 'perimeter'
    5 | total<T: Shape>(item: T): int { return item.perimeter(); }
      |          ^~~~~

A method that two constraints both declare is an error too ('name' is declared by both 'Named' and 'Titled'; call it through one of them).

Each use is still compiled for its type argument, so a call goes straight to that type’s own method, with no trait value in between. A parameter without a constraint keeps working as before: its uses are checked in each specialization. In a list that mixes the two, such as f<T: Shape, U>, only the uses of T are checked in the generic.

Constrained extensions

An extension of a generic struct can add a constraint the struct does not have: extend Box<T: Named> { ... }. Its members exist only on the specializations whose type argument meets it, so Box<Square> has label() and Box<String> does not. With with, the constraint makes a conditional conformance: after extend Box<T: Shape> with Shape, a Box<Square> is a Shape (it can be passed where T: Shape is required and converted to a Shape value), and a Box<String> is not.

trait Shape {
    area(): int;
}

trait Named {
    name(): String;
}

struct Square {
    area(): int { return 4; }
    name(): String { return "square"; }
}

extend Square with Shape {}
extend Square with Named {}

struct Box<T> {
    var item: T;
    construct(item: T) { this.item = item; }
}

# Only a Box of something Named has `label()`.
extend Box<T: Named> {
    label(): String { return "box of " + item.name(); }
}

# A Box of shapes is itself a shape.
extend Box<T: Shape> with Shape {
    area(): int { return item.area() * 2; }
}

main(): int {
    var box = Box<Square>(Square());
    assert(box.label() == "box of square", "constrained extension");

    Shape shape = box;
    assert(shape.area() == 8, "conditional conformance");

    # Box<String> is still a Box, without `label()` or `area()`.
    var text = Box<String>("plain");
    assert(text.item == "plain", "any Box");
    return 0;
}
  • Every Box<X> keeps the struct’s own members and constraints; an extension adds to them, it never removes any.
  • Inside the extension, T offers the struct’s constraints and the extension’s, as in any constrained generic.
  • A call of a member the specialization does not have names the constraint it misses:
main.pep:20:9: error: no member named 'label' in 'Box<Circle>'
   20 |     box.label();
      |         ^~~~~
main.pep:15:15: note: 'label' requires 'Circle' to conform to 'Named'
   15 | extend Box<T: Named> {
      |               ^~~~~

and a type argument that misses a conditional conformance says so too ('Box<String>' conforms to 'Shape' only when 'String' conforms to 'Shape').

  • Only the struct’s own parameters can carry an extension’s constraints: extend Box<int: Shape> is an error.
  • A conformance that holds for every Box needs its members on every Box: extend Box<T> with Named cannot rest on a name() that only extend Box<T: Named> provides. Make the conformance conditional instead (extend Box<T: Named> with Named).
  • Several extensions may declare the same trait with different constraints; a specialization conforms when it meets any of them.
  • Inside another generic, a call such as b.label() on a Box<T> is checked in each specialization, like any member of a generic struct.

Overriding a generic function for one type

You can give a generic function a separate definition for a specific type argument. Write the concrete type where the type parameter would go:

# The generic version handles every type...
describe<T>(value: T): String {
    return "something";
}

# ...and these definitions replace it for two specific types.
describe<int>(value: int): String {
    return "an int";
}

describe<String>(value: String): String {
    return "a String";
}

main(): int {
    assert(describe<float>(1.5) == "something", "the generic version");
    assert(describe<int>(7) == "an int", "the int override");
    assert(describe<String>("hi") == "a String", "the String override");

    # The standard library's hash<String> is such an override: it hashes
    # a String by its content instead of by identity.
    assert(hash<String>("pepper") == hash<String>("pepper"), "content hash");
    return 0;
}

A call whose type argument matches an override, such as describe<int>(7), uses the override; every other call uses the generic version. The standard library uses this to give hash<String> a content-based hash, while hash<T> hashes other structs by identity.

An override can name a built-in type (int, bool, String, and so on) or a struct, such as describe<Point>. It may be declared in any file that can see both the generic function and the struct: here main.pep overrides shapes.pep’s describe<T> for its own Point, and the generic code in shapes.pep uses the override too:

# A generic function, and code that calls it for any type.
export describe<T>(v: T): int {
    return 0;
}

export describe_twice<T>(v: T): int {
    return describe<T>(v) * 2;
}

import "shapes";

struct Point {
    var x: int;
    var y: int;
}

# Overrides shapes.pep's describe<T> for Point, from another file.
describe<Point>(p: Point): int {
    return p.x + p.y;
}

main(): int {
    var p = Point();
    p.x = 3;
    p.y = 4;
    assert(describe<Point>(p) == 7, "the override");
    assert(describe_twice<Point>(p) == 14, "generic code in shapes.pep uses it too");
    assert(describe<int>(5) == 0, "other types keep the generic version");

    # The standard library's generics, such as hash<T>, can be overridden
    # for a struct the same way.
    return 0;
}

A function whose type parameters all name types the file can see (its own, the ones it imports, under any name such as P after import [Point as P] from geo, and the standard library’s) is an override when the file can also see a generic function of that name and number of type parameters (its own, an imported one, or the standard library’s); otherwise a struct’s name is just the name of a type parameter. The generic may be spelled by any name the file has for it (show<Point> after import [describe as show]). A type argument must name a struct, not a type alias or a trait. A generic and another function of the same name in one file are overloads, unless they have the same parameters, or the generic’s type parameters all name structs the file can see without a generic of that name to override: either is an error, since it usually means an override whose type argument the file cannot see, or of a generic the file’s own function of that name hides.

To add methods to a generic struct from outside its declaration, use an extension.

Type aliases

A type alias gives an existing type another name. Use one to shorten a long type that you write often, such as HashMap<String, Array<int>>, or to say what a value means, such as Score instead of int.

Declaring an alias

Write type, the new name, =, and the type it stands for:

# An alias is another name for an existing type.
type Score = int;
type Names = Array<String>;
type Handler = (int) => int;

struct Player {
    var name: String;
    var best: Score = 0;        # aliases work in fields...
}

type Team = Player;

double_it(x: int): int {
    return x * 2;
}

# ...and in parameters and return types.
apply(h: Handler, x: Score): Score {
    return h(x);
}

main(): int {
    var s: Score = 21;
    var plain: int = s;         # Score and int are the same type
    assert(apply(double_it, plain) == 42, "function type alias");

    var names = Names();        # construct through the alias
    names.append("Ada");
    assert(names.count() == 1, "Names is Array<String>");

    var p = Team();
    p.best = s;
    var q: Player = p;          # Team and Player are the same type
    assert(q.best == 21, "struct alias");
    return 0;
}

An alias is only a spelling, not a new type. The compiler replaces every use of the alias with its target before it checks anything else, so Score and int are interchangeable: you can assign one to the other, pass one where the other is expected, and error messages name the target type.

You can use an alias anywhere a type can appear: local and module-level variables, parameters, return types, struct fields, generic arguments, and casts. An alias of a struct also works where the struct’s name would: to construct it (Team()) and to call its static methods.

Generic aliases

An alias can have type parameters of its own, including defaults, just like a generic struct:

# Generic aliases take their own type parameters.
type Predicate<T> = (T) => bool;
type Lookup<V> = HashMap<String, V>;
type Outcome<T, E=Error> = Result<T, E>;

is_even(x: int): bool {
    return x % 2 == 0;
}

count_matching(values: Array<int>, test: Predicate<int>): int {
    var n = 0;
    for (var v in values) {
        if (test(v)) {
            n += 1;
        }
    }
    return n;
}

parse_digit(text: String): Outcome<int> {
    if (text == "7") {
        return Outcome<int>.ok(7);
    }
    return Outcome<int>.err(Error("not a digit I know"));
}

main(): int {
    var values = Array<int>();
    values.append(1);
    values.append(2);
    values.append(4);
    assert(count_matching(values, is_even) == 2, "Predicate<int> is (int) => bool");

    var ages = Lookup<int>();   # HashMap<String, int>
    ages.insert("Ada", 36);
    assert(ages.contains("Ada"), "Lookup<int> is HashMap<String, int>");

    # Outcome<int> fills E with its default: Result<int, Error>.
    assert(parse_digit("7").value() == 7, "ok");
    assert(parse_digit("x").is_err(), "err");
    return 0;
}

The arguments at the use site fill the alias’s parameters in order, and omitted ones take their defaults. Outcome<int> becomes Result<int, Error>, and Lookup<int> becomes HashMap<String, int>. Aliases are especially handy for function types, which are long to write out: Predicate<int> reads better than (int) => bool.

Aliases across files

Like other top-level declarations, an alias is private to the file that declares it. Mark it export to let files that import it use it; see Visibility and Modules and imports.

Recursive aliases

An alias must not refer to itself, directly or through other aliases. The compiler reports the cycle at the alias, with a note at each alias it passes through:

type Celsius = Degrees;
type Degrees = Celsius;

main.pep:1:6: error: type alias 'Celsius' refers to itself
    1 | type Celsius = Degrees;
      |      ^~~~~~~
main.pep:2:6: note: through type alias 'Degrees', declared here
    2 | type Degrees = Celsius;
      |      ^~~~~~~

Traits and extensions

Pepper has no inheritance. Instead, you add behavior to a type with an extension, and describe a set of behavior that several types share with a trait. Extensions can be written anywhere, so you can add methods to a library type, such as String, from your own code.

A trait is also a type: a value of type Shape holds any struct that has the Shape trait, and calls its methods (see Traits as types).

Extensions

An extend block adds methods to a struct declared elsewhere, whether in the same file, another file, or the standard library:

struct Temperature {
    var celsius: float = 0.0;
    construct(this.celsius = 0.0) {}
}

# `extend` adds methods to a struct declared elsewhere.
extend Temperature {
    fahrenheit(): float {
        return celsius * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0;
    }

    static freezing(): Temperature {
        return Temperature(0.0);
    }

    bool ==(Temperature other) {
        return celsius == other.celsius;
    }
}

# Library types can be extended too.
extend String {
    exclaim(): String {
        var s = String();
        s.append(this);
        s.append("!");
        return s;
    }
}

# One specialization of a generic library type can be extended, and its
# methods can loop over `this`.
extend Array<int> {
    total(): int {
        var sum = 0;
        for (var x in this) {
            sum += x;
        }
        return sum;
    }
}

struct Box<T> {
    var value: T;
}

# Extending the generic struct adds the method to every Box<...>.
extend Box<T> {
    get(): T {
        return value;
    }
}

main(): int {
    var t = Temperature(100.0);
    assert(t.fahrenheit() == 212.0, "extension method");
    assert(Temperature.freezing() == Temperature(0.0), "static method and operator from an extension");

    assert("hello".exclaim() == "hello!", "String extension");

    var numbers = Array<int>();
    numbers.append(2);
    numbers.append(3);
    assert(numbers.total() == 5, "Array<int> extension loops over this");

    var b = Box<int>();
    b.value = 5;
    assert(b.get() == 5, "Box<int>");
    var s = Box<String>();
    s.value = "five";
    assert(s.get() == "five", "Box<String>");
    return 0;
}
  • An extension can hold anything a struct body can hold except fields, a constructor, and a destructor: methods, static methods, operators, and indexers.
  • Methods in an extension behave exactly like methods declared in the struct. They can use this and name the struct’s fields directly, and they are called the same way.
  • A type can have any number of extensions.
  • An extension method may share its name with the struct’s methods if its parameter types differ: it joins their overload set.
  • An extension in another file is usable only where that file (or its module) is imported, and only if it is exported; the standard library’s extensions are usable everywhere. See Visibility.

Extending generic structs

extend Box<T>, using the struct’s own type parameter name, adds the methods to every specialization: Box<int>, Box<String>, and so on. The example above does this.

When Box constrains its parameter (struct Box<T: Shape>), the extension keeps the constraint without restating it; extend Box<T: Shape> may restate it as documentation (see constraints). A constraint the struct does not have limits the extension to the specializations that meet it: extend Box<T: Named> { ... } adds its methods to Box<Square> but not to Box<String>, and extend Box<T: Shape> with Shape makes a Box of shapes a shape (see constrained extensions).

extend Box<int> targets one specialization: its methods exist only on Box<int>, and calling one on a Box<String> is an error (no member named 'doubled' in 'Box<String>').

A library type’s specialization can be extended the same way. The example’s extend Array<int> adds total(), which loops over this with for.

An extension cannot add fields; declare every field in the struct itself.

Traits

A trait names a set of methods. Declare one with trait and method signatures ending in ;. Then declare that a type has the trait with extend Type with Trait, and provide the methods in that extension:

# A trait names a set of methods that a type provides.
trait Shape {
    area(): int;
    name(): String;

    # A method with a body is a default: every type with the trait gets it.
    describe(): String {
        return "a " + name();
    }
}

struct Square {
    var side: int = 1;
    construct(this.side = 1) {}
}

# `extend ... with` declares that Square has the Shape trait, and adds the
# trait's methods to it.
extend Square with Shape {
    area(): int {
        return side * side;
    }

    name(): String {
        return "square";
    }
}

# A trait can be generic, and can declare static methods; `this` as a type
# stands for the type that has the trait.
trait From<T> {
    static this from(T value);
}

extend Square with From<int> {
    static Square from(int side) {
        return Square(side);
    }
}

main(): int {
    var sq = Square(3);
    assert(sq.area() == 9, "trait method called on the struct");
    assert(sq.name() == "square", "second trait method");
    assert(sq.describe() == "a square", "default method from the trait");
    assert(Square.from(4).area() == 16, "static method from a generic trait");
    return 0;
}
  • A trait can have type parameters, like From<T>.
  • A trait can declare static methods. In a trait, this used as a type stands for the type that has the trait.
  • extend Square with Shape, Printable { ... } attaches several traits at once.
  • A trait can declare several methods of one name with different parameter types; the type implements each with the method whose parameter types match (see Overloading).
  • The methods in the extension are ordinary methods of the struct, so you call them on a Square as usual.
  • A generic parameter can require a trait, total_area<T: Shape>, so that only types declared to have it are accepted (see constraints).
  • The runtime declares traits too. ToString (to_string(): String) makes a type usable in an interpolated string.

The compiler checks that the type has every method the trait declares, either in the extension or in the struct itself. A missing method is an error at the extension, with a note at the trait’s method:

main.pep:9:8: error: 'Square' does not implement 'area', required by trait 'Shape'
    9 | extend Square with Shape {
      |        ^~~~~~
main.pep:2:5: note: 'area' declared here
    2 |     area(): int;
      |     ^~~~

Default method bodies

A trait method can have a body. A type that has the trait and does not define that method gets the trait’s body as its own method; a type that defines the method keeps its own. Inside a default body, the trait’s type parameters and this stand for the types named in the with clause:

trait Shape {
    area(): int;
    sides(): int { return 4; }
}

extend Square with Shape {
    area(): int { return side * side; }
}

Here Square(3).sides() returns 4.

A default method can have type parameters of its own (see Generic methods). The runtime’s Iterator<T> uses this for its map<U> and filter adapters, which every type that declares Iterator<T> gets.

A default body sees only what its trait declares: a bare call to one of the trait’s methods calls it on this, and any other bare name means what it means where the trait is declared (a top-level function or variable), even when a conforming type happens to have a method or field of that name. Call through this explicitly only for the trait’s own methods.

Traits as types

A trait’s name is also a type. A variable, parameter, field, return value, or collection element of type Shape holds any struct that declares Shape, and calling a method on it runs that struct’s own method:

# A trait used as a type holds any struct that declares the trait.
trait Shape {
    area(): int;
    name(): String;
}

struct Square {
    var side: int = 1;
    construct(this.side = 1) {}
}

extend Square with Shape {
    area(): int { return side * side; }
    name(): String { return "square"; }
}

struct Rect {
    var width: int = 1;
    var height: int = 1;
    construct(this.width = 1, this.height = 1) {}
}

extend Rect with Shape {
    area(): int { return width * height; }
    name(): String { return "rect"; }
}

# One function accepts every Shape; each call runs the value's own method.
measure(shape: Shape): int {
    return shape.area();
}

main(): int {
    # A Square converts to a Shape wherever a Shape is expected.
    var s: Shape = Square(3);
    assert(measure(s) == 9, "square through a trait parameter");
    assert(s.name() == "square", "method of the concrete type");

    # Collections can hold different types that share a trait.
    var shapes = Array<Shape>();
    shapes.append(Square(2));
    shapes.append(Rect(2, 5));
    var total = 0;
    for (var shape in shapes) {
        total = total + shape.area();
    }
    assert(total == 14, "sum of areas");

    # Two trait values are equal when they refer to the same object.
    var same: Shape = s;
    assert(same == s, "same object");
    return 0;
}

  • Conversion is implicit. A Square becomes a Shape wherever a Shape is expected: an initializer, an assignment, an argument, a return value.

  • Conformance is declared. Only a type that declares the trait with extend Type with Trait converts. Having the right methods is not enough:

    main.pep:11:20: error: 'Circle' does not conform to trait 'Shape'
   11 |     var s: Shape = Circle();
      |                    ^~~~~~
main.pep:6:8: note: declare it with 'extend Circle with Shape'
    6 | struct Circle {
      |        ^~~~~~

  • A trait value is a shared reference to the struct, like any other struct value (see Memory). When the last reference goes away, whether it was a Shape or a Square, the struct’s own destructor runs.

  • Only instance methods are callable through the trait. Static methods, generic methods, and methods whose signature uses this as a type, need the concrete type; calling one through a trait value is an error.

  • Methods must match the trait’s signature. An implementation with different parameter or return types is an error. The one exception is a trait method that returns a trait type: the implementation may return a struct that declares that trait, as iterate() does in Iteration.

  • == and != on trait values compare identity: they are equal when they refer to the same object.

What traits do not do yet:

  • A trait value cannot convert back to its struct, or to another trait.
  • Atomic<Shape> is not supported. A trait value is two pointers wide and cannot be swapped atomically.
  • Weak<Shape> is not supported. Take the weak reference to the struct type instead.

Iteration

A for loop visits each element of a collection in turn. You can loop over an Array, over the code points of a String, and over any type of your own that follows the iterator protocol.

Looping over an array

for (var x in source) { ... } runs the body once per element, with x bound to the element:

struct Item {
    int value;
    construct(this.value = 0) {}
}

make_items(): Array<Item> {
    var items = Array<Item>();
    items.append(Item(20));
    items.append(Item(22));
    return items;
}

main(): int {
    var nums = Array<int>();
    nums.append(1);
    nums.append(2);
    nums.append(39);

    # The basic loop: x takes each element in order.
    var total = 0;
    for (var x in nums) {
        total = total + x;
    }
    assert(total == 42, "sum of the elements");

    # The loop variable may be typed, and the parentheses are optional.
    long wide = 0;
    for (long x in nums) {
        wide = wide + x;
    }
    for var x: int in nums {
        wide = wide - x;
    }
    assert(wide == 0, "typed loop variables");

    # break and continue work as in a while loop.
    var odd = 0;
    for (var x in nums) {
        if (x % 2 == 0) {
            continue;
        }
        if (x > 10) {
            break;
        }
        odd = odd + x;
    }
    assert(odd == 1, "only 1 is odd and below 10");

    # A struct element is shared: changing a field changes the element,
    # but rebinding the loop variable does not touch the array.
    var items = make_items();
    for (var item in items) {
        item.value = item.value * 10;
        item = Item(99);
    }
    assert(items[0].value == 200, "first element was updated");
    assert(items[1].value == 220, "second element was updated");

    # Iterating a temporary keeps it alive for the whole loop.
    var sum = 0;
    for (var item in make_items()) {
        sum = sum + item.value;
    }
    assert(sum == 42, "temporary array stays alive");

    # The loop is shorthand for driving the iterator yourself.
    var it = nums.iterate();
    var manual = 0;
    while (it.next()) {
        manual = manual + it.current();
    }
    assert(manual == 42, "the same elements, by hand");

    # Modifying the array after the loop is fine.
    nums.append(100);
    assert(nums.count() == 4, "appended after the loop");
    return 0;
}

The example shows each part of the loop:

  • The loop variable can be declared with var or with a type: for (var x in nums), for (long x in nums), and for (var x: int in nums) all work.
  • The parentheses are optional, as with if and while: for var x in nums { ... }. The braces are required.
  • break and continue work as they do in a while loop.
  • The loop variable is a copy, like any var. Assigning a new value to it does not change the collection. For a struct element, though, the copy is another reference to the same object (see Memory and reference counting), so item.value = ... does change the element.
  • A temporary source stays alive. The loop holds a reference to what it iterates, so for (var item in make_items()) is safe.

Looping over a string

A String yields its code points one at a time. Each one is a String holding a single code point, the same value that indexing gives you (word[i]):

main(): int {
    var word = "héllo ✓";

    # A String yields one code point at a time, as a one-code-point String.
    var count = 0;
    var copy = "";
    for (var c in word) {
        assert(c.length() == 1, "each piece is one code point");
        copy.append(c);
        count = count + 1;
    }
    assert(count == 7, "7 code points");
    assert(copy == word, "the pieces rebuild the string");

    # Each piece is the same value as indexing the string.
    var i = 0;
    for (var c in word) {
        assert(c == word[i], "same as word[i]");
        i = i + 1;
    }

    # An empty string runs the body zero times.
    for (var c in "") {
        assert(false, "never runs");
    }
    return 0;
}

The iterator protocol

The for loop is not tied to Array and String. It works with any type that has the right methods, described by two traits in the runtime (runtime/iterator.pep, documented in the Iterators reference):

export trait Iterator<T> {
    bool next();     # advance; true if there is a current element
    T current();     # the element next() just moved to
}

export trait Iterable<T> {
    iterate(): Iterator<T>;
}
  • An iterator steps through elements. next() moves to the next element and returns true, or returns false when there are no more (and keeps returning false after that). current() returns the element next() moved to.
  • An iterable is a collection that hands out a fresh iterator from iterate(). Array<T> returns an ArrayIterator<T>, String returns a StringIterator, and HashMap<K, V> and HashSet<K> return a HashMapIterator<K, V> and a HashSetIterator<K>.

for (var x in source) { body } behaves exactly like this:

{
    var it = source.iterate();   # or `var it = source;` when source is itself an iterator
    while (it.next()) {
        var x = it.current();
        { body }
    }
}

The loop chooses by the methods the source’s type has, like a C++ range-based for: it uses iterate() if the type has one, and otherwise uses the source itself as the iterator if it has both next() and current(). A type with neither is a compile error:

main.pep:4:19: error: type 'Foo' is not iterable: implement Iterable<T> (iterate()) or Iterator<T> (next() and current())
    4 |     for (var x in f) {
      |                   ^

HashMap<K, V> yields each entry as a tuple (K, V), so for (var (name, age) in ages) names both parts; HashSet<K> yields its members. Both visit entries in no particular order. Changing a value (ages[name] = … for a key already present) is fine while looping, but adding or removing an entry stops the program at the iterator’s next step.

Adapters

Iterator<T> has two default methods that wrap an iterator in another one. Each one works lazily, one element at a time as the loop asks for it:

  • map(transform) yields transform(x) for each element x; its element type is whatever transform returns.
  • filter(keep) yields only the elements for which keep(x) is true.

Both return iterators, so they chain, and a for loop can use the result directly:

struct Person {
    String name;
    int age;
    construct(this.name = "", this.age = 0) {}
}

main(): int {
    var people = Array<Person>();
    people.append(Person("Ada", 36));
    people.append(Person("Bo", 12));
    people.append(Person("Cyd", 40));

    # filter keeps the adults, map turns each one into a name.
    var names = Array<String>();
    for (var name in people.iterate().filter((p) => p.age >= 18).map((p) => p.name)) {
        names.append(name);
    }
    assert(names.count() == 2, "two adults");
    assert(names[0] == "Ada", "Ada first");
    assert(names[1] == "Cyd", "then Cyd");

    # Adapters work on any Iterator, including a String's.
    var kept = 0;
    for (var c in "hello".iterate().filter((c) => c != "l")) {
        kept += 1;
    }
    assert(kept == 3, "h, e, o");
    return 0;
}

Every type that declares Iterator<T> gets them: ArrayIterator<T> (from Array.iterate()), StringIterator, and your own iterators once you write extend YourType with Iterator<T> {}. The adapter holds a reference to the iterator it wraps, so a chain built from a temporary stays alive while the loop runs. They are generic methods (see Generics), so they are not callable through an Iterator<T> trait value.

Writing your own iterator

To make your own type work in a for loop, give it next() and current() (an iterator), or give it an iterate() method that returns such a type (an iterable):

# An iterator: next() advances, current() returns the element.
struct Countdown {
    int remaining;
    int now;

    construct(this.remaining = 0) {}

    bool next() {
        if (remaining == 0) {
            return false;
        }
        now = remaining;
        remaining = remaining - 1;
        return true;
    }

    int current() {
        return now;
    }
}

# Declaring the trait documents the intent; the loop goes by the methods.
extend Countdown with Iterator<int> {}

# An iterable: iterate() hands out a fresh iterator for each loop.
struct Evens {
    int limit;

    construct(this.limit = 0) {}

    EvensIterator iterate() {
        var it = EvensIterator();
        it.limit = limit;
        it.now = -2;
        return it;
    }
}

struct EvensIterator {
    int limit;
    int now;

    bool next() {
        now = now + 2;
        return now < limit;
    }

    int current() {
        return now;
    }
}

extend EvensIterator with Iterator<int> {}
extend Evens with Iterable<int> {}

# A generic function can loop over any type that supports the protocol.
sum<C>(C values): int {
    var total = 0;
    for (var v in values) {
        total = total + v;
    }
    return total;
}

main(): int {
    var total = 0;
    for (var n in Countdown(3)) {
        total = total + n;
    }
    assert(total == 6, "3 + 2 + 1");

    # A loop over an iterator in a variable uses that object up.
    var c = Countdown(2);
    for (var n in c) {
        total = total + n;
    }
    assert(!c.next(), "the countdown is exhausted");

    # An iterable starts a new pass every time.
    var evens = Evens(10);
    assert(sum<Evens>(evens) == 20, "0 + 2 + 4 + 6 + 8");
    assert(sum<Evens>(evens) == 20, "a second pass sees the same elements");

    var nums = Array<int>();
    nums.append(30);
    nums.append(12);
    assert(sum<Array<int>>(nums) == 42, "arrays work too");
    return 0;
}

Some things to keep in mind:

  • Declaring the trait is optional. The loop looks only at which methods a type has. Writing extend Countdown with Iterator<int> {} documents your intent, and the compiler then checks that Countdown has both next() and current() (see Traits and extensions). Declaring it also lets the type be used as an Iterator<int> value, and a for loop over such a value calls the methods through the trait. It also gives the type the adapters map and filter.
  • Looping over an iterator uses it up. When the source is itself an iterator stored in a variable, the loop drives that same object, so it is exhausted afterwards. An iterable starts a new, independent pass every time you loop over it.
  • Generic code can loop over a type parameter; each specialization checks the protocol for its own type (see Generics).
  • Calling current() out of turn panics in the runtime’s iterators: before the first next() you get ArrayIterator.current() before next(), and after next() returned false you get ArrayIterator.current() past the end. Your own iterators should follow the same rule.

Modifying a collection while you loop over it

Changing an Array or a String while a loop is iterating over it stops the program with a panic, because the iterator could otherwise skip or repeat elements, or read past the end:

var nums = Array<int>();
nums.append(1);
nums.append(2);
for (var x in nums) {
    nums.append(x);   # panics: Array modified during iteration
}

Every method that changes an Array counts, including storing an element with nums[i] = v. For a String, append and grow count, and the message is String modified during iteration. The check happens on the iterator’s next step, so modifying the collection after the loop is finished is fine.

To change elements as you go, loop over an index with while and store through it, or collect the changes in a second array and apply them after the loop.

Loop scope

The loop variable and anything declared in the loop body exist only inside the loop. Each pass gets a new loop variable, and struct values declared in the body are released at the end of every pass, whether the pass ends normally or by continue, break, or return. Leaving the loop early also releases the hidden iterator, so a destructor on a custom iterator runs at that point.

Using the loop variable or a body local after the loop is an error, the same as for any name that is out of scope:

main.pep:6:12: error: use of undeclared identifier 'i'
    6 |     return i;
      |            ^

The loop variable, or a local in the loop body, may have the same name as a variable declared before the loop. It hides the outer variable inside the loop, and the outer variable keeps its value afterwards.

Scoped blocks with with

A with block enters a scope object, binds what it hands out, and cleans up when the object is destroyed. It plays the role of Python’s with and C#’s using, but the cleanup is ordinary destruction: it runs through the same reference counting as every other object (see Memory and reference counting).

import async;

# A module-scope counter: const, and changed through an Atomic.
const open_sessions = async.Atomic<int>(0);

# A scope object: enter() hands out what the block works with, and the
# destructor calls exit() when the last reference goes away.
struct Session {
    var user: String;

    construct(this.user = "") {
        open_sessions.fetch_add(1);
    }

    destruct {
        this.exit();
    }

    Session enter() {
        return this;
    }

    exit() {
        open_sessions.fetch_sub(1);
    }
}

extend Session with Scoped<Session> {}

# enter() may return a null reference: then the body is skipped and the
# `else` block runs.
struct Lookup {
    var found: Session;

    construct(Session session) {
        found = session;
    }

    Session enter() {
        return found;
    }

    exit() {}
}

extend Lookup with Scoped<Session> {}

first_user(): String {
    with (var session = Session("ada")) {
        # `return` leaves the block too: the session still closes.
        return session.user;
    }
    return "";
}

main(): int {
    with (var session = Session("grace")) {
        assert(open_sessions.load() == 1, "open inside the block");
        assert(session.user == "grace", "bound to what enter() returned");
    }
    assert(open_sessions.load() == 0, "closed at the end of the block");

    assert(first_user() == "ada", "the value was returned");
    assert(open_sessions.load() == 0, "closed on return as well");

    var hits = 0;
    with (var s = Lookup(Session("linus"))) {
        hits += 1;
    } else {
        hits -= 100;
    }
    with (var s = Lookup(__null)) {
        hits -= 100;
    } else {
        hits += 1;
    }
    assert(hits == 2, "the body ran for a session, the else block for null");
    return 0;
}

The header

with (var name = scope) { ... } else { ... }
with (Type name = scope) { ... }
with (scope) { ... }
  • name is bound to scope.enter(), not to scope itself. A Session can hand out itself; a Weak<T> hands out a strong reference to the object it points at, or null once that object is gone.
  • Without a binding, the block still holds the result of enter() until it ends. An enter() that returns nothing (declared without a return type) has nothing to bind, and binding it is an error.
  • The parentheses are optional, as with if, while and for. The braces are required.
  • name cannot be reassigned inside the block.

Skipping the body

When enter() returns a struct reference that is null, the body is skipped and the optional else block runs instead. else is only allowed when enter() returns a struct type, since nothing else can be null.

The Scoped<T> protocol

A type works in a with block when it has the methods of the Scoped<T> trait (runtime/scoped.pep, documented in the Scoped reference):

export trait Scoped<T> {
    T enter();   # what the header binds; null skips the body
    exit();      # the cleanup; call it from the destructor
}

A with block goes by the methods a type has, not by the trait: a type without enter() is a compile error in a with header. Declaring the trait (extend Session with Scoped<Session> {}) documents the intent, and the compiler then checks that the type has both enter() and exit().

When exit() runs

The block keeps two locals: the scope object and the bound value. Both are released on every path out of the block (the end of the body, return, break and continue), the bound value first. Implementations call exit() from their destructor:

destruct {
    this.exit();
}

so exit() runs when the scope object’s last reference is released:

  • A scope object created in the header (with (var s = Session("grace"))) is released by the block, so exit() runs at the end of the block.
  • A scope object that something else also holds (a field, another local) lives on after the block, and exit() waits for its last owner. This is the same rule as any other object.
  • A copy of the bound value that outlives the block (stored in a field, returned) keeps that value alive, but not the scope object.

A panic stops the program without running destructors, so exit() does not run then.

Error handling with Result

An operation that can fail returns a Result: either Ok, holding the value you asked for, or Err, holding an error that says what went wrong. The caller checks which one it got before using the value. Pepper has no exceptions, so Result is how a function reports a failure the caller is expected to handle. For a failure that should stop the program, such as a broken invariant, use assert or panic instead.

Result and Error are part of the runtime, so you can use them without an import. The Result reference lists every member.

Creating and checking results

Result<TValue, TError> works like Rust’s Result<T, E>. It is an enum with two cases, Ok(value: TValue) and Err(error: TError). You build one with a case or with the static functions ok and err, and read it with match, is, or its methods:

# A function that can fail returns a Result instead of a plain value.
parse_digit(String s): Result<int> {
    if (s == "0") { return Result<int>.ok(0); }
    if (s == "1") { return Result<int>.ok(1); }
    if (s == "2") { return Result<int>.ok(2); }
    return Result<int>.err(Error("not a digit: " + s));
}

main(): int {
    var good = parse_digit("2");
    assert(good.is_ok(), "2 parses");
    assert(!good.is_err(), "is_err is the opposite of is_ok");
    assert(good.value() == 2, "value() returns the value");

    var bad = parse_digit("x");
    assert(bad.is_err(), "x does not parse");
    assert(bad.error().message == "not a digit: x", "the error explains why");

    # ok_or returns the value, or the fallback for an Err. It never panics.
    assert(good.ok_or(-1) == 2, "Ok gives its value");
    assert(bad.ok_or(-1) == -1, "Err gives the fallback");

    # Result<int> is short for Result<int, Error>.
    Result<int, Error> spelled_out = good;
    assert(spelled_out.value() == 2, "the same type");

    # Result is an enum: its cases build values too, and match reads them.
    var parsed = Result<int>.Ok(7);
    var doubled = match (parsed) { Ok(n) => n * 2, Err(e) => 0 };
    assert(doubled == 14, "match binds the value");
    if (bad is Err(e)) {
        assert(e.message.length() > 0, "is binds the error");
    }

    # An operation with no value to return uses void.
    var done = Result<void>.ok();
    var failed = Result<void>.err(Error("disk full"));
    assert(done.is_ok() && failed.is_err(), "Result<void> works like any other");
    return 0;
}

The pieces:

MemberWhat it does
Result<T>.Ok(value), Result<T>.ok(value)Creates an Ok result holding value.
Result<T>.Err(error), Result<T>.err(error)Creates an Err result holding error.
is_ok(), is_err()Report which kind the result is.
value()Returns the value; panics with Result.value on an Err value if the result is an Err.
error()Returns the error; panics with Result.error on an Ok value if the result is Ok.
ok_or(fallback)Returns the value, or fallback if the result is an Err. Never panics.

TError defaults to Error, so Result<int> means Result<int, Error>, and values of the two spellings can be assigned to each other freely (the compiler does generate a separate specialization for each spelling). Error is a struct with one field, String message: Error("boom").message is "boom".

Use value() when an Err would be a bug in your program, since it stops the program. When an Err is an expected outcome, match on the result, test it with is (if (r is Err(e)) { ... }) or is_ok(), or supply a fallback with ok_or.

Check before you read

A Result holds either its value or its error, never both. A match or an is test reads the one it holds, so it cannot pick the wrong one. value() and error() panic on the wrong one, so call value() only after checking is_ok(), and error() only after checking is_err().

A slot of type Result that is never given a value holds null, as for any enum whose cases carry values: Result<int>() is an error, since only the cases make values.

Results with no value

An operation that has nothing to return on success, such as deleting a file, uses void as its value type, like Result<(), E> in Rust. A void type argument erases what it types, so in Result<void> the case Ok carries nothing, ok() takes no argument, and value() returns nothing: calling it only checks that the result is Ok. Using that call as a value, as in var x = done.value();, is a compile error, as it is for any function that returns void.

var done = Result<void>.Ok;   # or Result<void>.ok()
var failed = Result<void>.err(Error("disk full"));
done.value();   # panics if `done` is an Err
match (failed) {
    Ok => {}
    Err(e) => { print(e.message); }
}

Custom error types and propagation
