  • Task<T>.spawn_local(body) starts a task on the running task’s worker and returns its Task<T>. The new task runs the next time the running task waits. T is the body’s result type; use Task<void> for a body that returns nothing.
  • task.join() waits for the task and returns a Result<T, TaskError>: the body’s value, or an error if the task was cancelled.
  • async.yield_now() lets every other ready task run first.
  • task.is_finished() says whether the body has returned.

A task from spawn_local stays on the thread of the task that started it, so it may use any value that task uses, as the closures above share log. Nothing needs to be thread-safe.

Several workers

run turns the calling thread into the first worker and starts one more thread per logical CPU after it (RuntimeOptions().workers(count) sets how many workers in all). async.spawn<T>(body) starts a task that whichever worker is free first runs, in parallel with the others:

import async;

sum(from: long, to: long): long {
    var total: long = 0;
    var i = from;
    while (i < to) {
        total = total + i;
        i = i + 1;
    }
    return total;
}

main(): int {
    async.run_with(async.RuntimeOptions().workers(4), () => {
        # Two halves of the work, on two workers at the same time.
        var low = async.spawn<long>(() => { return sum(0, 500000); });
        var high = async.spawn<long>(() => { return sum(500000, 1000000); });
        var total = low.join().value() + high.join().value();
        assert(total == 499999500000, "both halves were added");
    });
    return 0;
}

Because such a task may run on another thread, its body must be a shared function: it may capture only thread-safe values, as a thread’s body. Its result crosses threads too, so spawn constrains it T: Shared: a thread-safe type such as a number, a [Shared] struct, or a shared function type. async.spawn<String> is a compile error at String. join, cancel and is_finished work as for spawn_local, from the task that started it.

A task, once started, stays on its worker until it finishes, so the tasks it starts with spawn_local share values with it safely. An idle worker takes the next task that no worker has started yet. A task that computes without waiting still holds up the other tasks on its own worker (not the other workers), so a long computation should call yield_now() now and then.

async.spawn_on_each_worker(body) starts one task per worker, each on its own worker, and returns them in worker order. It is how a server runs an accept loop on every worker (see Sockets).

Blocking calls

Some work would hold a worker up: a call that blocks in the operating system (reading a file, a C library that waits) or a long computation. async.run_blocking<T>(body) runs body on a separate thread and parks the calling task until it returns, so the worker keeps running its other tasks meanwhile:

import async;

const ticks = async.Atomic<int>(0);

main(): int {
    async.run_with(async.RuntimeOptions().workers(1), () => {
        # Keeps running on the one worker while the blocking call waits.
        var ticker = async.Task<void>.spawn_local(() => {
            while (ticks.load() < 3) {
                async.sleep(5);
                ticks.fetch_add(1);
            }
        });
        var answer = async.run_blocking<int>(() => {
            async.Thread.sleep(50);   # blocks a pool thread, not the worker
            return 42;
        });
        assert(answer == 42, "the blocking call's result");
        assert(ticks.load() > 0, "the worker ran the ticker meanwhile");
        ticker.join();
    });
    return 0;
}

The runtime keeps a pool of threads for these calls. It starts one when a call finds none idle, up to RuntimeOptions().blocking_threads(count) (64 by default); past that, calls wait for a free one. As for spawn, body must be a shared function and T must be thread-safe. body always runs to the end: cancelling the task, or a timeout around the call, takes effect once the call has returned. Outside a task, run_blocking just calls body.

Waiting

async.sleep(milliseconds) puts a task to sleep and runs the others meanwhile, so many tasks can wait at the same time on one thread:

import async;

main(): int {
    var order = Array<int>();
    async.run(() => {
        var tasks = Array<async.Task<void>>();
        var i = 0;
        while (i < 3) {
            var n = i;
            # The later a task starts, the shorter it sleeps.
            tasks.append(async.Task<void>.spawn_local(() => {
                async.sleep(((3 - n) * 20) as ulong);
                order.append(n);
            }));
            i = i + 1;
        }
        for (var task in tasks) {
            task.join();
        }
    });
    # All three slept at the same time, on one thread.
    assert(order[0] == 2 && order[1] == 1 && order[2] == 0, "shortest sleep first");
    return 0;
}

Outside a task, sleep blocks the thread, and yield_now does nothing.

Tasks are never interrupted. A task that computes for a long time without waiting keeps every other task waiting, so a long loop should call yield_now() now and then.

Thread.sleep in a task is async.sleep.

Mutexes, channels and conditions

The synchronization types work in tasks too. When a task has to wait for a Mutex, for a value from a Channel or for room in a bounded one, or in Condition.wait, it parks and its worker runs other tasks, just as it does for a socket. The task that holds the lock or will send the value can be on the same worker, on another worker, or a plain thread:

import async;

struct Log {
    var lines: Array<String>;
    construct() {
        this.lines = Array<String>();
    }
}

const log = async.Mutex<Log>(Log());
const jobs = async.Channel<int>(2);

main(): int {
    # One worker: every task below shares one thread.
    async.run_with(async.RuntimeOptions().workers(1), () => {
        # The consumer parks in the channel until a value arrives.
        var consumer = async.Task<int>.spawn_local(() => {
            var total = 0;
            for (var job in jobs) {
                total = total + job;
            }
            return total;
        });
        # A task may hold the lock while it waits; the other task parks
        # until it is free.
        var writer = async.Task<void>.spawn_local(() => {
            with (var l = log.lock()) {
                l.lines.append("first");
                async.sleep(10);
                l.lines.append("second");
            }
        });
        async.yield_now();
        with (var l = log.lock()) {
            l.lines.append("third");
        }
        writer.join();

        # The producer parks while the bounded channel is full.
        var i = 1;
        while (i <= 5) {
            jobs.send(i);
            i = i + 1;
        }
        jobs.close();
        assert(consumer.join().value() == 15, "every job arrived");
    });
    with (var l = log.lock()) {
        assert(l.lines[2] == "third", "the lock waited for the writer");
    }
    return 0;
}
  • Each task counts as its own holder of a Mutex, so two tasks on one worker exclude each other, and a task may hold a lock across its own waits (a sleep, a socket call, another lock).
  • A cancel, or a timeout around the call, ends a channel wait: send returns false and receive returns an error (and a for loop over the channel ends). A task waiting for a Mutex still gets the lock, and Condition.wait still waits for a notification, since the caller’s loop would only wait again; wait_for returns when its own time runs out.
  • A Select parks its task on every channel at once, and a cancel or timeout ends its wait with an error. Condition.wait_while parks like wait.
  • Outside a task they block the thread, as before.

Task-local values

A TaskLocal<T> is a variable with a separate value in every task, as a ThreadLocal<T> has one per thread. Tasks that take turns on one worker share its thread, so only a TaskLocal can tell them apart:

import async;

# The id of the request the running task is handling.
const request_id = async.TaskLocal<long>();

# Deep in the call chain, without the id passed down as a parameter.
current_request(): long {
    return request_id.get();
}

main(): int {
    # One worker: the three tasks take turns on one thread, so a
    # ThreadLocal could not tell them apart.
    async.run_with(
        async.RuntimeOptions().workers(1),
        () => {
            var tasks = Array<async.Task<bool>>();
            for (var id in [1, 2, 3]) {
                tasks.append(
                    async.Task<bool>.spawn_local(
                        () => {
                            request_id.set(id);
                            async.yield_now();  # the other tasks set their ids meanwhile
                            return current_request() == id;
                        }
                    )
                );
            }
            for (var task in tasks) {
                assert(task.join().value(), "each task sees its own id");
            }
            # This task never set one.
            assert(!request_id.is_set(), "a task starts with no value");
        }
    );
    return 0;
}
  • set(value) stores the calling task’s value and get() returns it (the default of T, zero or null, until the task sets one). is_set() and clear() work as on a ThreadLocal.
  • A task starts with no value, even one started by a task that has one, and its values are released when it finishes.
  • Code outside any task (before async.run, or on a plain Thread) has one value per thread, like a ThreadLocal.
  • For a T that is not thread-safe, such as a String, reach the value with with (var value = local.enter()) { ... }, as for a ThreadLocal; get() is then a compile error.

Sockets

A socket call in a task that would have to wait (for a connection, for data, or for room to send) parks the task and lets the others run until the socket is ready. The socket API is the same one a plain program uses; only the waiting differs:

import async;
import io;

# Echoes everything a client sends until it closes the connection.
serve(stream: io.TcpStream) {
    var buffer = Array<u8>();
    while (true) {
        var r = stream.read(buffer, 4096);   # parks this task until data arrives
        if (r.is_err() || r.value() == 0) {
            return;
        }
        stream.write_all(buffer);
        buffer.clear();
    }
}

main(): int {
    async.run(() => {
        var listener = io.TcpListener.bind(io.SocketAddress.parse("127.0.0.1:0").value()).value();
        var address = listener.local_address().value();
        var clients = 10;

        # The server: one task per connection, all on this thread.
        async.Task<void>.spawn_local(() => {
            while (true) {
                var accepted = listener.accept();
                if (accepted.is_err()) {
                    return;   # cancelled when the first task returns
                }
                var (stream, peer) = accepted.value();
                async.Task<void>.spawn_local(() => { serve(stream); });
            }
        });

        # The clients, as tasks on the same thread.
        var replies = Array<async.Task<ulong>>();
        var i = 0;
        while (i < clients) {
            var k = i;
            replies.append(async.Task<ulong>.spawn_local(() => {
                var stream = io.TcpStream.connect(address).value();
                var message = $"hello from {k}";
                stream.write_string(message);
                var buffer = Array<u8>();
                stream.read_exact(buffer, message.size());
                return buffer.count();
            }));
            i = i + 1;
        }
        for (var reply in replies) {
            assert(reply.join().value() > 0, "the server echoed the message");
        }
    });
    return 0;
}

Outside a task, the same calls block the thread as before. A socket belongs to the worker whose task made it: tasks started with spawn_local can share it, and each spawned task makes its own.

Files

File.read, write and write_all in a task park the task until the system call is done, and the worker runs other tasks meanwhile. With the IoUring backend the kernel does the read or write itself; with the others a thread from run_blocking’s pool makes the blocking call. Opening, seeking, metadata and the other File calls still block the thread, as they are quick on local disks. A cancel or a timeout does not cut a read or write short: it takes effect once the call returns.

The array a read fills or a write sends from is in use until the call returns, so growing it from another task meanwhile panics (“Array: the buffer is in use by an I/O operation”). A String passed to write_all is copied first.

Accepting on every worker

An io.SharedTcpListener is a listening socket that any thread can accept on. Give each worker an accept loop with spawn_on_each_worker; each connection goes to one of the waiting workers, and the stream it returns belongs to that worker:

import async;

import io;

const served = async.Atomic<int>(0);

main(): int {
    async.run_with(async.RuntimeOptions().workers(4), () => {
        var listener = io.SharedTcpListener.bind(io.SocketAddress.parse("127.0.0.1:0").value()).value();
        var port = listener.local_address().value().port();

        # One accept loop per worker; each connection goes to one of them.
        async.spawn_on_each_worker(() => {
            while (true) {
                var accepted = listener.accept();
                if (accepted.is_err()) {
                    return;   # cancelled when the first task returns
                }
                var (stream, peer) = accepted.value();
                served.fetch_add(1);
                async.Task<void>.spawn_local(() => {
                    stream.write_string("hello").value();
                });
            }
        });

        var i = 0;
        while (i < 8) {
            var client = io.TcpStream.connect_host("127.0.0.1", port).value();
            var reply = Array<u8>();
            while (client.read(reply, 64).value() > 0) {
            }
            assert(reply.count() == 5, "greeted");
            i = i + 1;
        }
    });
    assert(served.load() == 8, "every connection was accepted once");
    return 0;
}

The listener has no close(), since other workers may be waiting on it. It closes when the last reference goes: here, once run has cancelled the loops.

Moving a stream to another worker

stream.into_transfer() moves a connection out of a TcpStream into an io.SocketTransfer, a thread-safe token that a shared function can capture or a Channel can carry, and io.TcpStream.adopt(transfer) takes it out again on the receiving worker. The old stream is closed afterwards, only the first adopt gets the connection, and a token no one adopts closes the connection when it goes:

import async;
import io;

main(): int {
    async.run_with(async.RuntimeOptions().workers(2), () => {
        var listener = io.TcpListener.bind(io.SocketAddress.parse("127.0.0.1:0").value()).value();
        var port = listener.local_address().value().port();
        var client = async.Task<ulong>.spawn_local(() => {
            var stream = io.TcpStream.connect_host("127.0.0.1", port).value();
            var reply = Array<u8>();
            while (stream.read(reply, 64).value() > 0) {
            }
            return reply.count();
        });

        var (stream, peer) = listener.accept().value();
        # A stream is not thread-safe; its transfer token is.
        var transfer = stream.into_transfer();
        var handler = async.spawn<void>(() => {
            var mine = io.TcpStream.adopt(transfer).value();
            mine.write_string("from any worker").value();
        });
        handler.join();
        assert(client.join().value() == 15, "the moved stream answered");
    });
    return 0;
}

When no task is ready to run, a worker blocks until a socket is ready, the next timer is due, or another worker wakes it; while tasks are running, it also checks the sockets every few dozen tasks, so a busy task cannot starve the network.

Backends

How the runtime waits for sockets is its I/O backend, an async.Backend:

BackendWhereHow
EpollLinuxepoll, edge-triggered
IoUringLinux 5.11 and laterio_uring, with a one-shot poll request per waiting socket; never picked automatically, since container seccomp profiles and hardened kernels often refuse it
KqueuemacOSkqueue, edge-triggered
IocpWindowsan I/O completion port, fed by AFD poll requests (as tokio and libuv do)
Polleverywherepoll() (WSAPoll on Windows), which looks at every waiting socket on each wait: fine for a few connections, slow for thousands

Backend.Automatic, the default, picks epoll, kqueue or IOCP, whichever the system has. RuntimeOptions().backend(kind) asks for one (and run_with panics if the system does not have it), and the PEPPER_IO_BACKEND environment variable (epoll, io_uring, kqueue, iocp or poll) overrides the automatic choice without changing the program, for testing and benchmarks. async.current_backend() says which one is running.

Timeouts

async.timeout(milliseconds) limits how long the waits inside a with block may take:

import async;
import io;

main(): int {
    async.run(() => {
        var listener = io.TcpListener.bind(io.SocketAddress.parse("127.0.0.1:0").value()).value();

        # Nobody connects, so the accept gives up after 50 milliseconds.
        with (var deadline = async.timeout(50)) {
            var accepted = listener.accept();
            assert(accepted.is_err() && accepted.error().is_timed_out(), "accept timed out");
            assert(deadline.is_expired(), "the limit has passed");
        }

        # A join gives up too; the task itself carries on until cancelled.
        var slow = async.Task<int>.spawn_local(() => {
            async.sleep(1000000);
            return 42;
        });
        with (async.timeout(20)) {
            var result = slow.join();
            assert(result.error().is_timed_out(), "join timed out");
        }
        slow.cancel();
    });
    return 0;
}

Once the limit passes, a socket call that has to wait fails with an IoError for which is_timed_out() holds, join fails with a TaskError for which is_timed_out() holds (the task it waited for carries on), and sleep returns early. Code that does not wait is never interrupted. The limit ends with the block. Timeouts nest, and an inner one cannot extend an outer one. deadline.is_expired() says whether the limit has passed. timeout panics outside a task.

Cancelling

task.cancel() asks a task to stop. Nothing stops it by force: from then on async.is_cancelled() is true inside it, sleep returns at once, and join on it fails with a TaskError whose is_cancelled() is true. A task waiting in join returns the same error when it is cancelled itself, and a socket call waiting in a cancelled task fails with an IoError whose is_cancelled() is true. When the first task of a run returns, every task still running is cancelled, on every worker, and run waits for each to finish:

import async;

main(): int {
    var polls = Array<int>();
    async.run(() => {
        var poller = async.Task<void>.spawn_local(() => {
            while (!async.is_cancelled()) {
                polls.append(1);
                async.sleep(5);
            }
        });
        async.sleep(30);
        poller.cancel();
        var result = poller.join();
        assert(result.is_err() && result.error().is_cancelled(), "a cancelled task's join fails");

        # A task still running when the first task returns is cancelled too,
        # and run waits for it to finish.
        async.Task<void>.spawn_local(() => {
            async.sleep(1000000);   # returns at once when cancelled
        });
    });
    assert(polls.count() > 0, "the poller ran until cancelled");
    return 0;
}

If every task is waiting for another task and none can continue, run panics instead of waiting forever.

How it works

Each task runs on a fiber: a stack of its own and a saved set of registers. Switching tasks saves the running task’s registers on its stack and restores the other’s, a few instructions of assembly on Linux and macOS (the __switch_context intrinsic) and the Fibers API on Windows. A task’s stack is reserved address space with a guard page below it; only the pages the task touches use memory, and a task that overflows its stack crashes the program as a thread would. Stacks are reused for later tasks.

Each worker has its own ready queue, timers and backend. Workers talk through a queue of messages each (a spawned task finished, was cancelled, or was woken by a Mutex, Condition or Channel) and a doorbell that ends a worker’s wait in its backend from another thread: an eventfd with epoll and io_uring, a user event with kqueue, a posted completion with IOCP, and a pipe (on Windows, a loopback UDP socket that a second socket sends to) with poll(). run_blocking’s pool threads are plain threads that report back through the same messages.

Current status

  • File calls other than read, write and write_all (opening, seeking, sync, directories) block the thread in a task.
  • On Windows, a ThreadLocal has a separate value in each task (it is built on fiber local storage); elsewhere the tasks of a thread share it.

The reference page documents every function.

Networking

The io module has TCP, UDP and Unix domain sockets, IP and socket addresses, and host name lookup; the tls module encrypts TCP connections, and the http module speaks HTTP over them. In a plain program every call blocks the calling thread until it completes, like File. To serve several connections at once, give each one its own thread, or its own task: in a task, a call that has to wait parks only that task.

Addresses

An IpAddress is an IPv4 or IPv6 address. A SocketAddress is an IP address and a port:

import io;

main(): int {
    var home = io.IpAddress.v4(127, 0, 0, 1);
    assert(home.is_loopback(), "127.0.0.1 is loopback");

    # Text is read strictly and printed in one canonical form.
    var six = io.IpAddress.parse("2001:DB8:0:0:0:0:0:1").value();
    assert(six.to_string() == "2001:db8::1", "IPv6 prints compressed and lowercase");
    assert(io.IpAddress.parse("256.1.1.1").error().is_invalid_input(), "256 is out of range");

    var service = io.SocketAddress.parse("[::1]:8080").value();
    assert(service.is_v6() && service.port() == 8080, "IPv6 with a port");
    assert(service.to_string() == "[::1]:8080", "brackets around IPv6");

    # A host name goes to the system resolver; an IP address is used as is.
    var local = io.resolve("localhost", 80).value();
    assert(local.count() >= 1 && local[0].address().is_loopback(), "localhost is loopback");
    return 0;
}
  • IpAddress.v4(a, b, c, d) and IpAddress.v6(a, ..., h) build an address from its bytes or its eight 16-bit groups. loopback_v4(), loopback_v6(), unspecified_v4() (0.0.0.0) and unspecified_v6() (::) are the well-known ones. IpAddress() is 0.0.0.0.
  • IpAddress.parse reads dotted decimal IPv4 and the RFC 4291 text form of IPv6, and to_string() prints the RFC 5952 form: lowercase, zeros compressed, ::ffff:1.2.3.4 for an IPv4-mapped address. Parsing and printing are the same on every platform.
  • SocketAddress(address, port) or SocketAddress.parse("1.2.3.4:80") make a socket address. IPv6 takes brackets: [::1]:80.
  • resolve(host, port) looks a host name up with the system resolver (the hosts file and DNS) and returns every address it has, with port attached. An IP address is returned as is. A name with no address fails with is_not_found().

TCP

A TcpListener waits for connections. Each TcpStream is one connection:

import io;

# A server and a client on this machine, taking turns on one thread: the
# system completes a connection before the server accepts it.
main(): int {
    # Port 0 asks the system for any free port.
    var listener = io.TcpListener.bind(io.SocketAddress.parse("127.0.0.1:0").value()).value();
    var address = listener.local_address().value();

    var client = io.TcpStream.connect(address).value();
    var (server, peer) = listener.accept().value();
    assert(peer == client.local_address().value(), "accept reports who connected");

    # The client sends a request and closes its sending side.
    assert(client.write_string("ping").is_ok(), "send the request");
    client.shutdown_write();

    # The server reads until the client is done: read returns 0 at the end.
    var request = Array<u8>();
    while (server.read(request, 4096).value() > 0) {
    }
    assert(request.count() == 4, "the whole request arrived");

    # It answers, and the client reads exactly the bytes it expects.
    server.write_string("pong");
    var reply = Array<u8>();
    assert(client.read_exact(reply, 4).is_ok(), "read the reply");
    assert(reply[0] == 'p' && reply[1] == 'o', "the reply is pong");
    return 0;
}
  • TcpListener.bind(address) listens on a local address. Port 0 lets the system pick a free port, and local_address() says which one it picked. accept() waits for the next connection and returns the stream and the peer’s address as a tuple.
  • TcpStream.connect(address) connects to an address. TcpStream.connect_host(host, port) resolves a name and tries each of its addresses in turn.
  • read(buffer, max) waits until some data arrives, then appends up to max bytes of it to buffer, the same way File.read does. It returns 0 once the peer has closed its side. read_exact(buffer, count) loops until count bytes have arrived.
  • write(data) sends what the system will take in one call. write_all(data) and write_string(text) loop until everything is sent.
  • shutdown_write() tells the peer that nothing more is coming, while this side can still read.
  • set_no_delay(true) sends small writes immediately instead of combining them.
  • local_address() and peer_address() return the two ends of the connection.

UDP

A UdpSocket sends and receives datagrams. Each one arrives whole or not at all, and in no guaranteed order:

import io;

main(): int {
    var loopback = io.SocketAddress(io.IpAddress.loopback_v4(), 0);
    var sender = io.UdpSocket.bind(loopback).value();
    var receiver = io.UdpSocket.bind(loopback).value();

    var datagram = Array<u8>();
    datagram.append(1);
    datagram.append(2);
    datagram.append(3);
    sender.send_to(datagram, receiver.local_address().value());

    # One receive takes one whole datagram and says who sent it.
    var buffer = Array<u8>();
    var (count, from) = receiver.receive_from(buffer, 1500).value();
    assert(count == 3 && buffer[2] == 3, "the datagram arrived whole");
    assert(from == sender.local_address().value(), "from the sender");
    return 0;
}
  • UdpSocket.bind(address) opens a socket on a local address.
  • send_to(data, address) sends one datagram. receive_from(buffer, max) waits for one datagram, appends it to buffer, and returns the byte count and the sender. The part of a datagram beyond max bytes is lost.
  • After connect(address), send and receive use that peer, and datagrams from anyone else are dropped.
  • set_broadcast(true) allows sending to a broadcast address.

Unix domain sockets

A Unix domain socket connects processes on the same machine through a path in the file system instead of an IP address and port. UnixListener and UnixStream work like TcpListener and TcpStream:

import io;

# A server and a client over a Unix domain socket, taking turns on one
# thread, as in the TCP example.
main(): int {
    var path = io.Directory.temp().join("pepper-networking-unix.sock");
    # Binding fails if the socket file is still there from an earlier run.
    io.File.remove(path);
    var listener = io.UnixListener.bind(path).value();

    var client = io.UnixStream.connect(path).value();
    var server = listener.accept().value();

    assert(client.write_string("ping").is_ok(), "send the request");
    var request = Array<u8>();
    assert(server.read_exact(request, 4).is_ok(), "read the request");
    server.write_string("pong");
    var reply = Array<u8>();
    assert(client.read_exact(reply, 4).is_ok(), "read the reply");
    assert(reply[0] == 'p' && reply[1] == 'o', "the reply is pong");

    # Closing the listener leaves the socket file; remove it when done.
    listener.close();
    assert(io.File.remove(path).is_ok(), "remove the socket file");
    return 0;
}
  • UnixListener.bind(path) creates a socket file at path and listens on it. Binding fails with is_address_in_use() if a file is already there, and closing the listener does not remove the file, so a server removes it with File.remove before binding and when it is done.
  • UnixStream.connect(path) connects to it. It fails with is_not_found() when there is no socket file, and with is_connection_refused() when the file is there but nothing listens on it.
  • accept() returns just the stream: the client’s end has no path.
  • Reading, writing, shutdown_write(), into_transfer() and adopt are the same as on a TcpStream, and SharedUnixListener is the counterpart of SharedTcpListener.
  • A path holds at most 107 bytes (103 on macOS); a longer or empty one fails with is_invalid_input().

Only stream sockets are supported, since Windows (10 version 1803 and later) has no Unix datagram sockets.

TLS

The tls module encrypts a TCP connection with TLS 1.2 or 1.3. A TlsConnector makes client connections and checks the server’s certificate. A TlsAcceptor serves them with a certificate and key. Both produce a TlsStream, which reads and writes like a TcpStream:

import async;
import io;
import tls;
import "test_certificate";

# A TLS server and client on this machine, in two tasks.
main(): int {
    var connector = tls.TlsConnector.create();
    if (connector.is_err()) {
        # On Windows, or where OpenSSL 3 is not installed.
        print(connector.error().message);
        return 0;
    }
    # A real server reads its certificate and key from files it was given.
    var certificate = io.Directory.temp().join("pepper-example-cert.pem");
    var key = io.Directory.temp().join("pepper-example-key.pem");
    io.File.write_text(certificate, test_certificate());
    io.File.write_text(key, test_private_key());

    async.run(
        () => {
            var acceptor = tls.TlsAcceptor.create(certificate, key).value();
            var listener = io.TcpListener.bind(io.SocketAddress.parse("127.0.0.1:0").value()).value();
            var port = listener.local_address().value().port();
            var server = async.Task<void>.spawn_local(() => {
                var (tcp, peer) = listener.accept().value();
                var stream = acceptor.accept(tcp).value();
                var request = Array<u8>();
                stream.read_exact(request, 4);
                stream.write_string("pong");
                stream.shutdown();
            });

            # The client trusts the test certificate as well as the system's.
            var client = connector.value();
            assert(client.add_root_certificate(certificate).is_ok(), "trust the test certificate");
            var stream = client.connect_host("localhost", port).value();
            stream.write_string("ping");
            var reply = Array<u8>();
            while (stream.read(reply, 4096).value() > 0) {}
            assert(reply.count() == 4 && reply[0] == 'p' && reply[1] == 'o', "the reply is pong");
            server.join();
        }
    );
    io.File.remove(certificate);
    io.File.remove(key);
    return 0;
}
  • TlsConnector.create() trusts the system’s root certificates, and add_root_certificate(path) adds more from a PEM file, such as a private certificate authority. Make one connector and share it: it is [Shared].
  • connector.connect(tcp, host) runs the handshake over a connected TcpStream. It checks that the certificate is valid and was issued for host, which is also sent to the server (SNI). connect_host(host, port) connects the TCP stream first. An IP address in host is checked against the certificate’s addresses.
  • TlsAcceptor.create(certificate_chain, private_key) reads PEM files, and acceptor.accept(tcp) runs the handshake over a connection a TcpListener accepted.
  • read, read_exact, write, write_all and write_string work on the decrypted bytes. shutdown() sends the TLS close_notify, and read returns 0 once the peer has sent one or closed the connection.
  • A failed handshake returns an error whose message says why, such as certificate verify failed: self-signed certificate.

On Linux and macOS the module uses OpenSSL 3, loaded when the first connector or acceptor is made: install it with the system’s package manager, or brew install openssl@3 on macOS. If it is missing, create() returns an error. On Windows it uses the system’s SChannel, which needs nothing installed; a server’s private key must be PKCS #8 (BEGIN PRIVATE KEY), and TLS 1.3 needs Windows 11 or Server 2022.

Errors

Every operation returns an IoResult. Besides the file-system predicates, IoError has these for networking:

PredicateWhen
is_connection_refused()nothing listens at the address
is_connection_reset()the peer reset or closed the connection (writing to a closed connection included)
is_address_in_use()another socket already has the address and port
is_address_not_available()the IP address is not one of this machine’s
is_timed_out()the peer never answered
is_not_found()resolve found no address for the name, or UnixStream.connect found no socket file

Writing to a closed connection never raises SIGPIPE, so it cannot kill the process. The write returns an error instead.

Closing

A socket closes when the last reference to it goes, like a File, and close() closes it earlier and reports any error. A socket cannot be copied, so it cannot go through a channel to another thread. Use it on the thread that made it, or move it: into_transfer() turns a TcpStream (or a UnixStream) into a thread-safe SocketTransfer that TcpStream.adopt (or UnixStream.adopt) takes on another thread, and a SharedTcpListener is a listener any thread can accept on (see Tasks).

On POSIX a listener sets SO_REUSEADDR, so a server can restart right away. On Windows it does not, because there that option would let another program take over the port.

Current status

  • Outside a task every call blocks its thread, with no timeout. In a task a call parks only the task, and async.timeout limits how long it may wait.
  • TLS clients cannot present certificates.
  • Unix datagram sockets are not supported.
  • IPv6 scope ids (fe80::1%eth0) are not supported.

The reference pages for addresses, sockets and Unix domain sockets and TLS document every method.

HTTP

The http module has an HTTP/1.1 client and server, over plain TCP or TLS. Both run in tasks: a request that waits parks only its task.

import async;
import http;
import io;

# Answers every request: `/hello` greets, anything else is not found.
handle(request: http.Request): http.Response {
    if (request.path() == "/hello") {
        var response = http.Response(200).set_text("hello, " + request.query());
        response.headers["Content-Type"] = "text/plain";
        return response;
    }
    return http.Response(404).set_text("nothing at " + request.path());
}

main(): int {
    async.run(
        () => {
            # Port 0 asks the system for any free port.
            var server = http.Server.bind(io.SocketAddress.parse("127.0.0.1:0").value()).value();
            var port = server.local_address().value().port();
            # serve() runs until async.run ends, so it gets a task of its own.
            async.spawn<void>(() => {
                server.serve(handle);
            });

            var base = "http://127.0.0.1:" + to_string(port);
            var client = http.Client();
            var response = client.get(base + "/hello?pepper").value();
            assert(response.status == 200, "found");
            assert(response.text() == "hello, pepper", "the handler's text");
            assert(response.headers["content-type"] == "text/plain", "names ignore case");

            var missing = client.get(base + "/elsewhere").value();
            assert(missing.status == 404 && missing.reason == "Not Found", "not found");

            var posted = client.post(base + "/hello", "text/plain", "a body").value();
            assert(posted.is_success(), "any method reaches the handler");
        }
    );
    return 0;
}

Messages

  • A Request has a method, a url, headers and a body. For a client the url is absolute (https://example.com/items?page=2); a server handler gets the request target (/items?page=2). uri() parses either as a Uri, and path() and query() return its parts.
  • A Response has a status, a reason, headers and a body. is_success() tests for a 2xx status.
  • Headers maps each field name to its values. Names ignore case (they are stored lowercased). headers["Accept"] reads the first value ("" when there is none) and headers["Accept"] = "text/html" replaces the field; get(name) returns an optional, add keeps earlier values, values(name) returns them all, and names() lists the fields in no defined order.
  • set_text and set_body fill a request or response and return it, so they chain. body() returns the bytes, for any body including binary ones; text() decodes them as UTF-8, replacing invalid bytes with U+FFFD.

URLs

Uri (in the prelude, so no import is needed) parses any URI reference following RFC 3986: an absolute URI with any scheme (https:, mailto:, file:) or a relative reference such as a request target. It splits the text into scheme, user_info, host, port, path, query and fragment; the parts that can be missing are optionals. Components keep their percent-escapes, and Uri.decode turns one into text.

main(): int {
    # Any scheme parses; the scheme is lowercased and nothing else changes.
    var uri = Uri.parse("HTTPS://user@example.com:8443/caf%C3%A9?page=2#top").value();
    assert(uri.scheme == "https" && uri.host.value() == "example.com", "scheme and host");
    assert(uri.port.value() == 8443 && uri.user_info.value() == "user", "port and user information");
    assert(uri.path == "/caf%C3%A9" && uri.query.value() == "page=2", "path and query keep their escapes");
    assert(Uri.decode(uri.path).value() == "/café", "decoded path");
    assert(uri.path_and_query() == "/caf%C3%A9?page=2", "what an HTTP request line names");

    # Missing parts are None: a mailto URI has no authority.
    var mail = Uri.parse("mailto:someone@example.com").value();
    assert(mail.host.is_none() && mail.path == "someone@example.com", "no authority");

    # A relative reference has no scheme, like a request target on a server.
    var target = Uri.parse("/items?page=2").value();
    assert(!target.is_absolute() && target.path == "/items", "relative");

    assert(Uri.parse("http://example.com/a b").is_err(), "a space must be percent-encoded");
    return 0;
}

Client

  • Client() trusts the system’s root certificates for https:// URLs. Client(connector) uses a tls.TlsConnector of your own, for instance one that trusts a private certificate authority.
  • get(url), post(url, content_type, body) and send(request) open a connection, send the request and read the whole response. The client adds Host, Content-Length and Connection: close.
  • Any status is a successful result: check status. An error means there was no response: the URL is not http:// or https:// (is_invalid_input()), the connection or TLS handshake failed, or the response was not valid HTTP.
  • Redirects are returned, not followed, and every request uses a new connection.

Server

  • Server.bind(address) listens for HTTP; Server.bind_tls(address, acceptor) serves HTTPS with a tls.TlsAcceptor’s certificate.
  • serve(handler) accepts connections on every worker of async.run and serves each in a task of its own, calling handler for each request with the body read in full. It returns when async.run ends. The handler is a shared (Request) => Response, since every worker calls it.
  • Connections stay open between requests unless the client asks to close or speaks HTTP/1.0. Chunked request bodies and Expect: 100-continue are understood.
  • The server adds Content-Length to each response, and the standard reason phrase when reason is empty (reason_phrase(status) returns it).
  • A request it cannot parse gets 400 Bad Request, header fields over 64 KiB get 431, and a body over MAX_REQUEST_BODY (16 MiB) gets 413.

Current status

  • Bodies are read into memory in full, up to 16 MiB for a request and MAX_RESPONSE_BODY (64 MiB) for a response; there is no streaming yet.
  • HTTP/2, connection reuse in the client, and following redirects are not supported yet.

The reference pages for messages, the client, the server and Uri document every method.

Calling C

Pepper programs can call functions written in C: the C standard library, your operating system’s API, or any other library with a C interface. You declare the C function’s prototype with extern, make sure the library that defines it is linked, and then call it like any Pepper function.

Declaring a C function

An extern declaration is a C prototype, written the way C writes it: the return type, the name, and the parameter types, each followed by a parameter name. It has no body.

extern ulong strlen(char* s);
extern int strcmp(char* a, char* b);
extern void* malloc(ulong size);
extern void free(void* p);

After that, strlen("hello") calls the C library’s strlen. The compiler does not check your prototype against any C header, so it must match the real C function exactly. A wrong parameter or return type compiles, and then passes or reads the wrong bits when the program runs.

Match C types with Pepper types of the same size:

CPepper
char, signed char, unsigned charchar or i8, u8 or byte
short, unsigned shortshort or i16, ushort or u16
int, unsigned intint or i32, uint or u32
long long, unsigned long long, int64_t, size_t (64-bit)long or i64, ulong or u64
float, doublefloat, double
T*T* in the prototype

Pepper’s long is always 64 bits. C’s long is 64 bits on Linux and macOS but 32 bits on Windows, so a C function that takes long needs a different prototype per platform (see [LinkName] below for an example).

Some things to know about extern declarations:

  • The prototype uses C syntax only. The name(parameter: type): type form that Pepper functions use is a parse error on an extern, and __ptr<T> as a parameter type is an error too: write char*, not __ptr<char>.
  • An extern is private to its file, like every declaration. Write export extern ... to let files that import this one call it (see Visibility).
  • Several files may declare the same extern, since every declaration names the same C function. The runtime already declares malloc, free and a few others privately, and your program can declare them again.
  • An extern is linked by name. If no linked library defines it, the program compiles and then fails to link, with the linker reporting an undefined symbol. See Linking for how to add libraries.

Passing strings

Pepper’s String is a reference-counted object, not a C string, so a String value cannot be passed where C expects char*.

  • A string literal passed to an extern is passed as a NUL-terminated C string, with no allocation: strlen("hello") is 5. The same is true wherever a literal flows into a __ptr<char>, __ptr<u8>, or __ptr<void> in Pepper code (a variable, field, argument, or return value), so String("hello") copies the literal’s five bytes.
  • A String value is passed with c_str(), which returns the String’s NUL-terminated buffer as a __ptr<char>. The pointer belongs to the String: it is valid until the String is destroyed or grows (for example with append or +=). An empty String() has no buffer, so its c_str() is __null; check before you pass it to a C function that does not accept NULL.
  • To turn a C string back into a String, pass the pointer to the constructor: String(p) copies a NUL-terminated C string, and String(p, size) copies size bytes. If you already know the number of code points, pass it as a third argument: String(p, size, String.length_of(p, size)). The constructor copies the bytes, so you still own (and may free) the C buffer. A C string is never passed or stored where a String is expected without this copy: that is an error.
# Passing strings to C, and turning C strings back into Strings.

extern ulong strlen(char* s);
extern int strcmp(char* a, char* b);
extern char* strchr(char* s, int c);

main(): int {
    # A string literal passed to an extern is a NUL-terminated C string.
    assert(strlen("hello") == 5, "a literal is passed as a C string");
    assert(strcmp("abc", "abc") == 0, "equal C strings compare as 0");

    # So is one stored in a __ptr<char>, or passed to the String
    # constructor, which copies it.
    __ptr<char> greeting = "hello";
    assert(strlen(greeting) == 5, "a literal in a __ptr<char> is a C string");
    assert(String("hello").size() == 5, "String(literal) copies its bytes");

    # A String value goes through c_str().
    var name = "Pepper";
    name += " and C";
    assert(strlen(name.c_str()) == name.size(), "c_str() is the String's bytes");

    # A char* result is a __ptr<char>. Copy it into a String with the
    # constructor: the byte size and the number of code points.
    var rest = strchr(name.c_str(), 32);   # 32 is ' '
    assert(rest != __null, "strchr found a space");
    var size = strlen(rest);
    var copy = String(rest, size, String.length_of(rest, size));
    assert(copy == " and C", "the copy holds the tail of the C string");
    return 0;
}

Passing a String value directly to an extern’s char* parameter is an error:

main.pep:4:19: error: cannot pass 'String' to parameter 1 of extern 'strlen' of type 'char*'; pass its 'c_str()'
    4 |     return strlen(name) as int;
      |                   ^~~~

The reverse is an error too: a char* (or any raw pointer, void* included) is never a String, so passing one where a String is expected, assigning it to a String variable, or returning it as one is rejected. Copy it into a String with String(p) first:

main.pep:3:19: error: cannot pass a value of type '__ptr<char>' as argument 2 of 'assert', which has type 'String'; use 'String(...)' to copy a C string

Variadic functions

A C function with a variable argument list, such as printf or snprintf, ends its prototype with ... after at least one named parameter:

extern int snprintf(char* buffer, ulong size, char* format, ...);

The call uses the C calling convention for variadic functions, which differs from a plain call on some targets (such as macOS on Apple silicon). Each argument past the named ones gets C’s default argument promotions: integers narrower than int widen to int, and float widens to double. Match your format string to the promoted type: %d for a u8, %f for a float, and %lld (not %ld) for a long, because C’s long is 32 bits on Windows.

... must come last and must follow a named parameter: extern int f(...); is a parse error.

# Calling a C function that takes a variable argument list.

extern void* malloc(ulong size);
extern void free(void* p);

# On Windows, snprintf lives in legacy_stdio_definitions.
[Target(OS(Windows))] [Link("legacy_stdio_definitions")]
extern int snprintf(char* buffer, ulong size, char* format, ...);
[Target(!OS(Windows))]
extern int snprintf(char* buffer, ulong size, char* format, ...);

main(): int {
    var buffer = malloc(64) as __ptr<char>;
    u8 small = 200;     # widened to int
    float half = 0.5;   # widened to double
    long big = 5000000000;
    var written = snprintf(buffer, 64, "%d %.1f %lld %s", small, half, big, "ok");
    var text = String(buffer, written as ulong, String.length_of(buffer, written as ulong));
    free(buffer);
    assert(text == "200 0.5 5000000000 ok", "snprintf formatted every argument");
    return 0;
}

On Windows, the C runtime defines snprintf and its relatives inline in its headers, so the linkable symbols live in a separate library, legacy_stdio_definitions. The example links it with [Link] on Windows only.

Pointers

C code deals in raw pointers, and Pepper has a raw pointer type for talking to it: __ptr<T>, such as __ptr<void>, __ptr<char> or __ptr<__ptr<int>>. A void* returned by an extern is a __ptr<void> in Pepper, and a __ptr<T> can be passed to an extern that takes a C pointer.

A pointer supports these operations:

OperationMeaning
p[i]reads or writes the element i places from p; its type is T, so var v = p[i] declares a T
p + nthe address n elements after p (n bytes for __ptr<void>)
p == __null, p != __nullcompares with the null pointer
p == q, p != qcompares two addresses (a pointer also compares with an integer address)
p as ulong, p as longthe address as an integer
p as __ptr<U>the same address, seen as pointing at U

__null is the null pointer. sizeof<T>() gives the size of a type in bytes, which you need to allocate memory for C.

T* spelling is for extern prototypes only, since they mirror C. Everywhere else (parameters, return types, struct fields, locals, globals, type aliases, generic arguments and casts) you write __ptr<T>, and T* is a compile error:

clear(p: void*, n: ulong) { }

main.pep:1:10: error: C pointer syntax `void*` is only allowed in extern declarations; use `__ptr<void>`
    1 | clear(p: void*, n: ulong) { }
      |          ^~~~

# Raw pointers: __ptr<T> in Pepper code, T* in extern prototypes.

extern void* malloc(ulong size);
extern void free(void* p);
extern void* memset(void* p, int value, ulong size);

struct Buffer {
    var data: __ptr<u8> = __null;
    var size: ulong = 0;
}

make_buffer(size: ulong): Buffer {
    var b = Buffer();
    b.data = malloc(size) as __ptr<u8>;
    b.size = size;
    memset(b.data, 0, size);
    return b;
}

sum(values: __ptr<int>, count: int): int {
    var total = 0;
    var i = 0;
    while (i < count) {
        total = total + values[i];
        i = i + 1;
    }
    return total;
}

# `var` takes the element type from the pointer: `big` is a ulong, so a value
# above 2^32 reads back whole.
first(values: __ptr<ulong>): ulong {
    var big = values[0];
    return big;
}

main(): int {
    # Indexing reads and writes elements of T.
    var numbers = malloc(4 * sizeof<int>()) as __ptr<int>;
    numbers[0] = 10;
    numbers[1] = 20;
    numbers[2] = 30;
    numbers[3] = 40;
    assert(sum(numbers, 4) == 100, "indexing reads what was written");

    var wide = malloc(sizeof<ulong>()) as __ptr<ulong>;
    wide[0] = 5000000000;
    assert(first(wide) == 5000000000, "var v = p[i] has the pointee's type");
    free(wide);

    # p + n moves by n elements, not n bytes.
    var third = numbers + 2;
    assert(third[0] == 30, "numbers + 2 points at the third element");
    assert((third as ulong) - (numbers as ulong) == 8, "two ints are eight bytes");

    # __ptr<void> strides by bytes; cast to see the memory another way.
    var raw = numbers as __ptr<void>;
    var bytes = raw as __ptr<u8>;
    assert(bytes[4] == 20, "the second int starts at byte 4 (little-endian)");
    free(raw);

    # Pointers can live in struct fields, and compare with __null.
    var b = make_buffer(16);
    assert(b.data != __null, "malloc returned memory");
    assert(b.data[15] == 0, "memset cleared it");
    free(b.data);
    b.data = __null;

    # A pointer to pointers: indexing yields the inner pointer, and indexing
    # again reads or writes through it.
    var rows = malloc(2 * sizeof<__ptr<int>>()) as __ptr<__ptr<int>>;
    var row = malloc(sizeof<int>()) as __ptr<int>;
    rows[1] = row;
    rows[1][0] = 7;
    assert(rows[1][0] == 7, "rows[1][0] reads through the row pointer");
    assert(row[0] == 7, "rows[1] is the row pointer");
    free(row);
    free(rows);
    return 0;
}

Pointers are not reference-counted and nothing checks them: indexing past the end of an allocation, using memory after free, or forgetting to free it behaves exactly as it would in C. Keep raw pointers inside small functions or structs that own the memory, and give the rest of your program ordinary Pepper types.

Passing a Pepper function to C

A Pepper function value is a reference-counted object, not a C function pointer. For C, Pepper has a separate type, extern (P...) => R: the address of a function that C calls with the C calling convention. Declare a callback parameter of a C function with it, and pass a named function, or a closure that captures nothing:

# `extern (P...) => R` is a C function pointer type: qsort calls `compare`
# with pointers to two elements.
extern void qsort(void* base, ulong count, ulong size, extern (void*, void*) => int compare);

ascending(a: __ptr<void>, b: __ptr<void>): int {
    __ptr<int> x = a;
    __ptr<int> y = b;
    return x[0] - y[0];
}

main(): int {
    __ptr<int> numbers = _pep_malloc(4 * sizeof<int>());
    numbers[0] = 30;
    numbers[1] = 10;
    numbers[2] = 40;
    numbers[3] = 20;

    # A named function converts to the C function pointer type.
    qsort(numbers, 4, sizeof<int>(), ascending);
    assert(numbers[0] == 10 && numbers[3] == 40, "ascending");

    # So does a closure that captures nothing; its parameter types come
    # from the C function pointer type.
    qsort(numbers, 4, sizeof<int>(), (a, b) => {
        __ptr<int> x = a;
        __ptr<int> y = b;
        return y[0] - x[0];
    });
    assert(numbers[0] == 40 && numbers[3] == 10, "descending");

    # A C function pointer is a value like a number: store it, call it.
    var compare: extern (__ptr<void>, __ptr<void>) => int = ascending;
    assert(compare(numbers, numbers + 1) > 0, "40 sorts after 30");

    _pep_free(numbers);
    return 0;
}

  • What converts. A named free function, a static method (Order.descending), or a closure literal that captures nothing, whose parameter and return types match the C function pointer type exactly. A closure literal takes its parameter types from the type, as it does from any function type.

  • Nothing captured. C calls the function with its arguments alone, so a closure that captures a value, or a bound method (p.get), cannot convert:

    main.pep:4:43: error: closure passed as C function pointer type 'extern (void*, void*) => int' captures 'bias'; a C function pointer cannot hold captured values
    4 |     qsort(_pep_malloc(4), 0, 4, (a, b) => bias);
      |                                           ^~~~
main.pep:3:9: note: pass what the callback needs through the C function's context argument instead
    3 |     var bias = 1;
      |         ^~~~

    Most C APIs that take a callback also take a void* context argument that they hand back to it; pass what the callback needs through that. A function value held in a variable does not convert either, since it may be a closure.

  • C types only. C knows nothing of reference counts, so the parameter and return types must be numbers, bool, pointers, or other C function pointer types. A struct is an error: C function pointer type 'extern (String) => int' cannot use 'String'; C passes only numbers, 'bool' and pointers. Write pointers as void* in an extern declaration and as __ptr<void> elsewhere, as for any pointer.

  • A value like a number. A C function pointer has no reference count. Store it in a variable, field or module-scope const, return it, pass it to other threads, or call it: compare(a, b) calls through it with the C calling convention. Calling a null one (from C) panics. It converts to void* but not to a Pepper function type; wrap it in a closure that calls it, (x) => f(x), to use it as one.

__function_pointer(name) also gives a function’s address, as an untyped __ptr<void>. It takes a free function, or a static method of the struct whose method uses it. Inside a generic struct the static method is the one for the current type arguments, which is how ThreadLocal<T> gives the operating system a destructor for its T. Prefer a C function pointer type where the signature is known, since the compiler then checks it.

Binding to a different symbol name

[LinkName("symbol")] binds an extern to a C symbol whose name differs from the declared one. Pepper code calls the extern by its declared name, and the object file refers to symbol. Use it to give a C function a clearer name, to avoid clashing with a Pepper name, or, together with [Target], to bind one Pepper name to a different symbol on each platform:

# [LinkName] binds a Pepper name to a C symbol with a different name.

# llabs takes a 64-bit long long on every platform.
[LinkName("llabs")] extern long absolute(long value);

# C's long is 64 bits on Linux and macOS but 32 bits on Windows, so
# the 64-bit labs is only right away from Windows.
[Target(OS(Windows))] [LinkName("llabs")] extern long abs64(long value);
[Target(!OS(Windows))] [LinkName("labs")] extern long abs64(long value);

main(): int {
    assert(absolute(-7) == 7, "absolute calls llabs");
    assert(abs64(-5000000000) == 5000000000, "abs64 calls a 64-bit abs");
    return 0;
}

Real uses of the per-platform form include macOS on Intel, where the 64-bit-inode version of stat is named stat$INODE64:

[Target(OS(Mac) && Arch(x64))] [LinkName("stat$INODE64")] extern int stat(char* path, void* buf);
[Target(OS(Mac) && Arch(aarch64))] extern int stat(char* path, void* buf);

LinkName takes exactly one non-empty string, and an extern may carry at most one. Anything else is an error, such as:

main.pep:1:34: error: LinkName on extern 'pep_abs' takes exactly one string: [LinkName("sym")]
    1 | [LinkName("a", "b")] extern long pep_abs(long v);
      |                                  ^~~~~~~

Linking the library

A C function is only callable if the library that defines it is linked into your program. The C library is always linked. For anything else, attach [Link("name")] to the extern or pass -l name to the compiler. The Linking chapter covers both.

[Target(OS(Windows))] [Link("gdi32")] extern ulong GetStockObject(int kind);

Calling Pepper from C

Pepper builds executables, and there is no supported way yet for C code to call Pepper functions. The parser accepts an [Export] attribute on a function, intended to give it a C interface with object references passed as opaque handles, but the compiler does not act on it yet: [Export] currently has no effect.

Do not confuse [Export] with the export keyword, which makes a declaration visible to other Pepper files (see Visibility).

Platform selection

Some code only makes sense on one platform: a Windows API call, a Linux-specific constant, a type whose size differs between operating systems. The [Target(...)] attribute keeps a declaration or a block only when you compile for a matching platform, so one source file can hold every platform’s version side by side.

The target is always the platform you compile on: Pepper does not cross-compile yet.

Writing a condition

Target takes one boolean condition built from two predicates:

  • OS(...) is true on the named operating system: Windows, Mac (or MacOS), or Linux.
  • Arch(...) is true on the named processor architecture: x64 or aarch64.

Values are matched case-insensitively, so OS(windows) works too. Combine predicates with && (or and), || (or or), !, and parentheses:

[Target(OS(Windows))]                     # Windows
[Target(!OS(Windows))]                    # Linux and macOS
[Target(OS(Linux) && Arch(x64))]          # Linux on x64 only
[Target(OS(Windows) || OS(Mac))]          # Windows and macOS
[Target(!(OS(Windows) || OS(Mac)))]       # Linux

An item may carry several attributes. They are combined with “and”: the item is kept only when every Target on it matches. Other attributes on the same item, such as [Link(...)], do not affect the selection.

What it applies to

Put [Target(...)] before any top-level declaration: a function, an extern, a struct, a trait, an extension, a type alias, a module-scope variable, an import, or a re-export. It also works on the methods inside a struct, trait or extension. When two declarations share a name, give them conditions that never match on the same platform, so exactly one survives:

# One name, a different declaration per platform.

# Type aliases: a Windows HANDLE is a pointer, a POSIX descriptor an int.
[Target(OS(Windows))] type Handle = __ptr<void>;
[Target(!OS(Windows))] type Handle = int;

# Module-scope variables (const and thread-safe, like every global).
[Target(OS(Windows))] const max_path = 260;
[Target(!OS(Windows))] const max_path = 4096;

# Functions.
[Target(OS(Windows))]
platform_name(): String { return "Windows"; }

[Target(OS(Mac))]
platform_name(): String { return "macOS"; }

[Target(OS(Linux))]
platform_name(): String { return "Linux"; }

# Structs, and methods inside them.
[Target(Arch(x64))]
struct Cpu {
    var name: String = "x64";
}

[Target(Arch(aarch64))]
struct Cpu {
    var name: String = "aarch64";
}

struct Word {
    [Target(Arch(x64) || Arch(aarch64))]
    bits(): int { return 64; }
}

main(): int {
    var name = platform_name();
    print(name);
    print(Cpu().name);
    assert(Word().bits() == 64, "every supported target is 64-bit");

    [Target(OS(Windows))] {
        assert(sizeof<Handle>() == 8, "a HANDLE is a pointer");
        assert(name == "Windows", "the Windows function was kept");
    }
    [Target(!OS(Windows))] {
        assert(sizeof<Handle>() == 4, "a descriptor is an int");
        assert(max_path == 4096, "the POSIX variable was kept");
    }
    return 0;
}

The attribute goes before export, not after it: [Target(OS(Windows))] export f(). Writing export [Target(OS(Windows))] f() is a parse error.

Blocks inside a function

Inside a function body, attach [Target(...)] to a block { ... }. The block is kept or removed like a declaration. Blocks may nest, and may appear inside if and loop bodies.

This is the usual way to wrap C functions that differ per platform: declare each platform’s extern with its own condition, and call each one from a block with the same condition.

# A portable wrapper over a C function that has a different name on
# each platform. kernel32 is linked by default on Windows, and getpid is
# in the C library everywhere else.

[Target(OS(Windows))] extern uint GetCurrentProcessId();
[Target(!OS(Windows))] extern int getpid();

process_id(): long {
    [Target(OS(Windows))] {
        return GetCurrentProcessId() as long;
    }
    [Target(!OS(Windows))] {
        return getpid() as long;
    }
}

main(): int {
    var id = process_id();
    print(id);
    assert(id > 0, "a running process has a positive id");
    return 0;
}

What happens to code that does not match

Code whose condition does not match is removed before type checking. That is what makes the examples above work: a call to GetCurrentProcessId, which exists only on Windows, is fine in a block that is removed everywhere else. Removed code is not checked for errors beyond parsing, so a typo in it goes unnoticed until you build on the platform that keeps it.

It still has to parse, and every Target condition is validated on every platform, even one inside removed code. A misspelled value is always an error, never a silent “no match”:

[Target(OS(Darwin))] f(): int { return 1; }

main.pep:1:1: error: unknown OS value `Darwin` (expected Windows, Mac, MacOS, Linux) in [Target(OS(Darwin))]
    1 | [Target(OS(Darwin))] f(): int { return 1; }
      | ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Other mistakes the compiler reports:

  • Target takes exactly one condition: [Target(OS(Windows), Arch(x64))] is an error; write [Target(OS(Windows) && Arch(x64))].
  • Only OS(...) and Arch(...) may appear inside it. A bare name ([Target(Windows)]), another call ([Target(Foo(x))]), not in place of !, or a nested Target is an error.
  • OS(...) and Arch(...) are only valid inside Target(...), and the brackets hold one attribute: [OS(Windows)] and [Target(OS(Windows)) && Export] are parse errors.
  • Struct fields cannot carry [Target(...)]. Select the whole struct instead, as Cpu does in the first example.

Linking

The Pepper compiler turns your program into a native executable in two steps: it compiles all of your files, and the runtime, into one object file, and then links that object file with the system libraries it needs. When you call C functions, linking is where their definitions come from, so this chapter explains what is linked by default and how to add more.

What the compiler links

The compiler uses clang as its link driver, rather than calling the platform’s linker directly, because clang already knows each platform’s startup files, C library and SDK locations. It uses the clang from the LLVM installation the compiler was built with when there is one, and otherwise the first clang on your PATH.

Every program is linked with:

  • Linux: the C library, which clang adds.
  • macOS: libSystem, which contains the C library, plus the SDK and platform-version flags. clang adds all of these, using the Xcode Command Line Tools.
  • Windows: the Microsoft C runtime (the UCRT, vcruntime and the CRT startup library), which clang adds, plus kernel32, user32 and shell32, which the Pepper compiler adds. clang finds the Visual Studio and Windows SDK libraries itself, so you do not need a Developer Command Prompt.

Any library file named lib<name>.a in the runtime directory is linked too.

Anything else must be linked explicitly. On Linux, that includes the math library (m) for functions such as pow, and pthread on older systems.

Linking a library from the source: [Link]

Attach [Link("name")] to an extern declaration to link the library that defines it. The compiler passes -lname to the linker, just like -l on the command line. Name the library the way the linker does: m for libm, gdi32 for gdi32.lib.

# [Link("name")] on an extern links the library that defines it.

# gdi32 is not one of the libraries Windows programs link by default.
[Target(OS(Windows))] [Link("gdi32")] extern ulong GetStockObject(int kind);

# pthread_self is in libpthread on older Linux systems, in libc on newer
# ones, and in libSystem on macOS; linking pthread works on all of them.
[Target(!OS(Windows))] [Link("pthread")] extern ulong pthread_self();

# The math library is separate from the C library on Linux.
[Target(OS(Linux))] [Link("m")] extern double pow(double base, double exponent);
[Target(!OS(Linux))] extern double pow(double base, double exponent);

main(): int {
    [Target(OS(Windows))] {
        # 5 is NULL_BRUSH, a stock object that always exists.
        assert(GetStockObject(5) != 0, "gdi32 was linked");
    }
    [Target(!OS(Windows))] {
        assert(pthread_self() != 0, "pthread was linked");
    }
    assert(pow(2.0, 10.0) == 1024.0, "the math library was linked");
    return 0;
}
  • The library is linked only if the extern survives platform selection. Combining [Link] with [Target], as above, links a library only on the platforms that need it.
  • Each library is linked once, however many externs name it.
  • The library is linked even when nothing calls the extern.

Putting [Link] in the source keeps the knowledge of which library a function comes from next to its declaration, so nobody building your program has to remember a command-line flag.

Linking a library from the command line: -l

The -l option links a library for one build:

pepper main.pep -l m -o main

Repeat it for more libraries (-l m -l pthread). There is no option to add a library search directory yet, so a library must be one the linker finds on its own: a system library, or one in a directory the linker searches by default.

When linking fails

If a function you declared with extern is not defined by any linked library, compilation succeeds and the link fails. The compiler prints what the linker said, which names the missing symbol:

error: Link failed: clang exited with exit status: 1
/usr/bin/ld: .pep/build/main.units/main.o: in function `main':
main:(.text+0x25ba): undefined reference to `no_such_function'
clang: error: linker command failed with exit code 1 (use -v to see invocation)

The object the linker names is the one for the file that made the call, in .pep/build/<name>.units/. Symbols of your own functions appear as the compiler spells them for the linker: main and a method such as Point.length keep their names, and any other name is written _P followed by the name with _ doubled and other characters as _ and two hex digits, so a function parse appears as _Pparse and Array<int>.count as _PArray_3cint_3e.count. That way a Pepper function never collides with a C library function of the same name, such as exit. extern functions keep their C names.

To fix it, check the spelling of the extern against the C function (or use [LinkName] when the names differ), then add the library that defines it with [Link] or -l.

If the compiler cannot run clang at all, the error says Link failed: cannot run clang. Install clang (on Linux, from your package manager) or the Xcode Command Line Tools on macOS.

Warnings from the linker are passed through unchanged, even when the link succeeds.

Output files

With no -o, the executable is named after the first source file, without an extension, in the directory where you run the compiler. Windows will not run a file without .exe, so pass -o main.exe there. The object files and other intermediate files go in .pep/build/ under the current directory, or in the directory you pass to --build: one object per file of the program in <name>.units/, and <name>.o, which runs the program’s global initializers. Unchanged objects come from the build cache in .pep/cache/ (--no-cache skips it).

Compiler errors

When the compiler cannot build your program, it tells you what is wrong and exactly where, in the same format as clang. This chapter shows how to read an error and lists some common ones.

Reading an error

Here is a program with a mistake in it:

struct Point {
    var x: int;
    var y: int;
}

main(): int {
    var p = Point();
    var total = p.x + p.z;
    return total;
}

Compiling it prints:

main.pep:8:25: error: no member named 'z' in 'Point'
    8 |     var total = p.x + p.z;
      |                         ^

An error has three parts:

  1. The header: the file, line and column, then error: and the message. Editors and terminals recognize file:line:column and can jump to it.
  2. The source line the error is on, with its line number.
  3. A caret (^) under the exact token you need to change, with ~ under the rest of the token when it is longer than one character. Here, the member name z, not the whole statement.

Messages follow clang’s style: they start in lowercase, put names and types in single quotes ('z', 'Point'), and say what to do when there is an obvious fix. The fixed program is:

# The program from "Reading an error", after the fix.

struct Point {
    var x: int;
    var y: int;
}

main(): int {
    var p = Point();
    p.x = 3;
    p.y = 4;
    var total = p.x + p.y;
    assert(total == 7, "x + y");
    return 0;
}

Notes

Some errors are explained by a second place in your code. The compiler shows that place as a note: after the error, in the same format. When one file calls a function that another file did not export, the note points at the declaration:

main.pep:4:12: error: 'helper' is private to lib.pep; declare it with 'export' to use it from another file
    4 |     return helper();
      |            ^~~~~~
lib.pep:1:1: note: declared here
    1 | helper(): int { return 1; }
      | ^~~~~~

When a brace is never closed, the error is at the end of the file, and the note shows the brace that opened the block:

main.pep:5:1: error: expected '}'
    5 | 
      | ^
main.pep:1:13: note: to match this '{'
    1 | main(): int {
      |             ^

One error at a time

The compiler stops at the first error it finds and exits with status 1, so fix that error and compile again. It never produces an executable from a program with an error.

On a terminal, errors are colored like clang’s. Set the NO_COLOR environment variable to turn colors off. Output that goes to a file or a pipe is never colored.

Warnings do not stop the build, and the compiler prints them whether or not it also finds an error. Besides the linker’s own warnings, which the compiler passes through (see Linking), the only warnings today are deprecations.

Deprecations

A use of a declaration marked [Deprecated("message")] warns at the name, with the message and a note at the declaration. When the attribute names a replacement, the warning shows the rename under the code, and the language server offers it as a quick fix. See Deprecation.

main.pep:9:15: warning: 'clone' is deprecated: use 'copy' instead [deprecated]
    9 |     var b = a.clone();
      |               ^~~~~
      |               copy
main.pep:4:5: note: 'clone' declared here
    4 |     clone(): Counter { return this.copy(); }
      |     ^~~~~

Syntax of the language itself that is on its way out keeps compiling for a while too, with a warning that names its replacement and shows the fix under the code it replaces:

main.pep:3:5: warning: `new` is deprecated; constructors are spelled `construct`, matching `destruct` [deprecated]
    3 |     new(this.x = 1) {}
      |     ^~~
      |     construct
DeprecatedReplacement
new(...) constructorconstruct(...)
io.Path.join_str(String)io.Path.join(Path), which accepts a String
String.clone()String.copy()
ThreadLocal<T>.get() for a T that is not thread-safe (now an error)with (var value = local.enter()) { ... }
io.Path.is_dir()io.Path.is_directory()
io.File.set_len(ulong)io.File.set_length(ulong)
io.File.write_string(String)io.File.write_all(String)
HashMap.cap(), HashSet.cap()capacity()
Channel.send(x), try_send(x) with a variable something else references (now an error: send no longer copies)send(move(x)), or send(copy(x)) to keep using x
[Sending] parameter attribute (now an error)[Move]
Atomic<T> without an import (now an error: it moved to the async module)async.Atomic<T> after import async, or import [Atomic] from async

Errors in the editor

The Pepper language server, used by the VS Code extension, reports the same errors at the same places while you type. It underlines the token the caret would point at, and shows each note as related information that you can click to jump to.

Common errors

These are some errors you are likely to meet, with the exact text the compiler prints.

A name that was never declared, often a typo:

main.pep:3:16: error: use of undeclared identifier 'nope'
    3 |     return a + nope;
      |                ^~~~

main.pep:2:12: error: call to undeclared function 'frob'
    2 |     return frob(1);
      |            ^~~~

A type name that does not exist, often a misspelled type or a missing import:

main.pep:2:12: error: unknown type name 'Frob'
    2 |     var x: Frob = 1;
      |            ^~~~

A field or method the struct does not have:

main.pep:6:7: error: no member named 'move' in 'Point'
    6 |     p.move(1);
      |       ^~~~

The wrong number of arguments. When the function has default parameters, the message gives the range:

main.pep:4:12: error: too few arguments to 'add': expected 2, have 1
    4 |     return add(1);
      |            ^~~

main.pep:3:12: error: too many arguments to 'f': expected at most 2, have 3
    3 |     return f(1, 2, 3) + f();
      |            ^

A call no overload fits, or that two fit equally well. Each note is a candidate, and says why it does not fit (see Overloading):

main.pep:3:22: error: call to 'f' is ambiguous
    3 | main(): int { return f(1); }
      |                      ^
main.pep:1:1: note: candidate function
    1 | f(x: long): int { return 1; }
      | ^
main.pep:2:1: note: candidate function
    2 | f(x: short): int { return 2; }
      | ^

A struct used as a condition without a truth-test operator. A struct is never tested for null implicitly: declare !!(): bool on it, or compare with __null (see Truth tests and conditions):

main.pep:6:9: error: 'Node' cannot be used as a condition: declare '!!(): bool' on it, or compare with '__null'
    6 |     if (node) {
      |         ^~~~
main.pep:1:8: note: 'Node' declared here
    1 | struct Node {
      |        ^~~~

A syntax error. The parser says what it expected at the first place the code stopped making sense:

main.pep:2:14: error: expected ')'
    2 |     if (true {
      |              ^

main.pep:2:13: error: expected expression
    2 |     var x = ;
      |             ^

A value of the wrong type. Numbers convert among themselves, as in C, but a number is never a struct and one struct type is never another, except that a struct converts to a trait it declares, and a value converts to a struct whose constructor from its type is [Implicit]. A raw pointer is never a struct either: a __ptr<char> is not a String (copy it with String(p)), and a String is not a __ptr<char> (pass its c_str()). The check applies wherever a value flows into a typed place: a variable’s initializer, an assignment, an argument and a return:

main.pep:2:13: error: cannot initialize variable 'x' of type 'int' with a value of type 'String'
    2 |     int x = "hello";
      |             ^~~~~~~

main.pep:3:12: error: cannot pass a value of type 'i32' as argument 1 of 'g', which has type 'String'
    3 |     return g(5);
      |            ^

main.pep:3:19: error: cannot pass a value of type '__ptr<char>' as argument 2 of 'assert', which has type 'String'; use 'String(...)' to copy a C string
    3 |     assert(false, p);
      |                   ^

main.pep:2:12: error: cannot return a value of type 'String' from 'f', which returns 'int'
    2 |     return "a";
      |            ^~~

A struct used as a trait it does not declare (see Traits as types):

main.pep:11:20: error: 'Circle' does not conform to trait 'Shape'
   11 |     var s: Shape = Circle();
      |                    ^~~~~~
main.pep:6:8: note: declare it with 'extend Circle with Shape'
    6 | struct Circle {
      |        ^~~~~~

A value that is not thread-safe given to another thread (see Threads): here a thread body, a shared function value, that captures a String:

main.pep:5:46: error: closure passed as 'shared () => void' captures 'name' of type 'String', which is not thread-safe
    5 |     var t = async.Thread.spawn(() => { print(name); });
      |                                              ^~~~
main.pep:4:9: note: capture a thread-safe value instead, such as an 'async.Atomic<T>' or a '[Shared]' struct
    4 |     var name = "worker";
      |         ^~~~

The same name declared twice in one scope:

main.pep:3:9: error: redefinition of 'n'
    3 |     var n = 2;
      |         ^
main.pep:2:9: note: previous definition is here
    2 |     var n = 1;
      |         ^

Looping over something that cannot be iterated (see Iteration):

main.pep:3:19: error: type 'int' is not iterable: implement Iterable<T> (iterate()) or Iterator<T> (next() and current())
    3 |     for (var i in 5) {
      |                   ^

An import that names nothing (see Modules and imports):

main.pep:1:8: error: cannot find "nope.pep" or the module folder "nope" next to this file
    1 | import "nope";
      |        ^~~~~~

Code nested too deeply. Parentheses, blocks, calls, and each operator of a chain (a + b + c is two levels) nest the program one level deeper, and a file may nest at most 256 levels. The error points at the token that crosses the limit, here the 255th + of a long sum:

main.pep:2:1030: error: code is nested too deeply: the limit is 256 levels; split it into smaller expressions or functions
    2 |     return 0 + 1 + 1 + ... + 1;
      |                             ^

Split the expression into steps (var part = ...;), or move the inner part into a function.

Errors while the program runs
