Some problems can only be found while the program runs, such as an array index out of range or a failed assert. These are not compiler errors: the program prints a message and stops immediately (it aborts, so it exits with a failure status instead of returning from main). See assert and panic.

Current limitations

The type check does not compare the type arguments of generic structs yet, so Array<int> a = Array<String>(); compiles. Read such code carefully: the resulting program has undefined behavior.

Deprecation

When an API is on its way out, mark it [Deprecated("message")]. Code that uses it still compiles, but every use gets a warning that shows your message, the same way clang reports [[deprecated]]. That gives the code that depends on the API time to move before you remove it.

struct Temperature {
    int celsius;

    # A method on its way out: it still works, but every call warns.
    [Deprecated("use 'fahrenheit' instead", "fahrenheit")]
    to_f(): int { return fahrenheit(); }

    fahrenheit(): int { return celsius * 9 / 5 + 32; }
}

# The second argument names the replacement: the warning carries a fix that
# renames the call.
[Deprecated("use 'boiling' instead", "boiling")]
boiling_point(): Temperature { return boiling(); }

boiling(): Temperature {
    var t = Temperature();
    t.celsius = 100;
    return t;
}

main(): int {
    # Both calls warn, and both still work.
    var old = boiling_point();
    assert(old.to_f() == 212, "the old API still works");

    var t = boiling();
    assert(t.fahrenheit() == 212, "100 C is 212 F");
    return 0;
}

Compiling this prints a warning at each use of a deprecated name, with a note at its declaration. The second of the two is:

main.pep:25:16: warning: 'to_f' is deprecated: use 'fahrenheit' instead [deprecated]
   25 |     assert(old.to_f() == 212, "the old API still works");
      |                ^~~~
      |                fahrenheit
main.pep:6:5: note: 'to_f' declared here
    6 |     to_f(): int { return fahrenheit(); }
      |     ^~~~

Warnings never stop the build. The program above compiles and runs.

The replacement

The attribute takes an optional second argument: the name that replaces the deprecated one.

[Deprecated("use 'copy' instead", "copy")]
clone(): Counter { ... }

With a replacement, the warning comes with a fix that renames the use. The compiler shows the new name under the old one, as in the warning above, and the language server offers the rename as a quick fix. The fix only renames, so give a replacement only when the new declaration can be used the same way. Otherwise leave it out and explain the change in the message.

An empty message is allowed. The warning then says only 'name' is deprecated.

What it applies to

Put [Deprecated(...)] before any declaration other code refers to by name:

  • a function or an extern
  • a struct, a trait, or a type alias
  • a module-scope variable
  • a field, a method, or a constructor of a struct
  • a method in a trait or in an extension (put it on each method, not on the extend block)

A doc comment goes above the attribute, as it does for any attribute.

Which uses warn

Every use of the declaration warns, at the name you wrote:

  • a call, a reference to a function or variable, or a construction S() (a deprecated constructor is reported at the struct’s name)
  • a type name, anywhere a type is written
  • a member access x.name, a method call x.name(), a static call S.name(), and a bare field or method name inside the struct’s own methods
  • an entry in an import list, import [name] from m, and a qualified use m.name, where the warning points at name

These do not warn:

  • the declaration itself
  • a use inside a declaration that is deprecated too, including the methods of a deprecated struct and closures written inside a deprecated function, so old code can keep calling old code without noise
  • a re-export, export name as other or export [name] from source, which passes the name on without using it

Mistakes in the attribute

A malformed attribute is an error at the attribute:

main.pep:1:1: error: 'Deprecated' expects a message string: [Deprecated("message")]
    1 | [Deprecated]
      | ^~~~~~~~~~~~

The other errors are 'Deprecated' expects the replacement as a string, the replacement 'a b' is not a name, too many arguments to 'Deprecated': expected at most 2, have 3, duplicate 'Deprecated' attribute, and 'Deprecated' cannot be applied to an extension or a destructor.

Limitations

  • The compiler does not report uses it writes for you: the next() and current() calls of a for loop, the enter() call of a with block, and a call to an operator overload such as a + b.
  • The language server shows the warnings for the file you are editing. It does not show them for other files the program imports.

Documentation comments

Comments explain code to the people who read it. Pepper has one comment syntax, #, and a convention on top of it for documentation: lines starting with ## directly above a declaration document that declaration. Your editor shows them when you hover over a use of the name, and the standard library reference in this book is generated from them.

Comments

A comment starts with # and runs to the end of the line. It can take a whole line or follow code:

# Count the lines that are not blank.
var count = 0;   # blank lines are skipped below

Pepper has no block comment syntax: to comment out several lines, start each with #. (// is not a comment in Pepper.)

Doc comments

A doc comment is a run of consecutive lines that start with ##, directly above the declaration it documents:

## Returns the larger of `a` and `b`.
##
## @param a the first value
## @param b the second value
## @returns `a` when it is at least `b`, otherwise `b`
larger(a: int, b: int): int {
    return a >= b ? a : b;
}
  • The text of each line is what follows ## . A line that is just ## is a blank line in the documentation, which separates paragraphs.
  • The comment must sit directly above the declaration, with no blank line in between. Attributes and export or static may come between the comment and the declaration, so put the comment above the attributes.
  • Only lines that start with exactly two # count. A single # is an ordinary comment, and a line starting with three or more, such as a decorative #######, is not documentation.
  • A doc comment works on functions, structs, traits, extensions, type aliases, module-scope variables, and the fields, constructors and methods inside a struct, trait or extension.

What to write

Start with a description: what the declaration does, in the third person (“Returns …”, “Appends …”), followed by what a caller needs to know, such as edge cases, who owns what, how long it takes, and differences between platforms. The description is Markdown, so put code in backticks.

After the description come tags, each starting a line with @. A tag’s text runs until the next tag.

TagUse it for
@typeParam T descriptioneach generic parameter of a generic struct, trait, type alias or function
@param name descriptioneach parameter of a function, method or constructor
@returns descriptionwhat the function returns, whenever it returns a value
@panics descriptioneach way a caller can make the function panic (a failed assert, a call to panic)
@examplesample code, indented on the lines that follow; line breaks are kept
@see namea related declaration
@note texta remark that does not fit elsewhere

Write tag descriptions like clang writes errors: lowercase start, no trailing period. A field or a type alias usually needs only one line: ## The number of bytes in the buffer.

Keep notes that matter only to the people maintaining the code in ordinary # comments inside the body. The doc comment is the contract with callers.

Here is a small documented library:

# A small library, documented the way the standard library is.
# This line and the one above are ordinary comments: they start with a
# single '#'. Doc comments start with '##'.

## A last-in, first-out collection.
##
## Elements come out in the reverse of the order they went in.
##
## @typeParam T the type of the elements
## @example
##     var s = Stack<int>();
##     s.push(1);
##     s.push(2);
##     var top = s.pop();   # top == 2
struct Stack<T> {
    ## The elements, bottom first.
    var items: Array<T> = Array<T>();

    ## Adds `value` on top of the stack.
    ##
    ## @param value the element to add
    push(value: T) {
        items.append(value);
    }

    ## Removes and returns the element on top of the stack.
    ##
    ## @returns the element that was pushed last
    ## @panics if the stack is empty
    ## @see Stack.push
    pop(): T {
        assert(items.count() > 0, "pop() on an empty Stack");
        return items.remove_at(items.count() - 1);
    }

    ## Returns the number of elements.
    ##
    ## @returns how many elements the stack holds
    count(): ulong {
        return items.count();
    }
}

## Returns the larger of `a` and `b`.
##
## @param a the first value
## @param b the second value
## @returns `a` when it is at least `b`, otherwise `b`
## @note ties return `a`
larger(a: int, b: int): int {
    # An implementation note for maintainers, not part of the docs.
    return a >= b ? a : b;
}

main(): int {
    var s = Stack<int>();
    s.push(1);
    s.push(2);
    assert(s.pop() == 2, "the last element comes out first");
    assert(s.count() == 1, "one element is left");
    assert(larger(3, 7) == 7, "larger returns the larger value");
    return 0;
}

Where doc comments appear

  • In your editor. The Pepper language server shows a declaration’s doc comment when you hover over its name, anywhere it is used. The description comes first, followed by sections for the type parameters, parameters, return value, panics, related declarations, notes and examples.
  • In the standard library reference. The reference pages are generated from the doc comments in the runtime, one page per runtime file. A ## block at the very top of a file, followed by a blank line, introduces that file’s page. Building this documentation explains how to regenerate them.

The standard library is fully documented

Every public declaration in the runtime must have a doc comment: every exported declaration whose name does not start with _, and every field, constructor and method of such a struct, trait or extension whose name does not start with _. Names starting with _ are internals shared between runtime files and are exempt.

A test enforces this, and reports a clang-style error for each gap: a missing doc comment, a comment with no description, a missing @param, @typeParam or @returns, a tag with no description, a @returns on a function that returns nothing, or a @param naming a parameter that does not exist. If you contribute to the runtime, run the test suite before you send a change. The compiler does not check the doc comments in your own programs, but following the same format gets you the same editor support.

Naming conventions

Pepper code, including the standard library, follows one set of naming rules. The compiler does not enforce them, but every example in this book, the runtime, and the tools in this repository follow them, and code you contribute should too.

WhatStyleExamples
Structs, traits, type aliasesPascalCaseString, HashMap, IoResult
Generic parametersone capital letter, or PascalCaseT, K, V, TValue, TError
Data members (fields)snake_caseunit_name, is_file
Methods and free functionssnake_caseappend, remove_at, read_to_string
Parameters and local variablessnake_casecapacity, best_so_far
Constants (a const holding a fixed value)SCREAMING_CASEMAX_REQUESTS, LINE_WIDTH
Other module-scope variablessnake_caserequest_count
Private data members and methods_ then snake_case_readings, _is_empty
 
# Types are PascalCase; acronyms are written as words (`HttpClient`, not `HTTPClient`).
struct TemperatureLog {
    # Public data members are snake_case.
    var unit_name: String = "celsius";
    # Private data members start with `_`.
    var _readings: Array<int> = Array<int>();
    var _total: int = 0;

    # Methods and their parameters are snake_case.
    add_reading(degrees: int) {
        _readings.append(degrees);
        _total = _total + degrees;
    }

    average(): int {
        return _is_empty() ? 0 : _total / (_readings.count() as int);
    }

    # A private method starts with `_` too.
    _is_empty(): bool {
        return _readings.count() == 0;
    }
}

# Generic parameters are a single capital letter or PascalCase.
struct Pair<TFirst, TSecond> {
    var first: TFirst;
    var second: TSecond;

    construct(TFirst first, TSecond second) {
        this.first = first;
        this.second = second;
    }
}

# Free functions and local variables are snake_case.
largest_of<T>(values: Array<T>): T {
    var best_so_far = values[0];
    for (var value in values) {
        if (value > best_so_far) {
            best_so_far = value;
        }
    }
    return best_so_far;
}

main(): int {
    var log = TemperatureLog();
    log.add_reading(20);
    log.add_reading(24);
    assert(log.average() == 22, "average of the readings");
    assert(log.unit_name == "celsius", "public member");

    var pair = Pair<String, int>("answer", 42);
    assert(pair.second == 42, "generic struct");

    var numbers = Array<int>();
    numbers.append(3);
    numbers.append(9);
    numbers.append(4);
    assert(largest_of<int>(numbers) == 9, "generic function");
    return 0;
}

Types

A type name is PascalCase: each word starts with a capital letter, and there are no underscores. Write an acronym as a word, so IoError and HttpClient, not IOError or HTTPClient.

An enum’s cases are PascalCase too (Color.Red, Status.NotFound).

A generic parameter is either a single capital letter (T, U, K, V) or a PascalCase name, which by convention starts with T (TValue, TError). Use a single letter when the parameter’s role is obvious, and a name when a declaration has several parameters that a reader has to tell apart.

Members, functions, and variables

Everything else a program names is snake_case: lowercase words joined by underscores. That covers a struct’s data members, its methods, free functions, parameters, local variables, and module-scope variables.

The exception is a constant: a const, at module scope or in a function, whose value is fixed, such as a number, string, or character. Its name is SCREAMING_CASE, uppercase words joined by underscores (MAX_REQUESTS, LINE_WIDTH). A module-scope const that holds an object, such as const request_count = async.Atomic<int>(0);, is a variable and stays snake_case.

Spell words out. A name is read far more often than it is typed, so prefer iterate, index, and directory to iter, idx, and dir. Keep an abbreviation only when it is the usual name for the thing, such as io or c_str.

An extern declaration keeps the name the C library gives the function, whatever its style (GetCurrentProcessId), because that name is what the linker looks up. The same goes for the fields of a struct that mirrors a C struct.

Private members

Pepper has no member-level private keyword; any code that can reach an object can name all of its members. A leading _ marks a data member or method as private to its struct instead: code outside the struct, and its extensions, should not use it. The rest of the name is snake_case, as for a public member (_readings, _is_empty).

The standard library relies on this convention: its generated reference leaves _ members out, and doc comments are required only on members without the prefix.

A top-level declaration does not need the prefix to be private: it is private to its file unless it is exported (see Visibility). The runtime also uses the prefix on top-level helpers that its own files export to each other, such as _pep_malloc: they are not part of its public API, and the reference leaves them out too.

Formatting with pep-fmt

pep-fmt rewrites Pepper source in one standard style, so that every Pepper file reads the same and nobody has to argue about layout. It changes only whitespace, line breaks, the order of imports, and the form of function declarations; the program means exactly what it meant before.

pep-fmt is written in Pepper. Its parser is a separate library, tools/syntax, that other tools can use.

Running it

Build it with the compiler, with the tools folder on the import path:

pepper -I tools tools/pep-fmt/main.pep -o pep-fmt

Give it files or directories, like gofmt:

pep-fmt main.pep            # print the formatted file to standard output
pep-fmt -w main.pep src/    # rewrite each file that is not formatted
pep-fmt --check src/        # list each file that is not formatted
pep-fmt < main.pep          # no files: standard input to standard output

A directory stands for every .pep file under it, in name order, skipping directories whose names start with . (such as .git and the .pep build cache). -w rewrites only the files whose formatting changes. --check changes nothing, prints the path of each file that -w would rewrite, and exits with status 1 if there is one, which suits a CI step. The two can be combined.

If a file does not parse, pep-fmt leaves it untouched, prints the first syntax error to standard error, and exits with status 1 after the other files. Standard input is named <stdin>:

main.pep:2:14: error: expected ')'

A file that cannot be read or written also exits with status 1, and an unknown option exits with status 2 after printing the usage (pep-fmt -h prints it too).

The style

Layout. Indentation is 4 spaces. A brace goes on the same line as the declaration or statement that owns it, and else goes between the braces:

if count > 0 {
    print(count);
} else {
    print("none");
}

A block stays on one line only when it holds a single break, continue or return and was written on one line: if done { return; }.

Line width. Lines are at most 120 columns. A list that does not fit (arguments, parameters, an import list) moves to its own indented line, and if it still does not fit, puts one item on each line:

report_values(
    first_argument, second_argument, third_argument, fourth_argument, fifth_argument, a_much_longer_argument
);
report_values(
    first_argument,
    second_argument,
    an_argument_so_long_that_the_whole_list_no_longer_fits_on_one_line_even_after_moving_it_down_one
);

A long expression breaks before each operator, and a chain of three or more method calls that does not fit breaks before each .:

if (first_condition_that_is_long(value) and second_condition_that_is_long(value)
    or third_condition_that_is_long(value)) {
    run();
}
total = first_value_that_is_long_enough
    + second_value_that_is_long_enough
    + third_value_that_is_long_and_longer_still;
var count = words
    .iterate()
    .filter((w) => w.length() > 4)
    .map((w) => w.length() * 2)
    .count_them_all();

Comments and string literals are never reflowed, so a line can stay longer than 120 columns when it has nowhere to break.

Attributes go one per line, each on its own line above the declaration:

[Target(OS(Linux))]
[Deprecated("use 'open' instead", "open")]
export open_file(path: String): int { return 0; }

A parameter’s attributes are the exception: they stay on the parameter’s line, in front of it, as in construct([Sending] T value).

Declarations. Pepper functions and methods are written with the parameter types after the names and the return type last, add(a: int, b: int): int. The C-style form, int add(int a, int b), is kept for extern functions, which mirror C prototypes; pep-fmt rewrites it everywhere else, including operator methods (bool ==(Point other) becomes ==(other: Point): bool, and bool !!() becomes !!(): bool), indexers (T [](ulong index) becomes [](index: ulong): T) and constructor parameters. A void return type is left out when the function has a body (void run() and run(): void both become run()); a declaration without a body, such as a trait method, keeps it.

Blank lines. At most one blank line in a row. Top-level structs, traits, extensions and functions with a body are separated by one blank line.

Comments stay where they are, attached to the code next to them. Trailing comments on consecutive lines are aligned, two spaces after the longest line:

var total = 0;      # the running sum
var count = 0;      # how many values
var average = 0.0;  # total / count

Imports that are next to each other (no blank line or comment between them) are sorted: modules first (import io;), then files of this module (import "util";), each by name.

Kept as written: parentheses around conditions (if x and if (x) are both fine), fields declared either way (int x; or var x: int;), and the file’s line endings (\n or \r\n).

Turning it off for a section

Code between a # format: off comment and a # format: on comment is left exactly as written, for layouts the style would undo, such as a table of numbers:

# format: off
const IDENTITY = matrix(1, 0, 0,
                        0, 1, 0,
                        0, 0, 1);
# format: on

Each comment goes on its own line, between declarations or statements, and the pair must be in the same block (or both at the top level). Without a # format: on, the region runs to the end of the block or file.

Standard library reference

The standard library is the Pepper runtime: the files under runtime/ that every program is compiled with. Everything here is available without an import, except the io module, which a program brings in with import io (or import [File, Path] from io).

These pages are generated from the doc comments in the runtime’s source (see Documentation comments), so they always match the version of Pepper they were built with. Use the version picker at the top of the page to read the reference for another release.

Built-in functions

Source: runtime/internals.pep

assert

assert(condition: bool, message: String)

Panics with message when condition is false; otherwise does nothing.

The check always runs; there is no release mode that removes it. A string literal message picks the __ptr<char> overload instead, which builds no String. Any other message is evaluated before the call.

Parameters

  • condition — the condition that must hold
  • message — the text to print on failure; a null String prints a generic message

Panics

  • if condition is false: prints message and aborts (see panic)

Example

    assert(count > 0, "count must be positive");

assert

assert(condition: bool, message: __ptr<char>)

Checks that condition holds; if not, panics with message, a NUL-terminated C string. A string literal message picks this overload, so an assertion that holds builds no String.

Parameters

  • condition — the condition that must hold
  • message — the text to print on failure, or __null for a generic message

Panics

  • if condition is false: prints message and aborts (see panic)

Example

    assert(count > 0, "count must be positive");

panic

panic(message: String)

Prints message and aborts the program. It never returns.

Writes message and a newline to standard output, or “Assertion failed with no additional information” when message is null. Then it flushes every C output stream, so the message is not lost when stdout is a pipe, and calls C abort(). No destructors or releases run, and the process ends abnormally (SIGABRT on POSIX).

Parameters

  • message — the text to print

Panics

  • always

Example

    panic("unreachable");

panic

panic(message: __ptr<char>)

Writes message, a NUL-terminated C string, and a newline to standard output (a generic message when it is __null), flushes every C output stream, and aborts, as panic(String) does. A string literal message picks this overload, so it allocates nothing.

Parameters

  • message — the text to print, or __null

Panics

  • always

Example

    panic("unreachable");

Arguments and exit

The running program: its command-line arguments and how it ends.

Source: runtime/process.pep

arguments

arguments(): Array<String>

Returns the program’s command-line arguments.

Element 0 is the program as it was started (usually its path), and the arguments typed after it follow in order, as the shell passed them: a quoted argument with spaces is one element. Each call builds a new array.

On Windows the arguments are in the process’s ANSI code page, so text outside it is not preserved.

main receives the same array when it is declared main(args: String[]): int; arguments() reads it anywhere else.

Returns

  • the program name followed by its arguments

Example

    verbose(): bool {
        for (var argument in arguments()) {
            if (argument == "-v") {
                return true;
            }
        }
        return false;
    }

exit

exit(code: int)

Ends the program at once with status code.

Flushes standard output and every other C output stream first, so text printed so far is not lost. Nothing else runs: locals are not released, destructors do not run, and other threads stop where they are. Returning from main is the usual way to end; exit is for ending from deep inside a call.

Parameters

  • code — the exit status: 0 for success, anything else for failure (only its low 8 bits reach a POSIX parent)

Example

    if (arguments().count() < 2) {
        print("usage: tool FILE");
        exit(2);
    }

String

Source: runtime/string.pep

String

struct String

A mutable, reference-counted string of UTF-8 text. String literals ("text") are String values.

Two measures describe a String, and each API says which one it uses:

  • Code points (Unicode characters): length(), empty(), the indexer s[i], substr, and iteration.
  • Bytes of UTF-8: size(), find, starts_with, and ends_with. The byte size is the authoritative length, so the data may contain NUL bytes. It is never derived from a terminator.

A String is a reference type: var b = a; shares one object, so append, +=, and grow are visible through every reference. Use copy() or + for an independent copy. Equality (==) compares content.

A StringIterator panics when the String has been changed by append, +=, or grow since the iterator was created, so modifying a String while a for loop iterates it panics.

To build text from values, use an interpolated string ($"{name}: {count:>4}") or String.format("{0}: {1:>4}", name, count), a compiler intrinsic whose braces name its arguments by position (see the String interpolation chapter).

Example

    var s = "héllo";
    assert(s.length() == 5, "5 code points");
    assert(s.size() == 6, "6 bytes: 'é' is 2");
    s.append(" world");
    assert(s.find("world") == 7, "find returns a byte offset");
    assert(s[1] == "é", "the indexer counts code points");
    for (var c in s) {
        print(c);   # one code point per line
    }

Constructor

String()

construct(data: __ptr<char> = __null, size: ulong = 0, length: ulong = 0)

Creates a String by copying size bytes of data into a new NUL-terminated buffer. With no arguments, it creates an empty String whose c_str() is __null.

When data is not __null and size is 0, data is treated as a NUL-terminated C string:

  • with length nonzero, size becomes the byte length of its first length code points (0 if the C string is not valid UTF-8);
  • with length 0, size becomes the C string’s whole byte length.

When length is 0, it is counted from the bytes. A nonzero length is trusted, not checked against the data. Runs in O(size).

Parameters

  • data — the bytes to copy; __null for an empty String (then pass no sizes, because they are stored as given)
  • size — the number of bytes to copy from data; 0 treats data as a NUL-terminated C string
  • length — the number of code points in those bytes

Example

    var empty = String();
    var s = "abc";
    var copy = String(s.c_str(), s.size(), s.length());

Static methods

length_of

static length_of(data: __ptr<char>, size: ulong): ulong

Returns the number of Unicode code points in the first size bytes at data. Runs in O(size).

Returns 0 when data is __null, when size is 0, or when the bytes are not valid UTF-8: any malformed or truncated sequence makes the whole count 0.

Parameters

  • data — the UTF-8 bytes to measure
  • size — the number of bytes to measure

Returns

  • the number of code points, or 0 for invalid UTF-8

Methods

bytes

bytes(): u8[]

Returns a new array holding the String’s UTF-8 bytes, without a terminating NUL. Runs in O(size()).

Returns

  • a new array of size() bytes

Example

    var data = "hi".bytes();
    assert(data.count() == 2 && data[0] == 104, "the bytes of 'h' and 'i'");

length

length(): ulong

Returns the number of Unicode code points. O(1).

Returns

  • the length in code points, not bytes

See also

  • size

grow

grow(new_size: ulong)

Extends the byte buffer to new_size bytes and fills the new bytes with zeros. Does nothing when new_size is not greater than size().

A low-level primitive for append. It updates size() but not length(), so the zero bytes it adds are not counted as code points until the caller overwrites them and fixes the length. When it grows the buffer, it invalidates running iterators and may reallocate the buffer, which invalidates pointers from c_str(). Runs in O(new_size).

Parameters

  • new_size — the new byte length

append

append(rhs: String)

Appends the content of rhs to this String in place, updating size() and length().

Always invalidates running iterators, even when rhs is empty, so appending during iteration panics. It may reallocate the buffer. Every reference to this String sees the change. Runs in O(size() + rhs.size()).

Parameters

  • rhs — the String to append; it is not modified

Example

    var s = "TEST";
    s.append("ING");   # s == "TESTING"

operator []

[](idx: int): String

Returns the code point at code-point index idx as a new one-code-point String.

A negative idx counts from the end (s[-1] is the last code point). length() is added until the index is non-negative, so any negative index wraps, and s[-7] of a 3-code-point String is s[2]. Runs in O(idx) because it walks the UTF-8 bytes. Use for (var c in s) to visit every code point in O(size).

Parameters

  • idx — the code-point index; negative counts from the end

Returns

  • a new String that holds the one code point

Panics

  • if idx is not less than length() after the negative index is normalized, which includes any index into an empty String

Example

    var s = "TEST";
    assert(s[0] == "T", "first");
    assert(s[-1] == "T", "last");

operator ==

==(rhs: String): bool

Returns whether this String and rhs have the same content, compared byte by byte. Strings with different length() are unequal without comparing bytes. Runs in O(size()).

Parameters

  • rhs — the String to compare with

Returns

  • true when both hold the same bytes

operator +=

+=(rhs: String): String

Appends rhs in place, like append, and returns this same String, not a copy. s += t modifies the object that every reference to s shares, and invalidates running iterators.

Parameters

  • rhs — the String to append

Returns

  • this String, after appending

Example

    var s = "a";
    s += "b";   # s == "ab"

size

size(): ulong

Returns the number of bytes of UTF-8, not counting the NUL terminator. O(1).

Returns

  • the length in bytes, not code points

See also

  • length

iterate

iterate(): StringIterator

Returns an iterator over the String’s code points, which makes String Iterable<String>: for (var c in s) visits each code point as a one-code-point String, the same value s[i] gives.

The iterator holds a reference to this String. The whole loop runs in O(size). Modifying the String during iteration makes the iterator panic.

Returns

  • a new iterator, positioned before the first code point

Example

    var n = 0;
    for (var c in "héllo") {
        n = n + 1;   # 5 iterations
    }

empty

empty(): bool

Returns whether the String has no code points. O(1).

Returns

  • true when length() is 0

c_str

c_str(): __ptr<char>

Returns the String’s buffer as a NUL-terminated C string.

The pointer is owned by the String. It is valid until the String is destroyed or append, +=, or grow reallocates it. It is __null for a String built with no data (String()), so check it before you pass it to C. C functions stop at the first NUL byte in the content.

Returns

  • the String’s NUL-terminated byte buffer, or __null

copy

copy(copies: Copies = __null): String

Returns a new String with the same content and its own buffer, so later changes to either String do not affect the other. Runs in O(size()).

This is also how copy(value) copies a String (the Copyable<String> implementation), which passes copies.

Parameters

  • copies — the objects copied so far, when copy(value) calls it; a String holds no other objects, so it is not used

Returns

  • an independent copy of this String

Example

    var a = "abc";
    var b = a.copy();
    b.append("d");   # a is still "abc"

clone

[Deprecated("use 'copy' instead", "copy")] clone(): String

Deprecated: use copy instead. Returns a new String with the same content and its own buffer.

Returns

  • an independent copy of this String

find

find(needle: String): long

Returns the byte offset of the first occurrence of needle, or -1 when it does not occur.

The offset counts bytes, not code points. To use it with s[i] or substr, convert it with String.length_of(s.c_str(), offset). An empty needle is found at 0 unless this String is empty, in which case the result is -1. The result is also -1 when either String is not valid UTF-8. Runs in O(size() * needle.size()).

Parameters

  • needle — the text to search for

Returns

  • the byte offset of the first match, or -1 when there is none

Example

    var s = "TESTING";
    assert(s.find("STI") == 2, "byte offset");
    assert(s.find("xyz") == -1, "absent");

contains

contains(needle: String): bool

Returns whether needle occurs in this String (find(needle) >= 0). Because of that, an empty String contains nothing, not even "". Runs in O(size() * needle.size()).

Parameters

  • needle — the text to search for

Returns

  • true when needle occurs

starts_with

starts_with(prefix: String): bool

Returns whether this String begins with the bytes of prefix. An empty prefix always matches. Runs in O(prefix.size()).

Parameters

  • prefix — the text to test for

Returns

  • true when the first prefix.size() bytes equal prefix

ends_with

ends_with(suffix: String): bool

Returns whether this String ends with the bytes of suffix. An empty suffix always matches. Runs in O(suffix.size()).

Parameters

  • suffix — the text to test for

Returns

  • true when the last suffix.size() bytes equal suffix

substr

substr(start: ulong, count: ulong): String

Returns a new String of up to count code points starting at code-point index start. Both arguments count code points, not bytes.

count is clamped to the code points that remain. When start is at or past length(), the result is an empty String. Runs in O(size()).

Parameters

  • start — the code-point index of the first code point to copy
  • count — the maximum number of code points to copy

Returns

  • a new String that holds the selected code points

Example

    var s = "TEST";
    assert(s.substr(1, 2) == "ES", "middle");
    assert(s.substr(0, 99) == "TEST", "count is clamped");
    assert(s.substr(4, 5) == "", "start past the end");

operator !=

!=(rhs: String): bool

Returns whether this String and rhs differ in content, the negation of ==. Runs in O(size()).

Parameters

  • rhs — the String to compare with

Returns

  • true when the contents differ

operator +

+(rhs: String): String

Returns a new String that holds this String followed by rhs. Neither operand is modified. Runs in O(size() + rhs.size()).

Parameters

  • rhs — the String to append to the copy

Returns

  • a new concatenated String

Example

    var greeting = "Hello, " + "world";

to_string

to_string(): String

Returns this String, so a String is ToString and can be interpolated ($"name: {name}"). The result is the same object, not a copy. O(1).

Returns

  • this String

byte_at

byte_at(index: ulong): byte

Returns the byte at byte offset index of the UTF-8 data. O(1).

The offset counts bytes, not code points, so a byte inside a multi-byte code point is returned as it is. Compare the result with a character literal (s.byte_at(0) == '#').

Parameters

  • index — the byte offset, less than size()

Returns

  • the byte at index

Panics

  • if index is not less than size() (“String byte_at index out of bounds”)

Example

    var s = "a=b";
    assert(s.byte_at(1) == '=', "second byte");

substr_bytes

substr_bytes(start: ulong, size: ulong): String

Returns a new String of the size bytes starting at byte offset start. Both arguments count bytes, not code points, so offsets from find can be used directly. Runs in O(size).

Parameters

  • start — the byte offset of the first byte to copy
  • size — the number of bytes to copy

Returns

  • a new String that holds those bytes

Panics

  • if start + size is greater than size() (“String substr_bytes range out of bounds”)
  • if start or start + size falls inside a multi-byte code point (“String substr_bytes splits a code point”)

Example

    var s = "key=value";
    var eq = s.find("=") as ulong;
    assert(s.substr_bytes(0, eq) == "key", "before '='");
    assert(s.substr_bytes(eq + 1, s.size() - eq - 1) == "value", "after '='");

compare

compare(other: String): int

Compares this String with other byte by byte, for sorting. For valid UTF-8 this is code-point order; a String that is a prefix of the other orders first. Runs in O(min(size(), other.size())).

Parameters

  • other — the String to compare with

Returns

  • a negative number when this String orders before other, 0 when both hold the same bytes, and a positive number when it orders after

Example

    assert("apple".compare("banana") < 0, "a before b");
    assert("ab".compare("abc") < 0, "a prefix orders first");
    assert("x".compare("x") == 0, "equal");

operator <

<(other: String): bool

Returns whether this String orders before other, as compare does.

Parameters

  • other — the String to compare with

Returns

  • true when compare(other) < 0

operator <=

<=(other: String): bool

Returns whether this String orders before other or equals it, as compare does.

Parameters

  • other — the String to compare with

Returns

  • true when compare(other) <= 0

operator >

>(other: String): bool

Returns whether this String orders after other, as compare does.

Parameters

  • other — the String to compare with

Returns

  • true when compare(other) > 0

operator >=

>=(other: String): bool

Returns whether this String orders after other or equals it, as compare does.

Parameters

  • other — the String to compare with

Returns

  • true when compare(other) >= 0

trim_end

trim_end(): String

Returns a new String without the whitespace at the end: spaces, tabs, carriage returns, line feeds, vertical tabs and form feeds (ASCII only). Runs in O(size()).

Returns

  • a new String with the trailing whitespace removed

Example

    assert("code;  \r\n".trim_end() == "code;", "trailing whitespace");
    assert("  indented".trim_end() == "  indented", "leading kept");

trim_start

trim_start(): String

Returns a new String without the whitespace at the start: spaces, tabs, carriage returns, line feeds, vertical tabs and form feeds (ASCII only). Runs in O(size()).

Returns

  • a new String with the leading whitespace removed

Example

    assert("  \tcode".trim_start() == "code", "leading whitespace");

trim

trim(): String

Returns a new String without the whitespace at either end, as trim_start and trim_end do. Runs in O(size()).

Returns

  • a new String with the leading and trailing whitespace removed

Example

    assert(" \t value \r\n".trim() == "value", "both ends");

lower

lower(): String

Returns a new String with the ASCII letters A to Z changed to a to z. Every other character, including non-ASCII letters, is kept as it is, so the result is valid UTF-8 of the same size. Runs in O(size()).

Returns

  • a new String in lowercase

Example

    assert("Content-Type".lower() == "content-type", "ASCII lowered");
    assert("Ärger".lower() == "Ärger", "non-ASCII kept");

upper

upper(): String

Returns a new String with the ASCII letters a to z changed to A to Z. Every other character, including non-ASCII letters, is kept as it is, so the result is valid UTF-8 of the same size. Runs in O(size()).

Returns

  • a new String in uppercase

Example

    assert("get".upper() == "GET", "ASCII raised");

lines

lines(): String[]

Splits the String into lines and returns them without their line endings. A line ends at "\n" or "\r\n". A final line with no ending is included, but the end of the String after a final line ending does not start another line, so "a\nb\n" and "a\nb" both give ["a", "b"], and "" gives no lines. Runs in O(size()).

Returns

  • a new Array with one new String per line

Example

    var lines = "first\r\nsecond\n\nfourth".lines();
    assert(lines.count() == 4, "four lines");
    assert(lines[1] == "second", "\\r\\n removed");
    assert(lines[2] == "", "an empty line");

repeat

repeat(count: ulong): String

Returns a new String that holds this String count times in a row. count 0, or an empty String, gives an empty String. Runs in O(size() * count).

Parameters

  • count — how many copies to join

Returns

  • a new String of size() * count bytes

Example

    assert("ab".repeat(3) == "ababab", "three copies");
    var indent = " ".repeat(8);   # eight spaces

to_string

to_string(value: long): String

Returns the decimal text of value, with a leading - when it is negative.

to_string is overloaded for every integer type, so a call with any integer picks its own overload.

Parameters

  • value — the number to convert

Returns

  • a new String such as "-42"

Example

    assert(to_string(-42) == "-42", "negative");
    var where = to_string(line) + ":" + to_string(column);

to_string

to_string(value: ulong): String

Returns the decimal text of value.

Parameters

  • value — the number to convert

Returns

  • a new String such as "18446744073709551615"

to_string

Returns the decimal text of value, with a leading - when it is negative.

Parameters

  • value — the number to convert

Returns

Returns the decimal text of value.

Parameters

Returns

Returns the decimal text of value, with a leading - when it is negative.

Returns the decimal text of value.

  • value — the value to convert

to_string

to_string<T>(value: T): String

Returns the text of value by calling its to_string() method: the overload for any type that is ToString.

Declare a concrete override for a type that has no to_string() method of its own, or whose interpolated text should differ from it; like hash<Point>, an override is used by the whole program, including interpolated strings.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of value; it must have a to_string() method unless an override to_string<T> exists

Parameters

  • value — the value to convert

Returns

  • the String that value.to_string() returns

Example

    struct Point {
        var x: int = 0;
        var y: int = 0;
        construct(this.x = 0, this.y = 0) {}
    }

    to_string<Point>(value: Point): String {
        var x = value.x;
        var y = value.y;
        return $"({x}, {y})";
    }

ToString

trait ToString

Something with a text form: a to_string() method returning a String.

An interpolated string ($"total: {a + b}") converts each value it holds with to_string(value), so a struct that implements ToString can be interpolated, as can the integers, bool, and String, which have to_string overloads. String, StringBuilder and io.Path implement it.

Example

    struct Point {
        var x: int = 0;
        var y: int = 0;
        construct(this.x = 0, this.y = 0) {}
    }

    extend Point with ToString {
        to_string(): String {
            return $"({x}, {y})";
        }
    }

    var p = Point(1, 2);
    assert($"p = {p}" == "p = (1, 2)", "interpolated");

Methods

to_string

to_string(): String

Returns the text of this value.

Returns

  • a String

StringBuilder

struct StringBuilder

Builds a String from many pieces without copying the text built so far on every append.

String.append grows its buffer to the exact new size, so a long run of appends can copy the text repeatedly. A StringBuilder doubles its buffer when it is full, so appending is amortized O(piece size). Call to_string() for the result; the builder can keep appending afterward.

Example

    var out = StringBuilder();
    out.append("line ").append(to_string(3)).append("\n");
    var text = out.to_string();   # "line 3\n"

Constructor

StringBuilder()

construct(capacity: ulong = 0)

Creates an empty StringBuilder, optionally with room for capacity bytes before it has to grow.

Parameters

  • capacity — the number of bytes to allocate up front

Methods

append

append(text: String): StringBuilder

Appends the text of text and returns this builder, so calls can be chained. Runs in amortized O(text.size()).

Parameters

  • text — the String to append; it is not modified

Returns

  • this StringBuilder

Example

    var b = StringBuilder();
    b.append("a").append("b");   # b.to_string() == "ab"

size

size(): ulong

Returns the number of bytes of UTF-8 appended so far. O(1).

Returns

  • the size in bytes

length

length(): ulong

Returns the number of code points appended so far. O(1).

Returns

  • the length in code points

empty

empty(): bool

Returns whether nothing has been appended since the builder was created or last cleared. O(1).

Returns

  • true when size() is 0

clear

clear()

Removes all the text and keeps the buffer for reuse. O(1).

to_string

to_string(): String

Returns a new String holding the text appended so far. The builder is unchanged. Runs in O(size()).

Returns

  • a new String

StringIterator

struct StringIterator

An Iterator<String> over a String’s code points, returned by String.iterate() and used by for (var c in s).

Call next() to advance, then current() for the code point it moved to. Both methods panic if the String has been modified since the iterator was created. Create it with String.iterate(): a default-constructed StringIterator() has no String to walk.

Example

    var it = "ab".iterate();
    while (it.next()) {
        print(it.current());   # "a", then "b"
    }

Methods

next

next(): bool

Advances to the next code point. Runs in O(1) per code point.

Returns false once it passes the end, and on every call after that. A malformed UTF-8 sequence is yielded, together with the rest of the bytes, as one final “code point”.

Returns

  • true when positioned on a code point, false at the end

Panics

  • if the String was modified since the iterator was created

current

current(): String

Returns the code point that the last successful next() moved to, as a new one-code-point String.

Returns

  • a new String that holds the current code point

Panics

  • if the String was modified since the iterator was created
  • if next() has not been called yet
  • if next() has returned false (the iterator is past the end)

Array

Source: runtime/array.pep

Array

struct Array<T>

A growable, contiguous, zero-indexed sequence of T values.

Elements live in one heap buffer that doubles when full (starting at 4 slots), so append is amortized O(1) and indexing is O(1). When T is a struct type, each slot holds a counted reference, exactly like a std::vector<std::shared_ptr<T>>: storing an element acquires it, overwriting or removing one releases the old occupant, and destroying the Array releases every element it still holds. Moving elements within the Array (insert, remove_at, swap, reverse) does not change their reference counts.

Array is itself a struct, so assigning it or passing it to a function shares the same Array rather than copying its elements; use clone() for an independent copy.

An Array is Iterable<T>: for (var x in a) visits each element in index order. Every mutating operation (an element store through [], append, insert, remove_at, pop, clear, a shrinking truncate, swap, and reverse of two or more elements) invalidates running iterators, and the next step of such a loop panics with “Array modified during iteration”.

Type parameters

  • T — the element type

See also

  • ArrayIterator

Example

    main(): int {
        var a = Array<int>();
        a.append(1);
        a.append(2);
        a[0] = 5;
        var total = 0;
        for (var x in a) {
            total = total + x;
        }
        return total;   # 7
    }

Constructor

Array()

construct(capacity: ulong = 0)

Creates an empty Array, optionally preallocating room for capacity elements.

With the default capacity of 0, nothing is allocated until the first element is added. Preallocating avoids the reallocations append would otherwise perform while the Array grows to a known size.

Parameters

  • capacity — the number of element slots to allocate up front; count() is still 0

Example

    var a = Array<int>(16);   # a.count() == 0, a.capacity() == 16

Methods

iterate

iterate(): ArrayIterator<T>

Returns an iterator over the elements in index order; this is what for (var x in array) calls (the Iterable<T> protocol).

The iterator holds a reference to the Array, so iterating a temporary keeps it alive for the whole loop. Modifying the Array while the iterator is in use makes the iterator’s next next() or current() panic.

Returns

  • a new iterator positioned before the first element

Example

    for (var x in a) {
        total = total + x;
    }

count

count(): ulong

Returns the number of elements in the Array.

Returns

  • the element count; 0 for an empty Array

capacity

capacity(): ulong

Returns the number of elements the Array can hold before its buffer must be reallocated.

Returns

  • the allocated slot count, which is at least count()

empty

empty(): bool

Reports whether the Array has no elements.

Returns

  • true when count() is 0

reserve

reserve(capacity: ulong)

Ensures the buffer has room for at least capacity elements, reallocating it when it is smaller.

Never shrinks the buffer: a capacity at or below the current one does nothing. Elements, their order, and their reference counts are unchanged, and running iterators stay valid. Growing copies the existing elements, which costs O(count).

Parameters

  • capacity — the minimum number of element slots required

Panics

  • if the buffer must grow while an I/O operation in a task is using it

Example

    var a = Array<int>();
    a.reserve(8);   # a.capacity() >= 8
    a.reserve(2);   # no effect: capacity never shrinks

grow

grow()

Makes room for one more element: when the buffer is full, doubles its capacity (to at least 4); otherwise does nothing.

append and insert call this themselves; callers rarely need it. Does not change the elements or invalidate iterators.

Panics

  • if the buffer must grow while an I/O operation in a task is using it

operator []

[](idx: ulong): T

Returns the element at idx; this is the indexer read a[idx].

Runs in O(1). For a struct T the result is the stored reference itself; binding it to a variable acquires it like any shared copy.

Parameters

  • idx — the zero-based position to read

Returns

  • the element at idx

Panics

  • if idx < count() does not hold (“Array index read out of bounds”)

Example

    var first = a[0];

operator []

[](idx: ulong, value: T): T

Replaces the element at idx with value; this is the indexer write a[idx] = value.

For a struct T the slot acquires value and releases its previous occupant; assigning an element to its own slot (a[i] = a[i]) leaves counts unchanged. Only replaces an existing element: use append to add one. Invalidates running iterators, even when the value is unchanged.

Parameters

  • idx — the zero-based position to overwrite
  • value — the new element

Returns

  • the element now stored at idx (that is, value)

Panics

  • if idx < count() does not hold (“Array index write out of bounds”)

Example

    a[0] = 42;

append

append(item: T)

Adds item to the end of the Array.

Amortized O(1): when the buffer is full it doubles (O(count) for that call). For a struct T the Array acquires a reference to item. Invalidates running iterators.

Parameters

  • item — the element to add

Panics

  • if the buffer must grow while an I/O operation in a task is using it

Example

    var a = Array<int>();
    a.append(1);
    a.append(2);   # a holds [1, 2]

insert

insert(idx: ulong, item: T)

Inserts item at position idx, shifting the element there and every later element up by one.

Runs in O(count - idx), plus a reallocation when the buffer is full. idx == count() appends. For a struct T the Array acquires a reference to item; shifted elements keep their reference counts. Invalidates running iterators.

Parameters

  • idx — the position item will occupy; from 0 through count()
  • item — the element to insert

Panics

  • if idx <= count() does not hold (“Array insert index out of bounds”)
  • if the buffer must grow while an I/O operation in a task is using it

Example

    var a = Array<int>();
    a.append(1);
    a.append(3);
    a.insert(1, 2);   # a holds [1, 2, 3]

remove_at

remove_at(idx: ulong): T

Removes and returns the element at idx, shifting every later element down by one.

Runs in O(count - idx). For a struct T the Array’s reference is transferred to the caller, so the element stays alive as long as the result is held; shifted elements keep their reference counts. The capacity is unchanged. Invalidates running iterators.

Parameters

  • idx — the position of the element to remove

Returns

  • the removed element

Panics

  • if idx < count() does not hold (“Array remove index out of bounds”)

Example

    var a = Array<int>();
    a.append(1);
    a.append(2);
    var x = a.remove_at(0);   # x == 1; a holds [2]

pop

pop(): T

Removes and returns the last element.

Runs in O(1). For a struct T the Array’s reference is transferred to the caller. The capacity is unchanged. Invalidates running iterators.

Returns

  • the element that was last

Panics

  • if the Array is empty (“Array pop on empty Array”)

Example

    var top = a.pop();

first

first(): T

Returns the first element without removing it; the same as a[0].

Returns

  • the element at index 0

Panics

  • if the Array is empty (“Array first on empty Array”)

last

last(): T

Returns the last element without removing it; the same as a[a.count() - 1].

Returns

  • the element at index count() - 1

Panics

  • if the Array is empty (“Array last on empty Array”)

clear

clear()

Removes every element, leaving the Array empty.

Runs in O(count). For a struct T each element’s reference is released. The capacity is kept, so refilling the Array does not reallocate. Always invalidates running iterators, even on an empty Array.

truncate

truncate(count: ulong)

Shortens the Array to its first count elements, removing the rest.

Runs in O(removed elements). For a struct T each removed element’s reference is released. A count at or above the current count() does nothing (the Array never grows) and leaves iterators valid; an actual shrink invalidates them. The capacity is kept.

Parameters

  • count — the number of leading elements to keep

Example

    a.truncate(1);   # keeps only a[0]
    a.truncate(5);   # no effect when a has fewer than 5 elements

swap

swap(a: ulong, b: ulong)

Exchanges the elements at positions a and b.

Runs in O(1). Reference counts are unchanged: the two references just trade slots. Swapping a position with itself is allowed and changes no element, but still invalidates running iterators like every swap.

Parameters

  • a — the position of the first element
  • b — the position of the second element

Panics

  • if a < count() does not hold (“Array swap index out of bounds”)
  • if b < count() does not hold (“Array swap index out of bounds”)

reverse

reverse()

Reverses the order of the elements in place.

Runs in O(count) using swap, so reference counts are unchanged. An Array of fewer than two elements is left untouched and its iterators stay valid; otherwise running iterators are invalidated.

Example

    a.reverse();   # [1, 2, 3] becomes [3, 2, 1]

sort

sort(compare: (T, T) => int)

Sorts the elements in place into the order compare defines. The sort is stable: elements that compare equal keep their relative order.

compare(a, b) returns a negative number when a belongs before b, 0 when their order does not matter, and a positive number when a belongs after b, the convention String.compare follows. It is a merge sort: O(count log count) calls to compare, plus a scratch copy of the elements. For struct T the references are copied into the scratch Array and back, which acquires and releases them but leaves every count as it was. Invalidates running iterators when there are two or more elements.

Parameters

  • compare — returns the order of its two arguments, as above

Example

    var names = Array<String>();
    names.append("pear");
    names.append("apple");
    names.sort((a, b) => a.compare(b));   # ["apple", "pear"]
    var numbers = Array<int>();
    numbers.append(3);
    numbers.append(1);
    numbers.sort((a, b) => b - a);        # descending: [3, 1]

find

find(item: T): long

Returns the position of the first element equal to item.

Runs in O(count), scanning from the front. Elements are compared with ==: when T declares an == operator (as String does) that operator decides; for any other struct T it compares references, so only the very same object matches.

Parameters

  • item — the value to look for

Returns

  • the index of the first match, or -1 when no element matches

Example

    var i = a.find(9);   # -1 if a holds no 9

contains

contains(item: T): bool

Reports whether any element equals item, compared as find does.

Runs in O(count).

Parameters

  • item — the value to look for

Returns

  • true when find(item) finds a match

append_all

append_all(rhs: Array<T>)

Appends every element of rhs, in order, to the end of this Array.

Runs in O(count of rhs), reserving the needed capacity once up front. rhs is unchanged, and it may be this same Array (a.append_all(a) doubles a). For a struct T each appended element is acquired once more, since both Arrays now hold it. Invalidates this Array’s running iterators when rhs is not empty.

Parameters

  • rhs — the Array whose elements are copied

Panics

  • if the buffer must grow while an I/O operation in a task is using it

See also

  • +=

clone

clone(): Array<T>

Returns a new Array holding the same elements in the same order.

Runs in O(count). The copy is shallow: for a struct T both Arrays refer to the same element objects (each acquired once more), but adding or removing elements in one does not affect the other. The new Array’s capacity equals this Array’s count().

Returns

  • an independent Array with the same elements

Example

    var b = a.clone();
    b.append(7);   # a is unchanged

copy

copy(copies: Copies): Array<T>

Returns a deep copy: a new Array holding a copy of each element, made with copies.copy. This is how copy(value) copies an Array (the Copyable<Array<T>> implementation); call copy(array) rather than this method.

Unlike clone(), which shares struct elements, the result shares no element that is not thread-safe with this Array. An element that appears twice is copied once. Runs in O(count) plus the cost of copying the elements.

Parameters

  • copies — the objects copied so far

Returns

  • the copy

Example

    var names = Array<String>();
    names.append("ada");
    var copied = copy(names);   # calls this method

operator ==

==(rhs: Array<T>): bool

Reports whether both Arrays have the same count and pairwise equal elements, compared with == as find does.

Runs in O(count); stops at the first difference. Two empty Arrays are equal. capacity() is not compared.

Parameters

  • rhs — the Array to compare with

Returns

  • true when the Arrays are element-wise equal

operator !=

!=(rhs: Array<T>): bool

Reports whether the Arrays differ in count or in any element; the negation of ==.

Parameters

  • rhs — the Array to compare with

Returns

  • true when the Arrays are not element-wise equal

operator +=

+=(rhs: Array<T>): Array<T>

Appends every element of rhs to this Array in place (a += b); the same as append_all.

a += a is allowed and doubles a.

Parameters

  • rhs — the Array whose elements are appended

Returns

  • this Array, after the append

See also

  • append_all

Example

    a += b;   # a now ends with b's elements

operator +

+(rhs: Array<T>): Array<T>

Returns a new Array holding this Array’s elements followed by those of rhs (a + b).

Runs in O(count + count of rhs). Neither operand is modified; like clone, the result shares struct elements with its operands.

Parameters

  • rhs — the Array whose elements come second

Returns

  • the concatenation of this Array and rhs

Example

    var c = a + b;

ArrayIterator

struct ArrayIterator<T>

An Iterator<T> over the elements of an Array, in index order; returned by Array.iterate() and driven by for (var x in array).

Holds a reference to the Array, so iterating a temporary keeps it alive for the whole loop. The iterator is fail-fast: if the Array is modified after the iterator was created (see Array for which operations count), its next next() or current() panics instead of skipping or repeating elements.

Type parameters

  • T — the element type of the source Array

See also

  • Array.iterate

Example

    var it = a.iterate();
    while (it.next()) {
        var x = it.current();
    }

Methods

next

next(): bool

Advances to the next element.

The first call moves to index 0. Once it returns false it keeps returning false.

Returns

  • true when there is a current element, false once past the end

Panics

  • if the Array was modified since the iterator was created (“Array modified during iteration”)

current

current(): T

Returns the element the last successful next() moved to.

Returns

  • the current element

Panics

  • if the Array was modified since the iterator was created (“Array modified during iteration”)
  • if next() was never called (“ArrayIterator.current() before next()”)
  • if next() already returned false (“ArrayIterator.current() past the end”)

HashMap and HashSet

Source: runtime/hash.pep

hash

hash<T>(value: T): u64

Returns a 64-bit FNV-1a hash of value, the hash HashMap and HashSet use for their keys.

  • POD types (integers, floats, pointers, bool) fold the value’s own bytes, so equal values hash equally.
  • Struct types hash by identity: the object’s address, folded through FNV-1a so that aligned addresses spread across buckets. Two distinct objects with equal fields therefore hash differently and are distinct keys. A null reference hashes to the FNV-1a offset basis.
  • String hashes by content through the concrete hash<String> override, so equal strings at different addresses collide.

The result is deterministic within and across runs of a program for POD values and strings; for other struct types it depends on where the object was allocated. Reading the address does no refcount work, and a temporary argument is released afterwards.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of the value to hash

Parameters

  • value — the value to hash

Returns

  • the 64-bit hash of value

See also

  • hash<String>

Example

    var a = hash<int>(5);
    var b = hash<int>(5);   # a == b

hash

hash<String>(value: String): u64

Returns a 64-bit FNV-1a hash of a String’s bytes, so equal strings hash equally wherever they are stored. Keeps equal String keys of a HashMap or HashSet in one bucket.

Hashes the size() bytes of the String (not the NUL terminator) in O(size). An empty String hashes to the FNV-1a offset basis.

Parameters

  • value — the String to hash; it must not be a null reference

Returns

  • the 64-bit hash of the String’s content

Example

    assert(hash<String>("hello") == hash<String>("hello"), "content hash");

HashMap

struct HashMap<K, V>

A hash table that maps keys of type K to values of type V.

Keys are hashed with hash<K> and compared with ==: POD keys by value, String keys by content, and other struct keys by identity (two distinct objects with equal fields are different keys). Any type can be a key.

The map holds one reference to each stored key and value. It acquires them when they are stored and releases them when they are overwritten, removed, cleared, or when the map is destroyed.

Lookups, inserts, and removals take expected O(1) time. The table doubles before an insert of a new key would fill half of it (live entries plus removed-slot tombstones), so it never shrinks, and churn (many inserts and removals of different keys) can keep growing it even while count() stays small.

iterate() visits the entries as (key, value) tuples, in no defined order.

Type parameters

  • K — the key type; hashed with hash<K> and compared with ==
  • V — the value type

Example

    var ages = HashMap<String, int>();
    ages["ada"] = 36;
    ages.insert("alan", 41);
    assert(ages["ada"] == 36, "lookup");
    assert(ages.get("grace") == 0, "a missing key reads as the default");
    assert(ages.remove("alan"), "removed");
    assert(ages.count() == 1, "one entry left");

Constructor

HashMap()

construct(initial_capacity: ulong = 8)

Creates an empty map whose table has room for at least initial_capacity slots.

The slot count is rounded up to a power of two, with a minimum of 8. The map holds up to half its slot count before the first grow, so pass about twice the expected number of entries to avoid regrowing. Allocates three arrays of that many slots.

Parameters

  • initial_capacity — the minimum number of slots in the table

Example

    var m = HashMap<int, int>(64);   # 64 slots, 32 entries before growing

Methods

grow

grow()

Doubles the table and reinserts every entry, dropping all tombstones.

insert calls it automatically. Calling it directly is safe but only costs memory. Runs in O(capacity). It replaces the table’s arrays and moves entries to new slots. Reference counts are unchanged overall: each entry is acquired by the new arrays and released by the old ones.

count

count(): int

Returns the number of entries in the map. O(1).

Returns

  • the number of live key-value pairs

empty

empty(): bool

Returns whether the map has no entries. O(1).

Returns

  • true when count() is 0

capacity

capacity(): ulong

Returns the number of slots in the table, a power of two and at least 8. The map grows before its entries and tombstones reach half of it. O(1).

Returns

  • the current slot count

cap

[Deprecated("use 'capacity' instead", "capacity")] cap(): ulong

Deprecated: use capacity instead. Returns the number of slots in the table.

Returns

  • the same as capacity()

clear

clear()

Removes every entry and releases the map’s references to their keys and values. The table keeps its capacity. Runs in O(capacity).

copy

copy(copies: Copies): HashMap<K, V>

Returns a deep copy: a new map holding a copy of each key and value, made with copies.copy. This is how copy(value) copies a HashMap (the Copyable<HashMap<K, V>> implementation); call copy(map) rather than this method.

The copied keys are hashed again, so a map keyed by struct identity finds its entries under the copied keys. Runs in O(capacity) plus the cost of copying the entries.

Parameters

  • copies — the objects copied so far

Returns

  • the copy

contains

contains(key: K): bool

Returns whether the map has an entry for key. Expected O(1).

Parameters

  • key — the key to look up

Returns

  • true when key is present

insert

insert(key: K, value: V): bool

Maps key to value, adding a new entry or overwriting the value of an existing one.

When the key is already present, only the value is replaced: the map keeps the key object it already stores and releases the old value. A new entry acquires both key and value, and may first grow the table (see grow). Expected O(1); a grow costs O(capacity).

Parameters

  • key — the key to add or update
  • value — the value to store for key

Returns

  • true when a new key was added, false when an existing key’s value was overwritten

Example

    var m = HashMap<int, int>();
    m.insert(1, 10);   # true: added
    m.insert(1, 20);   # false: overwritten; m.get(1) == 20

get

get(key: K): V

Returns the value stored for key, or the default of V when key is absent.

The default is 0 for numbers and a null reference for struct types, including String. A missing key is not an error and is not inserted. When V is a struct type, call contains first rather than using a null result. The caller gets its own reference to the stored value. Expected O(1).

Parameters

  • key — the key to look up

Returns

  • the value for key, or the default of V when absent

remove

remove(key: K): bool

Removes the entry for key, releasing the map’s references to its key and value. Does nothing when key is absent.

The slot becomes a tombstone: occupied for probing, empty for lookup. It counts toward the grow threshold until an insert reuses it or the table grows. Expected O(1).

Parameters

  • key — the key to remove

Returns

  • true when key was present and removed, false when absent

operator []

[](key: K): V

Reads m[key]: returns the value for key, or the default of V (0, or a null reference for struct types) when key is absent. The same as get. A missing key is not inserted.

Parameters

  • key — the key to look up

Returns

  • the value for key, or the default of V when absent

Example

    var m = HashMap<String, int>();
    var n = m["missing"];   # 0; m is still empty

operator []

[](key: K, value: V): V

Writes m[key] = value: inserts key or overwrites its value, the same as insert.

Parameters

  • key — the key to add or update
  • value — the value to store for key

Returns

  • value, the value of the assignment expression

Example

    var m = HashMap<String, int>();
    m["hello"] = 5;

iterate

iterate(): HashMapIterator<K, V>

Returns an iterator over the entries as (key, value) tuples, in no defined order; for (var (key, value) in map) drives it.

The iterator holds a reference to the map. Changing a value through an existing key while iterating is allowed; adding or removing an entry makes the iterator’s next next() or current() panic.

Returns

  • an iterator positioned before the first entry

Example

    var total = 0;
    for (var (name, age) in ages) {
        total += age;
    }

HashSet

struct HashSet<K>

A hash set of distinct elements of type K, built on the same table as HashMap but without values.

Elements are hashed with hash<K> and compared with ==: POD elements by value, String elements by content, and other struct elements by identity (two distinct objects with equal fields are both members). The set holds one reference to each member. It acquires the reference on insert and releases it on remove, on clear, or when the set is destroyed.

Membership tests, inserts, and removals take expected O(1) time. The table doubles before an insert of a new element would fill half of it (members plus tombstones), and it never shrinks. iterate() visits the members, in no defined order. The lowercase fields and the _find_slot and grow methods are the table’s internal state: they are public but may change, and writing to them breaks the set.

Type parameters

  • K — the element type; hashed with hash<K> and compared with ==

Example

    var seen = HashSet<String>();
    seen.insert("a");
    seen["b"] = "b";   # the same as seen.insert("b")
    assert(seen.contains("a"), "member");
    assert(!seen.insert("a"), "already a member");
    assert(seen.count() == 2, "two members");

Constructors

HashSet()

construct(initial_capacity: ulong = 8)

Creates an empty set whose table has room for at least initial_capacity slots.

The slot count is rounded up to a power of two, with a minimum of 8. The set holds up to half its slot count before the first grow.

Parameters

  • initial_capacity — the minimum number of slots in the table

HashSet()

[Implicit] construct(items: Array<K>)

Creates a set holding each element of items once.

The constructor is [Implicit]: an array converts to a set wherever a set is expected, so an array literal can initialize one.

Parameters

  • items — the elements to insert; duplicates are kept once

Example

    HashSet<String> keywords = ["if", "else", "while"];
    assert(keywords.contains("else"), "a member");

Methods

grow

grow()

Doubles the table and reinserts every member, dropping all tombstones.

insert calls it automatically. Calling it directly is safe but only costs memory. Runs in O(capacity). It replaces the table’s arrays and moves members to new slots.

count

count(): int

Returns the number of members in the set. O(1).

Returns

  • the number of members

empty

empty(): bool

Returns whether the set has no members. O(1).

Returns

  • true when count() is 0

capacity

capacity(): ulong

Returns the number of slots in the table, a power of two and at least 8. O(1).

Returns

  • the current slot count

cap

[Deprecated("use 'capacity' instead", "capacity")] cap(): ulong

Deprecated: use capacity instead. Returns the number of slots in the table.

Returns

  • the same as capacity()

clear

clear()

Removes every member and releases the set’s references to them. The table keeps its capacity. Runs in O(capacity).

contains

contains(key: K): bool

Returns whether key is a member of the set. Expected O(1).

Parameters

  • key — the element to look up

Returns

  • true when key is a member

insert

insert(key: K): bool

Adds key to the set if it is not already a member.

A new member is acquired, and the insert may first grow the table (see grow). When an equal member already exists, the set keeps the member it has and does not store key. Expected O(1); a grow costs O(capacity).

Parameters

  • key — the element to add

Returns

  • true when key was added, false when it was already a member

remove

remove(key: K): bool

Removes key from the set, releasing the set’s reference to the member. Does nothing when key is not a member. The slot becomes a tombstone (see _tombstones). Expected O(1).

Parameters

  • key — the element to remove

Returns

  • true when key was a member and was removed, false otherwise

operator []

[](key: K): K

Reads s[key]: returns the stored member equal to key, or the default of K (0, or a null reference for struct types) when key is not a member.

For String elements this returns the instance the set stores, which may be a different object than key with the same content. A missing element is not inserted.

Parameters

  • key — the element to look up

Returns

  • the stored member equal to key, or the default of K

operator []

[](key: K, value: K): K

Writes s[key] = value: makes key a member, the same as insert(key).

A set stores only keys, so value is ignored.

Parameters

  • key — the element to add
  • value — ignored

Returns

  • key (the argument, not an existing equal member), the value of the assignment expression

iterate

iterate(): HashSetIterator<K>

Returns an iterator over the members, in no defined order; for (var x in set) drives it.

The iterator holds a reference to the set. Adding or removing a member while iterating makes the iterator’s next next() or current() panic.

Returns

Example

copy(copies: Copies): HashSet<K>

Returns a deep copy: a new set holding a copy of each element, made with copies.copy. This is how copy(value) copies a HashSet (the Copyable<HashSet<K>> implementation); call copy(set) rather than this method.

The copied elements are hashed again, so a set of structs compared by identity finds the copied elements. Runs in O(capacity) plus the cost of copying the elements.

Iterators

Source: runtime/iterator.pep

Iterator

trait Iterator<T>

Something a for loop can step through, one element at a time.

for (var x in source) drives a source that declares next() and current() directly: it calls next() before each pass and binds current() to the loop variable while next() returns true. A type whose for loop should go through a separate iterator implements Iterable<T> instead. A type with neither protocol is a compile error in a for loop.

The loop goes by the methods a type has, so declaring the trait is optional. Declaring it (extend Foo with Iterator<int> {}) checks that the methods match and lets the type be used as an Iterator<int> value, which a for loop drives through the trait.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of the elements produced

See also

  • Iterable

Example

    struct Countdown {
        int remaining;
        int now;

        construct(this.remaining = 0) {}

        bool next() {
            if (remaining == 0) {
                return false;
            }
            now = remaining;
            remaining = remaining - 1;
            return true;
        }

        int current() {
            return now;
        }
    }

    extend Countdown with Iterator<int> {}

    main(): int {
        var total = 0;
        for (int n in Countdown(3)) {
            total = total + n;   # visits 3, 2, 1
        }
        return total;
    }

Methods

next

next(): bool

Advances to the next element.

The first call moves to the first element, if any. Once it returns false it must keep returning false.

Returns

  • true if there is a current element, false when the elements are exhausted

current

current(): T

Returns the element the last successful next() moved to.

Calling it before the first next(), or after next() returned false, is an error; the runtime’s iterators panic in that case.

Returns

  • the current element

map

map<U>(transform: (T) => U): MapIterator<T, U>

Returns an iterator over transform applied to each element, in order.

Lazy: transform runs once per element, as the result is advanced, and the result advances this iterator. Every type that declares Iterator<T> gets this method.

Type parameters

  • U — the type transform returns

Parameters

  • transform — the function applied to each element

Returns

  • a MapIterator<T, U> over the transformed elements

Example

    var names = Array<String>();
    for (var size in names.iterate().map((name) => name.size())) {
        print(size);
    }

filter

filter(keep: (T) => bool): FilterIterator<T>

Returns an iterator over the elements for which keep returns true, in order.

Lazy: keep runs once per element, as the result is advanced, and the result advances this iterator. Every type that declares Iterator<T> gets this method.

Parameters

  • keep — the test an element must pass

Returns

  • a FilterIterator<T> over the elements that pass

Example

    var nums = Array<int>();
    for (var even in nums.iterate().filter((n) => n % 2 == 0)) {
        print(even);
    }

trait Iterable<T>

Something that hands out an Iterator<T> over its elements, such as Array<T> and String (which yields one code point at a time, as a String).

for (var x in source) calls source.iterate() once, then drives the returned iterator with next() and current(). When a type declares both iterate() and next()/current(), the loop uses iterate().

See also

  • Iterator

Example

    var nums = Array<int>();
    nums.append(1);
    nums.append(2);
    var total = 0;
    for (var x in nums) {
        total = total + x;
    }

iterate(): Iterator<T>

Returns a new iterator positioned before the first element.

The result may be any type that satisfies Iterator<T> (for example ArrayIterator<T>); each call starts a fresh, independent pass.

Returns
